summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans for a major new wind farm near Mepal have reached another milestone, with the Planning Inspectorate launching a formal consultation on the scope of the environmental information that will be required before an application can be submitted. As previously reported by this newspaper, energy company Vattenfall is proposing a large-scale wind farm on Fenland farmland south of Chatteris, close to Mepal, Somersham and Sutton. The project has entered a key planning stage after the Planning Inspectorate received Vattenfall's scoping request, published this week on Huntingdonshire District Council's planning portal. A map showing the proposed sites of both the Redmere Wind Farm at Shippea Hill and the other at Chatteris. (Image: Vattenfall) The proposed scheme would comprise up to 15 wind turbines with a maximum tip height of 220 metres, alongside a battery energy storage system, an on-site substation and associated infrastructure. The development could generate up to 126MW of electricity. A Planning Inspectorate letter dated September 29 asks consultation bodies to comment on what should be included in the project's Environmental Statement. Responses are due by October 27. The Environmental Statement will assess the impact on wildlife, birds, heritage, landscapes, traffic, noise, flooding, tourism and local communities. According to the scoping report, the site covers land approximately 2.5km south of Chatteris within the Fenland landscape and extends across parts of both East Cambridgeshire and Fenland districts. The report identifies a number of environmental issues that will require detailed assessment. These include the nearby Ouse Washes, which lies around 468 metres from the site and is protected as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, Special Protection Area, Special Area of Conservation and Ramsar wetland. Landscape impacts are also expected to be a significant consideration. The assessment will examine views from locations across the Fens, including Ely Cathedral, where the report notes the cathedral is a prominent landmark visible across the surrounding landscape. The wind farm would be a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project because it is expected to generate more than 100MW, so the Secretary of State—not local planning authorities—would decide its fate. The Planning Inspectorate said the project is still at the pre-application stage and no decision has been made on whether it can go ahead. The consultation will help decide the scope and detail of the Environmental Statement submitted with any application. Vattenfall has named Burwell Main Electricity Substation as the connection point, but the route for any off-site grid link has not been decided. After the consultation, the Planning Inspectorate will issue a scoping opinion listing the environmental issues the application must address. Vattenfall will hold a drop-in event at Mepal Village Hall, School Lane, Mepal, from 4pm to 8pm on October 14. Vattenfall has also announced it wants to build a wind farm with up to 32 turbines capable of generating 303MW—enough to power 218,084 homes - at Redmere Farm near Shippea Hill. The company said the development would be located on land to the north and south of Shippea Hill railway station, and to the west of Feltwell and Lakenheath villages.

metadata.title: Hundreds march in protest against Cambridgeshire puppy breeding facility
metadata.contentSnippet: More than 200 people have marched in protest against the breeding of dogs for laboratory testing at MBR Acres in Huntingdon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hundreds march in protest against Cambridgeshire puppy breeding facility
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 200 people have marched in protest against the breeding of dogs for laboratory testing at a Cambridgeshire facility. Organised by Save The Dogs UK, the five-mile march began at Huntingdon railway station at 1pm on September 26 and attracted supporters from Cambridgeshire, across the UK and Europe. Event organiser Sarah Gard welcomed the crowd before organisers read out a code of conduct urging a peaceful, lawful demonstration. The march passed through Huntingdon town centre, where Save The Dogs UK media lead Hazel Williams addressed protesters outside the town hall. The five-mile march began at Huntingdon railway station and continued to MBR Acres (Image: Vegan Photographs) Ms Williams said: "We have been completely blown away by the support and engagement from the local people of Huntingdon. "This isn’t just a national issue; it’s a local one." She raised concerns about using beagles in research and said many residents did not know dogs were being bred nearby for it. Ms Williams called for non-animal research and pointed to Cambridgeshire’s scientific expertise. Ms Williams claimed many residents did not know dogs were being bred nearby for that purpose (Image: Vegan Photographs) The march continued along the B1090 towards the MBR Acres facility, with demonstrators carrying placards and chanting in support of the beagles. Organisers said passing motorists sounded their horns as the group approached the site. The protest was organised by Save the Dogs UK (Image: Vegan Photographs) At the march’s end, protesters left dog collars and messages of kindness outside MBR Acres for the animals inside. Hundreds of protesters turned out for the event (Image: Vegan Photographs) The protest was livestreamed on social media (Image: Vegan Photographs) Ms Gard said she was "super proud of the peaceful and lawful event" and thanked the marshals, first aider, safety-vehicle driver and photographers who helped organise it. The event was livestreamed on TikTok and Instagram and reached supporters in Australia and Malaysia, according to Save The Dogs UK social lead Natalie Beach. Ms Beach called the atmosphere "incredible" and said the march united familiar faces with new supporters. Marshals, first aiders, photographers and a safety-vehicle driver took part (Image: Vegan Photographs) A spokesperson for MBR Acres said: "While animal research is a sensitive topic, the development of new human and veterinary medicines is strictly governed by UK and international regulatory frameworks, which legally require animal safety testing. "Our lawful role is to breed and supply healthy dogs for regulated scientific research—a lawful critical component of the UK medical development process. "Disrupting this vital work only risks delaying essential research and, ultimately, the treatments that patients and families are waiting for. "Every medicine used by families and their pets today relies on this critical work. "Under UK and international regulatory frameworks, safety testing remains a strict requirement to prove that new treatments are safe before they can ever progress to human clinical trials or veterinary use. The protest took place on September 26 (Image: Vegan Photographs) "We are fully committed to the development of non-animal alternatives and strongly support the advancement of New Approach Methodologies (NAMs). "However, while these technologies are maturing, they cannot yet fully replicate the complex biological systems of a living human or animal. "Until new alternatives are fully capable of ensuring absolute safety, these studies remain an irreplaceable step in protecting loved ones. The demonstration was intended to be peaceful and lawful (Image: Vegan Photographs) "Those calling for the closure of our facilities are not considering the severe consequences that this would have on research and development in the UK. "We will not tolerate unlawful behaviour, or the intimidation of our dedicated team, our absolute priority remains the compliance, safety and security of the animals in our care."

metadata.title: Initial report into fatal Elstow train crash reveals driver passed red signal
metadata.contentSnippet: The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) has published its latest findings on the fatal collision between two East Midlands Railway trains near Elstow.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Initial report into fatal Elstow train crash reveals driver passed red signal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The driver of a passenger train that crashed into another service near Bedford passed a red signal while accelerating, according to an interim investigation report. The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) has published its latest findings on the fatal collision between two East Midlands Railway trains near Elstow, Bedfordshire, on June 19. The crash happened at around 5.13pm when a Corby to London St Pancras service struck the rear of a stationary Nottingham to London St Pancras train on the Midland Main Line about 2.5 miles south of Bedford station. An image showing the impact of the two trains. The driver of the Corby service suffered fatal injuries and more than 160 people were injured. Investigators estimate that 257 passengers and staff were aboard the two trains when the collision occurred. Both trains derailed and suffered significant damage. The report confirms that the Nottingham to London train had come to an unexpected stop after an automatic emergency brake application. The scene just south of the Elstow interchange between the A421 and the A6 in Bedford South after two East Midlands Railway (EMR) trains were involved in a collision around 5.15pm on Friday, June 19. (Image: Chris Radburn/PA Wire) Signal WH154, the signal protecting the stationary train, was displaying a red danger aspect. Forward-facing CCTV footage from the Corby train showed the signal was correctly displaying red as the train approached. Investigators found the train was travelling at about 58mph and accelerating when it passed the signal. An image showing the impact of the two trains. Data recovered from the train's on-board recorder showed the driver first applied the brakes around 10 seconds before impact while travelling at approximately 76mph. The train's speed had reduced to around 50mph at the point of collision. RAIB said its investigation remains focused on understanding why the Corby service passed the red signal. The report also exposes problems with the Nottingham train before the crash. Investigators found it received an Automatic Warning System (AWS) warning indication despite approaching a signal showing green. The warning was not acknowledged within the required time, triggering an emergency brake application and bringing the train to a stand. The train's driver subsequently reported an AWS fault to the signaller. Witness evidence suggests neither the driver nor an instructor travelling in the cab recognised a continuous alarm as an AWS warning indication. Investigators also found a second incident on July 9, when another train wrongly received an AWS warning at the same green signal. Further checks found part of the AWS equipment was outside the required tolerance. The point of impact between the two trains. (Image: RAIB) The report notes there had been no previous recorded incidents of trains passing signal WH154 while it was displaying red since records began in 1985. Analysis by the Rail Safety and Standards Board indicated no train had encountered a red aspect at the signal before the accident in 2026. RAIB stressed that its job is to improve railway safety, not assign blame or liability. The scene just south of the Elstow interchange between the A421 and the A6 in Bedford South after two East Midlands Railway (EMR) trains were involved in a collision. (Image: Jamie Lashmar/PA Wire) The investigation will examine the actions of those involved, why the Corby train passed the signal at danger, the braking and warning systems, why the Nottingham service stopped, signal WH154’s status and visibility, the trains’ crashworthiness and the emergency response.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Five homes could be built on Grade II listed farm in Hunts village
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans have been submitted for five new homes on land near a Grade II listed farm in a Huntingdonshire village. Sue and Dominic Rice have lodged an application with Huntingdonshire District Council for five dwellings to be built on land at Christs College Farm, Green Lane, Upton, near Huntingdon. The plans would demolish a barn and stables and add three detached homes, two semi-detached homes, gardens, an adapted drive and biodiversity areas. The site is located roughly in the centre of Upton, which has a population of around 200, with Green Lane to the north and Upton Hill to the east. The dwellings would be built on grassy land on the farm and would be two storey, with a small area at one and a half storey on one house. The plans seek to provide mixed accommodation of two to four bedroom houses and would be "respectful of the listed dwellings in their vicinity". According to the heritage statement, the existing barn and stables are not historic structures associated with Christs College Farm and instead date from the 1980s. However, the barn is located 30 metres from Grade II listed Christs College Farm and 48 metres from Grade II* listed St Margaret's Church. The heritage statement reads: "Overall it is respectfully submitted that the setting of these assets would at least be preserved and may be considered enhanced through the removal of the barn and stables." If approved, all five homes would have sizeable private rear gardens. The Design & Access Statement says: "The houses are scaled to be of a reasonable height, which, given the benefit of the downward slope of the site, enables generously scaled houses, without them becoming overly imposing on the sensitive surroundings." No decision has yet been made on the plans. Full details are available on the Huntingdonshire District Council planning portal under reference 26/01761/FUL.

metadata.title: Lawyers welcome Bedford rail crash findings as compensation efforts continue
metadata.contentSnippet: Lawyers representing victims of the Bedford rail crash near Elstow welcomed the Rail Accident Investigation Branch's (RAIB) interim report, saying it offers early answers about the collision.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Lawyers welcome Bedford rail crash findings as compensation efforts continue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Lawyers representing victims of the Bedford rail crash welcomed the Rail Accident Investigation Branch's (RAIB) interim report, saying it offers early answers about the collision. Published today, the report examines the crash near Elstow and identifies factors that may have contributed to it. The wider investigation continues. Des Collins, senior partner at Collins Solicitors, represents several passengers affected by the crash. Mr Collins said clients would be pleased that the RAIB had produced "a relatively swift interim report" and that his firm would now be advising victims on their legal options. He highlighted the report's findings regarding a signal passed at danger (SPAD) and the apparent absence of a Train Protection Warning System (TPWS) on the stretch of railway where the collision occurred. Mr Collins said: "It is already clear from today's report that the fact of a signal passed at danger (SPAD) was compounded by a lack of a Train Protection Warning System (TPWS) on that stretch of railway. "This system is specifically designed to automatically bring a train to a safe stop, which would have prevented this accident." He also questioned previous assessments that the location was considered low risk and suggested lessons from previous rail disasters had not been fully implemented. The solicitor said his firm had invited both East Midlands Railway and Network Rail to accept liability in principle, with discussions ongoing. He said an early admission of liability could help passengers access interim payments to cover lost earnings and other immediate financial pressures while longer-term compensation claims are assessed. Mr Collins added that the full value of any claims would depend on the final investigation findings and the extent of individual injuries and losses. Stephanie Clarke, a personal injury partner at Stewarts, also welcomed the interim report but stressed that it does not determine blame. She said the role of the RAIB is to investigate technical and operational issues and identify measures that could prevent similar incidents from happening again. Ms Clarke said the report pointed to a possible problem with the train's Automatic Warning System (AWS) and likely human error in the crash. "These are important findings for the rail companies and network providers at the centre of the Bedford incident," she said. "They also help personal injury lawyers like myself representing victims as we seek to learn the reasons for their injuries." She said understanding the crash could help injured passengers and bereaved families come to terms with what happened. Ms Clarke said her team represents a family involved in the collision and is advising them on the investigation, rehabilitation and possible claims. She said many victims face long recoveries, with some suffering serious physical injuries and others psychological trauma, anxiety or post-traumatic stress. The lawyer stressed that today's report is only interim and that investigations by the British Transport Police and Office of Rail and Road continue. "Nevertheless today's report is very valuable and an important milestone," she said. The RAIB's final report is expected to explain the collision in more detail and recommend ways to improve rail safety. The crash killed driver Shaun Burton, 60, and injured more than 160 of the approximately 257 people on board; 102 passengers were taken to hospital. RAIB said the Corby-to-London St Pancras train acknowledged a red signal but continued accelerating, reaching 76mph, before emergency braking was applied about 200 metres from the stationary train. The stationary train had stopped unexpectedly after a fault with its Automatic Warning System equipment caused its brakes to apply, which turned the signal behind it red.

metadata.title: 325 young people supported to help prevent serious violence in Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: Early intervention is helping to prevent crime before it happens, according to Cambridgeshire’s police and crime commissioner.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 325 young people supported to help prevent serious violence in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Early intervention is helping to prevent crime before it happens, according to Cambridgeshire’s police and crime commissioner. Darryl Preston told members of the Police and Crime Panel in Peterborough that early intervention schemes were reducing offending and protecting vulnerable people, including women and girls. He said: "I have always been clear that prevention is better than cure and intervening earlier is better than responding after harm has occurred. "By addressing the underlying root causes that contribute to offending behaviour and by providing support at the earliest opportunity, we can help prevent crime, reduce future victimisation, and build safer communities." In his update, Mr Preston highlighted the Respect Programme, which supports families experiencing child-to-parent abuse, and the Drive programme, which targets domestic abuse and stalking perpetrators. He also pointed to the Safer Corridors Toolkit, developed with schools to identify and challenge harmful behaviours. Between April and June, 325 young people under the age of 24 received support through the Serious Violence Reduction Programme to help prevent involvement in serious violence. Mr Preston said: "While crime prevention remains a core part of policing, it cannot be delivered by police alone. "Success requires strong partnership working across all agencies within the local criminal justice system." Other recent initiatives include the selection of Cambridge Crown Court as an Intensive Supervision Court pilot site, and the delivery of trusted adult schemes, detached youth work, and diversionary activities funded through the Serious Violence Duty. Efforts to tackle serious and organised crime include the SOC Fusion knowledge events, which bring together agencies to identify threats and strengthen joint responses. Mr Preston said: "I cannot stress enough the importance of strong partnerships, targeted investment, and a shared focus on reducing harm before it occurs." Full reports and updates from the Police and Crime Panel meeting are available on the commissioner’s website.

metadata.title: Young advocate wins Centrepoint Award for her work to change the care system
metadata.contentSnippet: A 22-year-old advocate from Kent will be recognised for her work to improve the housing system for care leavers at a London awards ceremony this month.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Young advocate wins Centrepoint Award for her work to change the care system
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A 22-year-old advocate from Kent will be recognised for her work to improve the housing system for care leavers at a London awards ceremony this month. Hayleigh went into care when she was 10 years old and since then has navigated a number of challenges. “Growing up, the situation at home wasn’t working so my grandma stepped in and gave up her job as a nurse of 18 years to look after us,” explains Hayleigh. Hayleigh remembers that it was hard to trust adults trying to provide help as there was a lack of consistency in the system: “When I was younger, there were a lot of social workers involved at different times.  I struggled to connect with them as I thought they were all just doing it because it was their job -not because they wanted to help me.  For me, that was a big struggle.” There is currently inadequate support for young care leavers looking to secure affordable and stable housing, and Hayleigh struggled with this huge turning point in her life. But over the past decade, The Young Lives Foundation in Kent – a valued partner of Centrepoint’s - have consistently supported Hayleigh with independence and helped her to find her voice as she worked towards securing her own home. Through the charity’s programmes, the support she received helped her to identify that she lacked confidence in her own abilities and often judged herself harshly.  As she started to find her voice, she began to see that her natural empathy and warmth towards others were two of her greatest skills, and wanted to put these to good use advocating for other young people from similar backgrounds. Hayleigh is now an active member of the Children in Care Council and both officials and councillors defer to her to be the voice of care experienced young people. She is also continuing to work with The Young Lives Foundation, becoming an inspiration for the charity’s younger members. Describing Hayleigh, her Leaving Care Mentor Amy said: “I met Hayleigh four years ago and was immediately impressed.  Seeing her talk so passionately about other young people and wanting to support them is so admirable.  I look up to her – I’m just really proud.” Hayleigh was nominated for Centrepoint’s ‘Partner’ award by her Young Lives Foundation team. She is looking forward to attending the awards with one of her biggest supporters – her grandma. Hayleigh said: “When I found out that I won an award, I was speechless.  It’s really rewarding as it shows you are doing something right.  When I was younger, it was hard for me to express myself but now people are recognising me.  It’s not just for me, but for other young people as well.” (Image: Centerpoint) A new Housing Benefit rule comes into effect this month, making it easier for young people in supported housing to start and stay in work. It follows campaigning from youth homelessness charity, Centrepoint, to end a long-standing benefit trap which was preventing young people in supported housing from entering the workforce. The flaw in the system meant that these young people were actually left worse off when taking on more hours of work. Centrepoint estimated this was limiting opportunities for over 30,000 young people in supported housing. However, this October the government introduces a new earned income disregard in Housing Benefit for claimants in supported housing and temporary accommodation. It means that more of a young person's earnings will be ignored when their Housing Benefit is calculated, allowing them to keep more of what they earn. This will remove the quirk in the system that disincentivises work, and reduce the financial cliff edge when moving into, or progressing in, employment. Lisa Doyle, Head of Policy and Public Affairs at Centrepoint, said: “This is a significant victory for those trying to escape homelessness, particularly young people at the start of their careers, who have so far found their ambitions blocked by the system." She added, “This would not have been possible without our partners and campaigners, particularly those who have joined our calls for the government to make work pay. “We are incredibly grateful to them and would like to thank each of them on behalf of the young people we support.” Last year, over 118,000 young people faced homelessness. That’s one young person every four minutes. At a time of life when most of their peers are trying new things and taking their first steps into adulthood, these young people found themselves alone and afraid, and unsure where to turn. It doesn’t have to be like this, with the right support at the right time, these young people can escape homelessness or avoid it altogether. At Centrepoint, provide more than a bed for the night. We provide a safe place to rebuild, support into education and work, and the confidence to believe in a better future. Youth homelessness is not inevitable. With the right help at the right time, it can be prevented and it can be ended. Our mission is to end youth homelessness – and you can help us. Whether it’s running a marathon or holding a sleep out, you, your friends, family and co-workers can join our movement to end youth homelessness and give vulnerable young people a brighter future. To find out more, donate or get involved, please visit our website http://www.centrepoint.org.uk/newspaper (Image: Centerpoint) Centreprise - an innovative programme, designed to inspire a new generation of business leaders - has been launched by the youth homelessness charity, Centrepoint. 16 young people from London and Bradford were given the opportunity to develop entrepreneurial skills, build confidence and develop business ideas that could one day grow to become the UK’s next big company. It culminated in a Dragon's Den-style final, during which participants pitched their ideas to a panel of respected business leaders and entrepreneurs including; Centrepoint donor Alison Fortescue; founder of Amber Labs, James Bennet; and Co-founder of Little Moons, Vivien Wong. Sadie Odeogberin, Head of Centrepoint Works, said: “All young people want to work but there are some who aren’t given the support or opportunities to do so. Centreprise is changing that. "The past few weeks have been amazing, and I’m incredibly proud of what the young people have achieved.” The initiative was made possible thanks to the extraordinary generosity of Alison Fortescue, whose late husband Alex Fortescue left a £1 million legacy gift. The money will fund Centreprise for the next five years and this year was put towards equipment, software and professional services which judges allocated at the end of the day to help young people build their businesses. They will also have access to weekly 1-to-1 mentoring sessions, plus check-in calls with their mentors for three months. Alison Fortescue said: “I was so impressed by the enthusiasm of the young people participating in Centreprise, their commitment and ambitions are truly inspiring.”

metadata.title: New local media planning tool Raid launches today
metadata.contentSnippet: The local news media sector's new audience measurement platform Regional Audience Intelligence Data (Raid) has officially launched today, enabling media planners to see local more clearly.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New local media planning tool Raid launches today
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The local news media sector's new audience measurement platform Regional Audience Intelligence Data (Raid) has officially launched today, enabling media planners to see local more clearly. The new Raid platform, the only place to find UK local news media’s total brand audience, offers a host of new benefits including more immediate and accurate audience data, a reduction in modelled readership data, and a new bespoke user interface. News Media Association chief executive Theo Bamber said: “Local news media presents a unique and compelling proposition for advertisers. Local titles are highly trusted environments with deep connections to the communities and people they serve. “Raid gives planners a clear and dynamic view of this market, allowing them to see the scope and scale of local media and connect brands with the right audiences. It's an important innovation at a time when the advertising model is evolving, and will deliver significant benefits to publishers and agencies alike.” (Image: Raid) Developed by the international research agency RAM Penetrace on behalf of local publishers, Raid launches today with an advertising campaign across the media trade press and local news media sector. Over the past month, more than 100 local publishers and media planners have been introduced to Raid through a series of webinar training sessions. The system offers users readership insights right down to the postcode level. Tags deployed by the RAM Platform across local news websites capture the reach, frequency and demographics of the sector’s digital audiences, with additional readership surveys used to capture print readership data, powering Raid’s total brand audience data. CEO RAM Penetrace UK Ltd Dianne Newman said: “Raid has been designed with the flexibility to adapt quickly as the local news sector evolves while offering media agencies the rigour required to plan with complete confidence. "We look forward to continuing our work with publishers, agencies and advertisers as the rollout of this exciting new tool progresses over the coming weeks and months.” Raid replaces JICREG, which will continue to be available as a legacy system for the time being.

metadata.title: Cambs man charged with firearms offences after dawn raids targeting crime gang
metadata.contentSnippet: A man from Duxford, Cambridgeshire, has been charged with firearms offences following a major police operation.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs man charged with firearms offences after dawn raids targeting crime gang
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire man has been charged with firearms offences following a major police operation targeting a suspected organised crime group. Andreas Nicolas, 64, of Duxford, was charged with possession of a firearm (a revolver) and possession of a weapon to discharge a noxious thing, namely electricity. He was remanded in custody and will appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on October 1. Mr Nicolas was arrested in the early hours of Tuesday as part of a wider operation that saw 17 people arrested during raids at 24 properties across Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire, London, Essex and Suffolk. More than 800 Met officers took part in the arrest operations. Mr Nicholas was initially bailed on Tuesday evening but was re-arrested on Wednesday after officers discovered weapons during property searches that were suspected of belonging to him. He is the fourth person to be charged in connection with the operation. Charles Charalambous, 56, from Cockfosters, was charged with wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm to resist arrest, relating to an incident in which a police officer was stabbed while executing a warrant. Carl Robinson, 49, from Essex, was charged with possession of offensive weapons in a private place, namely three knives. Bradley Byford, 37, from Bishop’s Stortford, was charged with possession of a weapon to discharge a noxious thing, namely electricity. All three men appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, September 30. Mr Charalambous was remanded in custody to appear at Southwark Crown Court on Thursday, October 29. Mr Byford was bailed to appear at the same court on the same date. Mr Robinson’s case was adjourned for discussion of a legal matter, and he was bailed to appear again at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Thursday, October 1. All four men remain under investigation as part of the wider operation and have been bailed for those offences, along with the other 14 individuals arrested on Tuesday.

metadata.title: New order tackles anti-social behaviour, street drinking and vandalism in Huntingdon
metadata.contentSnippet: Police have introduced a new Public Spaces Protection Order in Huntingdon to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New order tackles anti-social behaviour, street drinking and vandalism in Huntingdon
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new Public Spaces Protection Order is now in force in Huntingdon to tackle crime and anti-social behaviour. Huntingdon District Council introduced the order with Cambridgeshire Constabulary on October 1 after residents and businesses raised concerns about rising anti-social behaviour. The order gives council officers and police powers to tackle disruptive behaviour in public spaces. Neighbourhood PCSO Jim Gardner with senior community safety officer Georgia Patterson from Huntingdonshire District Council (Image: Police) Colin Norden, neighbourhood inspector for Huntingdonshire, said: "This PSPO gives us the tools we need to address persistent issues, such as anti-social behaviour including street drinking, public urination and defecation, vandalism and other activities that disrupt public spaces. "With this order in place, we can respond more effectively to the concerns of residents and businesses, working together to create an environment and a space that are enjoyable and accessible for all." The order covers Huntingdon town centre and the area inside the ring road. The order will last three years and be reviewed every year. Debbie Mickelburgh, executive councillor for communities, health and leisure, said: "This Public Spaces Protection Order demonstrates our commitment to working in partnership with Cambridgeshire Constabulary and the local community to tackle anti-social behaviour. "Residents and businesses have been clear that action is needed, and this order provides additional tools to help address behaviours that impact people’s enjoyment of Huntingdon town centre. "Together, we can help ensure Huntingdon remains a safe and welcoming place for all."

metadata.title: Inquest opens into death of Cambs motorcyclist, 19, who died in crash
metadata.contentSnippet: An inquest has been opened into the death of a 19-year-old who died in a crash between two motorbikes on the A605 near Cardea in Peterborough.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Inquest opens into death of Cambs motorcyclist, 19, who died in crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An inquest has been opened into the death of a 19-year-old who died in a crash between two motorbikes in Cambridgeshire. Rolas Saskovas, of Lawson Avenue, Peterborough, was injured in the crash on August 31 and later died in hospital. Police were called to the head-on collision on the A605 Stanham Way, near Cardea, at around 5.20pm. Mr Saskovas was riding a blue Yamaha MT-03 which collided with a black BMW S100. The BMW rider, a 32-year-old man from London, sustained serious but not life-threatening injuries. He was taken to hospital after the crash. Area Coroner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Simon Milburn opened Mr Saskovas' inquest on October 1 at Vantage House in Huntingdon. The brief hearing heard how Mr Saskovas was the rider of a motorcycle that was involved in a collision, and as a result he suffered a number of injuries. The provisional cause of death was given as 1A multiple severe traumatic injuries with the toxicology results pending. Mr Milburn adjourned the hearing for an inquest on March 11, 2027, at Vantage House.

metadata.title: Broadcaster and Childline founder Dame Esther Rantzen has died aged 86
metadata.contentSnippet: Broadcaster and Childline founder Dame Esther Rantzen has died aged 86 following a lung cancer diagnosis.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Broadcaster and Childline founder Dame Esther Rantzen has died aged 86
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen has died aged 86. Dame Esther had previously shared that she was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer in May 2023. In a statement, her family said: “Our adored mother Dame Esther Rantzen died today. “Her legacy of compassion and understanding will live on in her charities Childline and the Silverline, and through those of us who were lucky enough to love and be loved by her. “We are grateful she is finally at rest with her beloved husband, Desmond Wilcox, but we will miss her immeasurably. She was our sunshine. “We will always remember her endless capacity for joy, her ability to comfort every heartache, her beautiful way with words and her expert guidance in all things." Dame Esther became a household name in the UK during her time on the BBC; she was best known for presenting That’s Life! – a programme featuring a mix of investigations, topical issues and entertainment – from 1973 to 1994. Alongside her successful career as a journalist and broadcaster, she also set up children’s charity Childline in 1986. Dame Esther created Childline to help offer counselling and support for children and young people in the UK up until the age of 19, in 2006 the charity became part of The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC). The late broadcaster also set up The Silver Line in 2013, a charity which supports elderly people in the UK who are battling loneliness. In 2015, Dame Esther was made a DBE by the late Queen Elizabeth II for services to children and older people due to her charity work. During her lung cancer diagnosis, Dame Esther had been very open with her thoughts on death and in December 2023 she shared she had joined the assisted dying organisation, Dignitas. Dame Esther had also called for a free vote on assisted dying, sharing: “I think it’s important that the law catches up with what the country wants.” Dame Esther Rantzen is survived by her three children, Rebecca, Miriam and Joshua Wilcox.

metadata.title: Red Arrows flying over Cambridgeshire this week — here's when and where to see them
metadata.contentSnippet: The Red Arrows are set to fly over Cambridgeshire this week — here's how and where you can see them.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Red Arrows flying over Cambridgeshire this week — here's when and where to see them
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The famous Red Arrows are set to fly over Cambridgeshire this week — here's when and where you can see them. The jets will be appearing in the skies over the county on Friday (October 2), as they make a short 18-minute flight from RAF Waddington to RAF Mildenhall. They will take off from Lincolnshire at 1.47pm, fly south and enter Cambridgeshire around 1.56pm, north-west of Wisbech. The Red Arrows will fly south-west before turning south-east over Thorney, near Peterborough, at 1.58pm. A minute later, at 1.59pm, the seven jets will roar directly over Chatteris. They will fly over Mepal, Wilburton and Stretham around 2.01pm before heading east to RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk. The timings and route could change before Friday afternoon’s flight. It has been a turbulent year for the Red Arrows, after the RAF confirmed in May that their famous nine-jet formation would be cut to seven. The change was blamed on shortages of parts and engines for the ageing BAE Systems Hawk T1 jets, which have been used by the team since 1980 and are due to retire in 2030. The team was also stranded in Canada during July and August after displaying in the US for the country’s 250th anniversary celebrations. Prolonged bad weather prevented its return to the UK. All Hawk aircraft, including those used by the Red Arrows, were grounded last week after a training jet crashed in Wales. The RAF has now cleared them to fly again. Friday's flight will be one of the last chances to see the Red Arrows this year, with the jets displaying at IWM Duxford's Flying Finale on Saturday (October 3) as the UK airshow season wraps up for another year.

metadata.contentSnippet: Plans have been submitted to turn a historic outbuilding beside Grade I listed building Bodsey House in Ramsey into a five-bedroom home.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans have been submitted to turn a historic outbuilding beside a Grade I listed building into a five-bedroom home. Mick Hilless has applied to Huntingdonshire District Council to turn a barn and office building linked to Bodsey House into a home on Bodsey Toll Road, Ramsey. Bodsey House is Grade I listed, meaning it is of exceptional interest. The property was once a 13th-century hermitage belonging to Ramsey Abbey but has since been altered and turned into a family home. The plans would turn the barn and office building at the rear of the site into one five-bedroom home. The historic barn is curtilage listed, which means it is legally protected as it sits within the grounds of a listed building. Documents by Scroxton Architects say the barn and office building are dilapidated and no longer suitable for modern agricultural or commercial use. The plans would demolish the modern open-sided portal barn at the rear and replace it with a two-storey extension forming a five-bedroom home. The site is about 1.8km north-east of Ramsey and covers 0.2 hectares. The planning documents state: "The demolition of the unsightly, open-sided concrete portal barn and its replacement with the sensitive and subservient timber-clad proposal would significantly enhance the immediate setting, helping to restore the model-farm character of the historic farmstead. "By removing the non-historic modern portal barn and replacing it with a subservient, high-quality extension, the development secures the long-term visual preservation of the historic barn while significantly enhancing the setting of the Grade I listed Bodsey House." The plans also include three parking spaces, secure storage for five bicycles and new biodiversity-friendly landscaping. Access would remain through the existing entrance on Bodsey Toll Road. The applicant says in a heritage statement that the development would secure the historic buildings’ future while preserving the setting of the neighbouring listed property. Full details are available on the Huntingdonshire Planning Portal under reference 26/01763/FUL.

metadata.title: Woman arrested after 'burglary' at Cambs puppy breeding facility
metadata.contentSnippet: A woman has been arrested following a break-in at beagle breeding facility MBR Acres in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Woman arrested after 'burglary' at Cambs puppy breeding facility
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A woman has been arrested following a break-in at a beagle breeding facility in Cambridgeshire. Police were called to MBR Acres in Wyton, near Huntingdon, at 11.10pm on September 29, after reports of a burglary. A spokesperson for the force confirmed that a 43-year-old woman from Inverness was arrested on suspicion of burglary. She remains in custody. The incident is believed to be linked to an "open rescue" at the site, where beagles are bred for use in laboratory testing. Campaign group Camp Beagle, the UK's longest-running permanent animal rights protest camp, has maintained a continuous presence outside the facility since the summer of 2021. The organisation demands that the facility close and end the use of beagles for research purposes. MBR Acres previously told The Hunts Post: "Our operations are entirely legal and carried out under strict UK Home Office regulatory oversight. "We remain committed to meeting all required welfare and operational standards." Footage shared with Camp Beagle appears to show people entering the facility and reaching sheds where the dogs are kept. Police did not confirm what was taken during the burglary.

metadata.title: NINE areas of Cambs where crime rise is 'concerning'
metadata.contentSnippet: Nine areas of Cambridgeshire have been highlighted after a ‘concerning’ rise in crime was reported.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: NINE areas of Cambs where crime rise is 'concerning'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nine areas of Cambridgeshire have been highlighted after a ‘concerning’ rise in crime was reported. South Cambridgeshire District Council has reported ‘concerning trends’ after a rise in rural crime in a number of areas. The council’s cabinet has approved a new plan to combat shoplifting with a focus on specific wards. A report said the focus should be on areas which “are flagging on multiple crime and activity types” or where “professional concern indicates a need for a focus”. These include Cambourne, Histon and Impington with a focus on Orchard Park, Northstowe, Milton and Waterbeach, Fen Ditton and Fulbourn and any other areas where “the data shows spikes or concerning trends”. It will allow the South Cambridgeshire Community Partnership – a joint effort between the council and emergency services and voluntary groups – to work to address the problem. Cllr Dr Lisa Redrup, lead cabinet member for healthy communities, said there were “several new priorities” for the partnership this year. The Liberal Democrat councillor said this included looking at rural shoplifting as “rates have been rising” and it is a “really difficult problem”. She said the partnership would help to find different ways to tackle it. It also said that there was a “concerning” and “large increase” in drug offences over the last year, but this may have been down to how they were recorded. Cllr Bridget Smith, leader of the council, said she was “very pleased” that tackling rural shoplifting was made a priority as she has witnessed it herself. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “The gall with which it is carried out is quite mind boggling actually. “It makes shop workers feel incredibly vulnerable and actually makes other people going to shops where this is happening in such a laden fashion feel very very vulnerable as well.” She said small supermarkets were particularly at risk as they sell “some quite high value goods” and asked if advice could be given to them. She said: “Now that food prices are so very high, stealing a steak is actually quite an expensive thing to nick really. If there’s any more that could be done that would be really helpful.” The cabinet approved the new operational and communications plan for the community safety partnership for 2026/27. A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire Constabulary said: “We’re aware shoplifting can have a huge impact on those involved in the business community as well as local residents, and this is one of the reasons why it is a key issue for officers across the county. “We work closely with retailers concerning shoplifting and seeking prosecutions where possible. For repeat offenders, we are applying for Criminal Behaviour Orders preventing them from entering areas where they have previously committed crime. “We have a Spree Offender Team who proactively arrest and seek to charge prolific shoplifters. “The force would also encourage businesses to reporting shoplifting to us as it helps our officers build a bigger picture of what is happening across the county. “This can be done online (https://www.cambs.police.uk/ro/report/ocr/af/how-to-report-a-crime/), calling 101 or 999 in an emergency.” They also said that drug-dealing “remains a priority” for their teams and said the rise in offences could be due to “two factors – proactive policing work and a change in recording practices.” They said police across the country have been carrying out “proactive stop-searches in hotspot areas”, but also that all reports from border forces of drugs intercepted coming into the country are now recorded as crimes rather than intelligence items.

metadata.contentSnippet: A sheep stuck in a river sparked a rescue operation in St Ives, Huntingdonshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A sheep stuck in a river sparked a rescue operation in St Ives. Firefighters from Huntingdon and Cambridge were called to Meadow Lane after the animal became trapped in the water. Crews used a sled to reach the sheep and safely brought it back to dry land. Sheep rescue (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service) A spokesperson for Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service said: "Whilst these types of incidents can't always be avoided, we would like to urge those that have animals to please ensure fences and gates are secure to reduce the chances of animals becoming stuck in places like rivers. "We train to be able to help animals who have found themselves stuck in a variety of scenarios so that we can free them safely. "If you spot an animal stuck in water, do not attempt to rescue them yourselves. "Dial 999 and ask for the fire service."

metadata.title: Aerial photos show scale of new David Lloyd health club in Huntingdonshire
metadata.contentSnippet: Aerial photos show the scale of a new David Lloyd premium health and wellness club in St Neots ahead of its grand opening.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Aerial photos show scale of new David Lloyd health club in Huntingdonshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Aerial photos show the scale of a new premium health and wellness club in Huntingdonshire ahead of its grand opening. The new David Lloyd club will officially launch on October 6, bringing fitness, swimming, racquet sports and spa facilities to St Neots. The club will have more than 100 workout stations, heated indoor and outdoor pools, and racquet sports areas. Its courts will include cushioned acrylic tennis courts and padel courts. Aerial photos by Maciek Platek at St Neots Gallery show the scale of the new club, which is located on Nuffield Road in Wintringham. The new club will feature workout stations, indoor and outdoor pools and racquet sports areas Children will get fun, safe coaching through the Swim Stars and Tennis Stars programmes. Facilities in the club's spa retreat will include a Himalayan salt sauna, crystal steam room, cold plunge pools and a swim-in, swim-out hydro pool. The retreat will also feature heated beds and a spa garden. The club will also feature a spa retreat Matt Borer has been appointed club general manager for the St Neots location after 16 years with David Lloyd Clubs. Mr Borer said: "I’m so excited to be joining David Lloyd St Neots as the Club General Manager. "There’s already a great deal of excitement surrounding the new Club and I’m really looking forward to welcoming members through the doors later this year. The new David Lloyd club in St Neots will open on October 6 "Throughout my 16 year career with David Lloyd Clubs, I’ve had the opportunity to work across several fantastic Clubs and I can’t wait to bring my passion for delivering a great member experience to St Neots. "I’m looking forward to meeting members and becoming part of the St Neots community." The opening is expected to create local jobs in hospitality, fitness and spa services. Membership prices to David Lloyd clubs vary between locations but can be up to £100 a month, whilst standard day passes can be around £20.

metadata.title: Cambs paedophile who sent explicit images to decoy account jailed
metadata.contentSnippet: A Cambridge paedophile who believed he was talking to a 13-year-old girl online has been jailed after being caught by a decoy account.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs paedophile who sent explicit images to decoy account jailed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire paedophile who believed he was talking to a 13-year-old girl online has been jailed after being caught by a decoy account. David Clark, 52, from Akeman Street in Cambridge, shared explicit messages and images with an account he believed to belong to a 13-year-old girl. He had contacted the account on Snapchat in September 2025, not realising it was operated by an online child abuse activist group. Clark continued to engage in sexual conversations despite being told multiple times that the girl was only 13. He asked about her sexual experiences, described sex acts and sent an explicit picture of himself. He also asked her to send indecent images and sent a picture of two adults having sex. Clark was arrested in November 2025. David Clark was jailed for three years and two months (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Officers seized several devices and found Clark had tried to delete the chat history. He pleaded guilty to attempting to engage in sexual communication with a child, causing a child to look at an image of sexual activity, and attempting to cause or incite a girl to engage in sexual activity. Clark was jailed for three years and two months at Huntingdon Law Courts on Friday, September 25. Detective Constable Bethany Reynolds, from the Online Child Abuse Safeguarding Team (OCAST), said: "Clark is clearly a risk to children. "He advised the 'child' in this case to delete the messages in case her parents found them, proving he knew what he was doing was wrong. "Although thankfully a decoy account, Clark still attempted to prey on and groom what he believed was a child. "Protecting young people from harm is one of our top priorities and we will do all we can to bring offenders to justice." For more on child abuse, including how to report it and spot the signs, visit the dedicated pages on the Cambridgeshire Police website.

metadata.title: Police release sketch of man wanted in connection with serious sexual assault
metadata.contentSnippet: Police have released an artist’s impression of a man wanted in connection with a serious sexual assault in Little Paxton.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Police release sketch of man wanted in connection with serious sexual assault
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have released an artist’s impression of a man wanted in connection with a serious sexual assault in Huntingdonshire. A woman in her 20s was attacked between 9pm and 9.30pm on August 27 on Mill Lane, Little Paxton, near St Neots. Cambridgeshire Constabulary stepped up patrols in the area after the attack. The suspect is described as a white man with a pale complexion and very dark short hair. He is believed to have been wearing a black T-shirt, black shorts, and white trainers at the time of the assault. Anyone who recognises the man is urged to come forward after the force released an artist’s impression. The suspect is described as a white man with a pale complexion and very dark, short hair (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Detective Constable James Howard, the investigating officer, said: "The victim has shown considerable courage in assisting our investigation and has worked with a forensic artist to produce this image. "I am asking the public to carefully look at the drawing and consider whether they recognise the person depicted. "Even if you think the information you hold may be insignificant, I encourage you to come forward. "Small details can often make a significant difference in helping us identify a suspect. "We are particularly interested in speaking with anyone who was in the area at the time, may have captured footage on CCTV, dashcam or mobile devices, or who recognises the individual shown in this drawing." Officers also want to hear from anyone who saw a dark Tesla near Mill Lane around the time of the incident. As of September 30, no arrests have been made and the investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information or footage is asked to contact police via the force website, quoting reference 35/66280/26. Those without internet access can call 101. Information can also be provided anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or through the Crimestoppers website.

metadata.title: Curious guinea pig rescued from poor conditions seeks new home in Cambridgeshire
metadata.contentSnippet: A "curious little guinea pig" is searching for a new home in Cambridgeshire after being rescued from poor living conditions.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Curious guinea pig rescued from poor conditions seeks new home in Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "curious little guinea pig" is searching for a new home in Cambridgeshire after being rescued from poor living conditions. Jarek, a one-year-old guinea pig, is currently being cared for at the RSPCA Block Fen Animal Centre. He was removed from a multi-animal household and is now looking for a loving forever home. A spokesperson for the centre said: "Jarek is a very curious little guinea pig with a lovely personality and a big appetite. "He loves mealtimes and is always keen to see what tasty treats are on offer. "He is becoming a confident boy. "He is still learning that everyone can be trusted and will benefit from patient owners who are willing to continue building his confidence through gentle, regular handling." Jarek is looking to be rehomed with a single female or a group of females. He has not yet been neutered, so temporary separate accommodation will be required until this is complete. Last year, 419 guinea pigs were taken into RSPCA national centres in England and Wales (Image: RSPCA) The RSPCA recommends a minimum space of 10 square feet for a pair of guinea pigs and will ask to see photos of the enclosure as part of the rehoming process. The adoption fee is set at £25. Anyone interested in rehoming Jarek is encouraged to complete the centre’s online application form. The RSPCA has reported a rise in guinea pigs being surrendered, citing overbreeding, the cost-of-living crisis, and a general lack of owner knowledge as contributing factors. Last year, 419 guinea pigs were taken into RSPCA national centres in England and Wales—an increase of 181 from the previous year. Guinea pigs typically live five to six years and are active for up to 20 hours a day. They are social animals that require companionship and should never be kept alone.

metadata.title: 24 fined after waste dumped beside Cambourne charity bring banks
metadata.contentSnippet: Twenty-four people have been fined for fly-tipping in Cambourne, where waste was dumped next to charity bring banks.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 24 fined after waste dumped beside Cambourne charity bring banks
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Twenty-four people have been fined for fly-tipping in Cambourne, where waste was dumped next to charity bring banks. South Cambridgeshire District Council issued the fines after repeated incidents at the recycling area in the Morrisons car park, outside Home Bargains. A range of items, including vacuum cleaners, TVs, mattresses, furniture, and child seats, were left at the site, prompting the removal of the bring banks. Laurence Damary-Homan, lead cabinet member for environment at South Cambridgeshire District Council, said: "We know people in Cambourne were frustrated by rubbish being left beside these bring banks and it is an issue nationally. "Most residents use them responsibly, they provide income for good causes, and they’re a convenient recycling option. Residents are being urged not to leave waste beside bring banks (Image: South Cambridgeshire District Council) "But leaving items next to full bring banks or dumping unwanted goods is fly-tipping and is simply not acceptable. "If there is no room in a container, please take your items home and return another day or use a Household Recycling Centre. "If they get misused, they’ll be removed as we’ve seen in Cambourne. "Our officers investigate to identify those responsible wherever possible, and we will continue to issue fines and pursue prosecutions where we can." Over the past two years, the council’s envirocrimes officers issued 14 Fixed Penalty Notices for fly-tipping, eight for littering, and sent seven warning letters. Six prosecutions have been brought forward, with two Duty of Care Fixed Penalty Notices issued and 11 further cases under investigation. The council is taking action against fly-tipping in South Cambridgeshire. (Image: South Cambridgeshire District Council) The envirocrimes team is now visiting recycling and charity bank sites across South Cambridgeshire to offer advice, identify problems, and work with site operators to prevent further dumping. Leaving waste beside bring banks can attract more fly-tipping, vermin, and creates a burden for those maintaining the sites. Residents are asked to check for space before depositing items and to use Household Recycling Centres if banks are full.

metadata.title: East Anglia Clean & Green Awards judges reveal what makes a winning entry
metadata.contentSnippet: The East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027 judges reveal what they seek in Project of the Year and Sustainability Strategy entries, closing November 8.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: East Anglia Clean & Green Awards judges reveal what makes a winning entry
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Businesses that are championing greener ways of working will be put in the spotlight at the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027. The Project of the Year and Sustainability Strategy Award categories will focus on the specific, measurable schemes that have made a substantial impact on the environment. Here, the judges for these categories tell us more about what they bring to the process. Paul Ager, divisional port manager, East Anglia at Associated British Ports, which sponsors the Project of the Year award (Image: ABP) Sponsored by Associated British Ports Sponsor judge: Paul Ager, divisional port manager, East Anglia, Associated British Ports Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? I joined ABP (Associated British Ports) in June 2016, having previously spent more than 14 years in leadership positions in logistics, supply chain and the construction sector. In June 2022, I joined the Suffolk Chamber of Commerce Board and I sit on the Suffolk Business Board, which allows me to contribute to the development of the region. Why were you keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards? As someone who was born and raised in Suffolk, I am passionate about supporting businesses that are investing in the region, creating opportunities and driving positive change. What do you bring to the judging process? My experience allows me to assess projects from both a strategic and practical perspective. I understand the challenges involved in taking a project from concept to completion, managing stakeholders and delivering measurable outcomes. Through ABP’s recent delivery of the Lowestoft Eastern Energy Facility, we’ve seen first-hand what it takes to deliver a complex infrastructure project that creates long-term value for both industry and the wider community. What will you be looking for in the winner? I will be looking for a project that has delivered clear and lasting benefits, whether that is for the environment, the economy, the community or a particular industry. The winner should be able to show how their project has made a meaningful difference and created value beyond its immediate objectives. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? Don’t underestimate the value of sharing your story. Many organisations deliver impressive projects but are often too modest about their achievements. Focus on clearly explaining the challenge you set out to address, what made your approach unique and the results you achieved. Why should those entering be able to demonstrate community and/or industry involvement? The most successful projects rarely happen in isolation. Strong projects create benefits that extend beyond a single organisation and often rely on effective collaboration with customers, suppliers, local communities, industry partners or public bodies. Demonstrating this shows that a project has generated wider value, built meaningful partnerships and delivered outcomes that others can learn from. Those qualities are often what turn a good project into a truly outstanding one. Johnathan Reynolds, managing director of Opergy Group, which sponsors the Sustainability Strategy Award (Image: Opergy) Sponsored by Opergy Group Sponsor judge: Johnathan Reynolds, managing director, Opergy Group Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? I have spent much of my career working across sustainable development, energy, infrastructure, innovation and skills. I advise businesses, public bodies and major projects on turning complex evidence and ambition into practical strategies, investment and delivery. Why were you keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards? East Anglia has a strong community of organisations doing serious, practical work on sustainability. I wanted to support an award that recognises that effort, shares good practice and gives businesses and organisations of different sizes a platform to demonstrate what they are achieving and learning. Have you ever been judged for an award yourself? Yes. I have experienced multiple awards processes from both entrant and judging perspectives, so I understand the work that sits behind a strong submission and the importance of a process that is rigorous, fair and focused on evidence rather than presentation alone. How will you use that experience when judging this award? I will focus on what sits behind the polished submission: the evidence, decisions, delivery and outcomes. Having experienced award processes myself, I know entrants often invest considerable effort in telling their story, so I will approach each submission carefully, consistently and with respect for what has actually been achieved. What will you be looking for in the winner? A clear, credible strategy that has moved into delivery and produced evidence of real change. I will be looking for strong leadership, measurable outcomes, collaboration and a willingness to tackle difficult trade-offs rather than simply present a perfect story. Why is it important for entrants to demonstrate the scalability of their strategy? Scalability shows that a strategy can create value beyond a single pilot, site or short-term initiative. That does not always mean becoming bigger; it can mean being repeatable, adaptable or capable of influencing others. We want to understand whether the approach can sustain momentum and deliver greater impact over time. The deadline for entries to the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards is Sunday, November 8 at midnight. For more information or to enter, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk

metadata.title: Andy Burnham announces plans to end pension triple lock to fund social care service
metadata.contentSnippet: The state pension triple lock could be scrapped as Andy Burnham discusses difficult choices around funding a national care service.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham announces plans to end pension triple lock to fund social care service
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
The state pension triple lock is being drawn into the debate over how the Government could fund a national care service, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham putting care as a key priority. The triple lock ensures the state pension rises each year by whichever is highest out of inflation, average wage growth or 2.5 per cent. But changing the policy could free up money for other Government priorities at a time when ministers are considering how to tackle the long-running pressures facing social care. Burnham is calling for an “honest conversation” about some of the difficult choices facing the country. In his first conference speech as Prime Minister, he said that the triple lock will be honoured for the rest of this term, but added: "From there, in April 2030, we will adjust it. The state pension will continue to rise every year, at least by prices, or 2.5 per cent, and it will hold its value relative to earnings over time, so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation." Today's Poll: Would you support scrapping State Pension triple lock (amount its guaranteed to rise by) to pay for universal social care?
    
    NB. This is a vibe question. There are many other routes, options & things money could go to. Yet given a straight choice what's your view? — Martin Lewis (@MartinSLewis) September 28, 2026 The link between pensions and social care is emerging as ministers consider how a national care service could be funded. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) estimates that the triple lock currently adds around £16 billion a year to state pension spending compared with uprating pensions in line with average earnings. That does not mean £16 billion could simply be transferred to social care if the triple lock were changed. The eventual saving would depend on what replaced the existing system, how pension increases were calculated and the wider impact on Government finances. But the size of the figure illustrates why the triple lock is being discussed as ministers look at competing demands on public spending. The debate comes against a backdrop of substantial increases in state pension payments since the guarantee was introduced. Press Association analysis of DWP data found that the average annual state pension increase between 2012/13 and 2026/27 was 4.1 per cent. That compares with an average of 3.5 per cent during the previous 15 years, from 1997/98 to 2011/12. The IFS estimates that if flat-rate state pensions had risen in line with average earnings since 2010 rather than under the triple lock, they would now be around 12 per cent lower - equivalent to approximately £1,500 a year less. The think tank says the triple lock has therefore played an important role in increasing pensioner incomes, although it is not the only factor. State pension spending is now around £154 billion a year, according to the IFS. That is equivalent to around 4.9 per cent of national income, compared with 4.3 per cent in 2010 and 3.6 per cent in 2006/07. The IFS estimates the triple lock itself accounts for around £16 billion of additional annual spending compared with an earnings-linked alternative. The triple lock will remain until 2030. The Budget on 28 October will provide a key opportunity for the Government to set out more of its spending plans. For pensioners, the crucial question will be whether they are better off with the triple lock, or with a fully funded social care service.

metadata.title: Pensioners given major tax promise as Andy Burnham reveals new care plan
metadata.contentSnippet: Andy Burnham has pledged that low-income pensioners will not be dragged into paying Income Tax during this Parliament as he sets out his national care service plans.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Pensioners given major tax promise as Andy Burnham reveals new care plan
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Pensioners living mainly on the state pension have been given a fresh tax promise by Andy Burnham as he set out plans for a national care service. The Prime Minister said low-income pensioners will not be “dragged into paying income tax” during this Parliament, as he linked the pledge to his wider offer of a rising state pension and no care charges. Under the current rules, the standard Personal Allowance is £12,570 – the amount of income an individual can receive before they normally start paying Income Tax. The allowance is currently frozen at that level. Burnham told Labour conference: “Some may not realize it, but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care charges today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen. “I can also confirm today our commitment to ensure that the low-income pensioners won't be dragged into paying income tax in this Parliament. “So this is the deal: a state pension that rises every year, no care charges, and a high-quality national care service to give peace of mind in later life. Conference, I am going to go out and argue for that-a good deal for our pensioners and for older people in the 21st century” The Personal Allowance is the amount of income people can normally receive each tax year before Income Tax becomes due. For 2026/27, it stands at £12,570 and is due to remain at that level for 2027/28 under existing legislation. Someone whose total annual income is below their Personal Allowance will not normally pay Income Tax. This includes pension income. The full new state pension is currently below the Personal Allowance, meaning someone receiving only the full new state pension would not normally have an Income Tax bill on that pension alone. However, people with other taxable income can have a tax liability once their total income exceeds their available allowance. The issue is particularly significant because the state pension is increasing while the Personal Allowance has remained frozen. Burnham's pledge means the Government is committing to ensuring that low-income pensioners are not pulled into Income Tax during this Parliament. The precise mechanism for achieving that commitment was not set out in the speech. The Personal Allowance is currently £12,570, while the full new state pension is £241.30 a week, or around £12,548 a year when paid for 52 weeks. That leaves only a small gap between the full new state pension and the current tax-free allowance. Burnham presented the tax pledge as one part of a broader package for older people. He said his plan would combine a state pension that continues to rise each year with no care charges and a national care service. His comments come as the Government faces a major debate over how such a service would be funded. Burnham has also put the future of the state pension triple lock into the wider conversation, although the Government has said the existing commitment will remain during this Parliament. The triple lock currently guarantees that the state pension rises each year by whichever is highest of inflation, average wage growth or 2.5 per cent. If someone's taxable income is above £12,570, Income Tax can be due on the amount above the allowance, depending on their circumstances and tax bands. For 2026/27, the basic Income Tax rate in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is 20 per cent on taxable income within the basic-rate band. This means pensioners with a state pension plus private or workplace pension income, earnings or other taxable income may have to pay tax even if their state pension itself is below the Personal Allowance. Burnham's conference pledge puts the Personal Allowance alongside the state pension and social care at the heart of his offer to older people.
