summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A church in Southoe has officially launched its new community hub. The celebrations on September 12 took place at St Leonard’s Church, marking the opening of a flexible space for year-round events. The community and church members have worked on the project since 2021. Major repairs and interior reordering began in November 2026. The project, supported by 15 grant-making bodies, includes two new toilet cubicles, a new bell-ringing floor and staircase, a refurbished floor, and a ramp into the south porch. The National Lottery Heritage Fund contributed £245,082, while Hunts District Council provided £20,082 for new solar panels. The community gathered at St Leonard’s Church for the celebrations (Image: St Leonard’s Church) Upgraded water, sewerage, and power supplies were also required. About 150 people attended the celebrations, with local MP Ben Obese-Jecty cutting a ribbon to announce the opening. The project team has secured funding for a new electric green energy heating scheme, complementing the solar panels, from the Church of England Net Zero Boiler Replacement Fund (£38,804) and the National Lottery Community Fund (£19,464). This installation should be completed by early November. The space is already in use, with the local community choir rehearsing, along with a coffee morning and a weekend quiz night.

metadata.title: Cambs police officer dismissed and barred after gross misconduct
metadata.contentSnippet: A Cambridgeshire police officer has been dismissed without notice and placed on the barred list for dishonesty amounting to gross misconduct.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs police officer dismissed and barred after gross misconduct
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire police officer has been dismissed without notice for dishonesty amounting to gross misconduct. The officer, referred to as PC A, was dismissed from Cambridgeshire Constabulary following an accelerated misconduct hearing held at Lysander House in Bedfordshire on September 21. PC A resigned on September 16 but was still a serving officer when the hearing took place. She denied all the allegations. The hearing centred on PC A’s links to Person B, her former partner, and his brother, Person C. Person C had previously been jailed for a serious offence. After becoming a police officer, PC A told Northamptonshire Police she had suffered domestic abuse and that Person B had forced her to hide the clothes Person C wore during the offence. In 2024, PC A told the chief constable she had ended all contact with Person B in 2019, apart from unwanted contact he initiated. She also denied ever having contact with Person C. However, phone records and evidence from Person B indicated that she had been in touch with both individuals. In his written decision, Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: "I find that she would have been aware that the Chief Constable would rely upon her truthfulness in retaining her in the Constabulary. "This included the importance of her providing a full and accurate account of contact with Persons B and C. "This was essential, given her knowledge as a police officer of the seriousness of Person C's criminal behaviour. "I find that she was aware that the accounts provided were not accurate. "In my view, this was not misremembering, as alleged by her, but the deliberate misleading of a senior police officer in a formal hearing. "I then applied the standards of ordinary decent members of the public, who in my view, would consider such conduct by PC A to be dishonest." The panel found that PC A had repeatedly misled the chief constable and the Professional Standards Department. The panel found that PC A’s actions amounted to gross misconduct and breached the honesty standards expected of officers. Aggravating factors included repeated dishonesty, conduct during formal investigations, and the personal gain involved in attempting to remain employed as a police officer. Limited weight was given to personal mitigation, despite PC A’s reported history of domestic abuse. Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: "In my view there was no mitigation for the misconduct. "Having carefully considered the difficult personal life and the impact on PC A, I am still minded to place limited reliance, in determining the appropriate sanction, on personal mitigation. "However it is my view such misconduct is at the upper end of seriousness, causing significant harm to confidence in the Constabulary." As well as dismissal without notice, PC A will be placed on the College of Policing’s public barred list. Chief Constable Simon Megicks said: “PC A deliberately misled investigators and senior officers during formal proceedings about her associations and contact with individuals linked to a serious crime matter. “Honesty is fundamental to policing. "When an officer fails to uphold those standards, it risks undermining public confidence in the police service. "The outcome reflects the seriousness with which we treat such conduct.”

metadata.title: 10 Cambridgeshire pubs named among UK's best real ale venues
metadata.contentSnippet: CAMRA’s latest Good Beer Guide names dozens of Cambridgeshire pubs among the best places to enjoy real ale.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 10 Cambridgeshire pubs named among UK's best real ale venues
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: CAMRA’s latest Good Beer Guide names dozens of Cambridgeshire pubs among the best places to enjoy real ale. The Campaign for Real Ale’s 2027 guide celebrates the UK’s best pubs and independent breweries, with 812 new entries chosen by volunteers. The £16.99 Good Beer Guide 2027 is available from CAMRA’s website and showcases cask-beer venues across the country, including Cambridgeshire. (Image: CAMRA) Ash Corbett-Collins, CAMRA’s chairman, said: "The Good Beer Guide is fiercely independent, just like the brewers making the best beer. "It is the result of the time and effort of our volunteers across the UK to find the pubs serving the best kept cask beer. "This year, we released our flagship report, Beer in the UK, alongside our campaign to expose how ‘Big Beer’ is dominating the UK beer market, and how ordinary drinkers and independent brewers lose out as a result. "Because of that, we need the Competition and Markets Authority to start a formal investigation of the UK on-trade beer market. "If you agree with us, please join CAMRA, buy the Guide, and find amazing independently brewed beers for yourself." Sir Ian Rankin, author of the foreword for this year’s guide, said: "What makes the perfect pub? "Ask 50 people, and you might get 50 different answers. "My preferences might not be yours, but there are a few things we can probably agree on. "We want the beer to be good and the welcome to be friendly. "We want to see signs that the bar represents the best of its community or neighbourhood. "We want to feel like we fit in." The guide features 4,500 pubs, 1,700 brewers and 5,000 beers, all selected through an independent volunteer-led process. The 2027 guide highlights a mix of Cambridgeshire city-centre favourites and rural gems. This 16th-century former coaching inn on Market Hill is said to have been Oliver Cromwell’s recruiting station. CAMRA highlights its ever-changing range of beers, served from up to 14 handpumps. The ivy-clad Old Bridge Hotel overlooks the River Great Ouse from an 18th-century former private bank. The Old Bridge Hotel in Huntingdon is named in the CAMRA Good Beer Guide 2027. (Image: BID Huntingdon) The Pig ’n’ Falcon serves up to six changing beers, often including unusual and dark brews. Nelson’s Head sits on Merryland in the town centre, with two drinking areas and a large outdoor patio. This city-centre micropub is one of Ely’s top destinations for beer lovers. It was named local Pub of the Year in 2025 and Cider Pub of the Year in 2026. The West End House in Ely is named in the Good Beer Guide 2027, pictured here after being named Pub of the Year for Ely and district earlier this year. (Image: CAMRA Ely and District) Known locally as "The Westie", this traditional pub is just a short walk from Ely Cathedral. The guide describes it as a snug and welcoming local. It was named local CAMRA Pub of the Year 2026. The Draper’s Arms occupies a converted 19th-century draper’s shop on Cowgate and is listed among Wetherspoon’s top 10 real-ale pubs. This community pub has served customers for around 150 years. The Blue Bell overlooks Werrington village green and offers a traditional pub atmosphere, spacious garden and regular entertainment. The thatched 17th-century Ship Inn sits beside the River Nene and has featured in the guide for 17 years. The Good Beer Guide 2027 has all the details of the Cambridgeshire pubs and entries from across the UK.

metadata.title: Officer stabbed as police arrest 17 during dawn raids targeting crime gang
metadata.contentSnippet: Seventeen people have been arrested after police raids targeting an organised crime group across five areas, including Hertfordshire and Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Officer stabbed as police arrest 17 during dawn raids targeting crime gang
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Seventeen people have been arrested after dawn raids targeting an organised crime group across five areas, including Hertfordshire and Cambridgeshire. The arrests were made this morning (September 29), during raids at 24 properties across Hertfordshire, Cambridgeshire, London, Essex and Suffolk. More than 800 Met officers took part in the arrest operations. A Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "These arrests mark a significant point in this investigation. "Those arrested are suspected of leading or being involved at a senior level in serious and organised crime and related financial offending." The operation follows a months-long investigation by specialist Met detectives working with HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Officers from both agencies helped search the properties. The FCA has also disrupted seven firms and is pursuing a further 30 as part of the wider operation. A spokesperson for the FCA said: "Tackling financial crime requires the type of partnership shown by today’s joint action and the many months of close cooperation leading to it. "We’ll continue to work with the police and others to identify and disrupt organised crime groups who abuse our financial system to launder dirty money." Those arrested included a 65-year-old man suspected of taking part in an organised crime group, conspiracy to commit grievous bodily harm, money laundering and tax evasion. A 31-year-old woman was arrested on suspicion of conspiring to commit GBH and taking part in an organised crime group. A 56-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of GBH over the stabbing of a police officer, as well as taking part in an organised crime group, money laundering, tax evasion, false accounting and failing to report suspected money laundering. Others were arrested on suspicion of money laundering, cheating the public revenue, false accounting and breaching anti-money-laundering rules. A spokesperson for HMRC said: "Today’s action highlights the importance of close collaboration between HMRC and other law enforcement partners in tackling serious and organised crime, including suspected money laundering and other criminal activity." An officer was stabbed in the leg while executing a warrant at a property in Cockfosters, Barnet, during the raids. Colleagues and paramedics treated him at the scene before he was taken to hospital with injuries that were not life-changing. The Met said: "We will ensure he gets all the support he needs." The force also warned that organised crime harms whole communities. A spokesperson said: "We know the impact of serious and organised crime stretches well beyond those at senior levels of the organisations involved. "Lines can often be drawn from the top, all the way to those involved in the criminality that blights communities, including serious violence and exploitation." Organised crime investigations are among the Met’s most complex operations, demanding time, resources and expertise from police and partner agencies. The spokesperson said: "We hope these arrests show how determined we are to ensure organised crime groups cannot operate freely in London. "We will work tirelessly to identify them, to gather evidence and to take action." Searches are continuing at several properties, with police warning of a visible presence in affected areas for days. Met, HMRC and FCA officers are continuing to gather evidence and build cases against those arrested.

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire first in UK to pilot AI-powered crime reporting tool
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire has become the first place in the UK to pilot AI-powered crime reporting technology.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire first in UK to pilot AI-powered crime reporting tool
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire has become the first place in the UK to pilot AI-powered crime reporting technology. Cambridgeshire Constabulary is trialling Citizen Assist, an artificial intelligence system that guides users through reporting non-urgent crimes via a conversational, text-based tool on the force’s website. The pilot launched on September 24 as part of a national scheme led by the National Police Chiefs' Council to improve digital public contact. Simon Megicks, chief constable of Cambridgeshire Constabulary, said: "This scheme is ultimately about utilising new technology to improve the service we can provide to the public, by developing and enhancing the reporting options already available to them. "As we move through an increasingly digital world, as a constabulary, we recognise the importance of embracing AI in a way that means we’re able to provide another, convenient way to report crime digitally." Citizen Assist is designed specifically for policing and supports the entire reporting process. It gathers information, builds a structured crime report, and submits it directly into police systems. Simon said: "Citizen Assist is a great opportunity to harness modern technology to help ensure crime reports reach us with accurate, high-quality information from the outset, benefiting both the public and the force. "Whilst the AI technology will help to collect and collate relevant information and turn it into a crime report, all decisions about the report will remain firmly with police staff and officers, just as it does with existing online crime reports." He emphasised that the technology is intended to supplement, not replace, existing reporting channels. Members of the public can now use Citizen Assist to report non-urgent crimes through the ‘report a crime’ section of the force’s website. Further details about the system and its use in Cambridgeshire are available on the Cambridgeshire Constabulary website.

metadata.title: Andy Burnham announces VAT cut on energy bills 'from this Thursday' in keynote speech
metadata.contentSnippet: Andy Burnham has announced that VAT will be removed from domestic energy bills from 'this Thursday', October 2026.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Andy Burnham announces VAT cut on energy bills 'from this Thursday' in keynote speech
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Andy Burnham has announced VAT will be removed from domestic energy bills from 'this Thursday', October 2026. The move, worth £850 million, is expected to save the average household around £45 a year, giving families extra help as colder weather approaches, and the energy price cap increases. At his first party conference speech since becoming Prime Minister, Mr Burnham said the Government wanted to provide immediate support for households facing ongoing cost-of-living pressures. From this Thursday, October 1 2026, VAT on domestic electricity bills will fall from 5% to 0%. The Government says energy suppliers are expected to pass the saving directly on to customers, including those on fixed tariffs. Officials estimate the measure will help millions of households from this week: While the exact saving will depend on individual energy use, the announcement is expected to provide welcome relief for millions of families heading into winter. The Government explained the moves in July, saying the measure will be funded by cancelling the previous digital ID programme and reprioritising existing departmental budgets, allowing households to benefit without introducing new taxes. Chancellor John Healey said this summer the announcement would provide reassurance for families while helping to tackle the cost of living: "For too long, too many people have struggled with the cost of living. "Today's energy tax cut will give families some breathing room on bills and provide reassurance this winter."

metadata.title: Boy, 14, missing from home in Cambs as police launch appeal
metadata.contentSnippet: Police have launched an appeal to trace a 14-year-old boy missing from his home in Grafham, near Huntingdon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Boy, 14, missing from home in Cambs as police launch appeal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have launched an appeal to trace a 14-year-old boy missing from his home in Cambridgeshire. Delton was last seen in the early hours of September 29 after leaving his home on Inhams Way, Grafham, near Huntingdon. He is described as slim, 5ft 10in tall, with brown hair and green eyes. He is believed to be wearing a green hoodie, blue jeans or black tracksuit bottoms, and light grey Sketchers trainers. Delton may also be carrying a large khaki-green Mountain Warehouse rucksack. Anyone who sees Delton should call 999 immediately, quoting incident 73 from September 29.

A very warm welcome back to Abbey College. 
As part of our school community, you play an important role in helping our young people 
succeed. This weekly bulletin helps us stay connected as we work together to support more

metadata.contentSnippet: A councillor has been named Young Councillor of the Year for his work in Huntingdon.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon councillor Nathan Hunt named Young Councillor of the Year
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A councillor has been named Young Councillor of the Year for his work in Huntingdon. Nathan Hunt, a town councillor for Huntingdon, received the honour from the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Association of Local Councils (CAPALC) in recognition of his contributions to town and parish council work. Cllr Hunt said: "I am honoured to receive this award and would like to thank CAPALC and Cllr Cushman for the nomination. "One of my priorities as a councillor is ensuring that young people feel represented and encouraged to engage with local democracy. "I hope this award highlights the important contribution that younger councillors can make to their communities, and I look forward to continuing to serve the residents of Huntingdon." Originally elected to Huntingdon Town Council’s Central ward in July 2024, Cllr Hunt was re-elected to the Huntingdon East ward in May 2026. The award was collected on his behalf by the Mayor of Huntingdon, Cllr Patrick Kadewere, at the CAPALC Awards on Friday, September 18 and was formally presented to Cllr Hunt at a council meeting on Tuesday, September 22. Cllr Kadewere said: "Nathan's award is thoroughly deserved and reflects the positive contribution he has made since joining Huntingdon Town Council. "He and our other younger members have shown that age is no barrier to making a meaningful difference in the community, bringing enthusiasm, fresh ideas, and a genuine commitment to representing residents. "We are proud to see his work recognised by CAPALC and hope his achievement inspires other young people to consider getting involved in local government." Cllr Hunt was nominated by Deputy Mayor Freya Cushman, who praised his efforts to promote inclusivity within the council. Huntingdon Town Council is currently inviting applications from residents aged 18 or over to fill a co-option vacancy in the Hinchingbrooke ward.

metadata.title: 18-year-old who died after car crashed into tree in Woburn named
metadata.contentSnippet: A teenager who died in a crash in Woburn has been named as 18-year-old Megan Durham.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 18-year-old who died after car crashed into tree in Woburn named
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A teenager who died in a crash when her car hit a tree has been named as 18-year-old Megan Durham. Megan, from Milton Keynes, was killed when her Fiat 500 left the road and hit a tree in Sheep Lane, Woburn on Sunday, September 13. In a tribute, her family said she was "loved beyond words by family members and friends" and "will be deeply missed by all who knew her." "Our thoughts remain with Megan's family and loved ones who have requested privacy at this incredibly difficult time," said a spokesperson for Bedfordshire Police. "Officers from the Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Roads Policing Unit are continuing their investigation and are preparing a file for the coroner." Police want witnesses who saw the vehicle before the crash or have information about it to come forward. The collision happened at around 11pm, and police believe other vehicles may have passed the scene. Drivers are being asked to check dashcam footage and quote Operation Herring when reporting information to police at www.beds.police.uk/ro/report.

metadata.title: Godmanchester Apple Day to feature 20 heritage varieties and supersized surprises
metadata.contentSnippet: Godmanchester's annual Apple Day is set to return next month.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Godmanchester Apple Day to feature 20 heritage varieties and supersized surprises
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Godmanchester is set to celebrate its annual Apple Day. The free event takes place at Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery on Saturday October 10 from 10am to 3pm. The nursery, run by Godmanchester Town Council, boasts a heritage orchard with 20 apple varieties, many of which were first cultivated before 1900. This event gives families—and well-behaved pets—the opportunity to explore the nursery and taste apples that cannot be found in supermarkets. The celebration goes beyond apples, with a variety of local traders also expected to attend, offering free activities for children. The Godmanchester Miniature Railway will be on site, and attendees can enjoy live music from the Collaboration Choir and the Carpe Diem Band. Moores Mobile Farm will also be present, bringing goats, guinea pigs, ducks, and rabbits. Attendees can participate in traditional apple pressing and taste the fresh results. This year, the event welcomes 'Supersize Ken', who became famous last year for making everyday items in large proportions. The nursery's Muddy Trowel Café will serve cakes and their renowned hot pulled pork rolls with apple sauce. Belle’s GF Bakes will provide a variety of gluten-free and vegan options. Three local businesses will provide cider, spirits, and locally grown and pressed fruit juice. Saragusta Spirits and Meadow Lodge Farm have teamed up to create the event's first-ever Apple Day cocktail and mocktail. The nursery encourages visitors to walk, cycle, or take the bus to the event due to limited parking. The community plant nursery is powered almost entirely by volunteers and has established itself as an integral part of the Godmanchester community, not only as a plant nursery but also as a place people can visit for free to enjoy nature. The nursery's Facebook event page has more information.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have released CCTV images of a man they would like to speak to in connection with a spate of arsons in Huntingdon. The incidents happened on August 11, including in St Germain Street, where a skip was set on fire. Another two incidents occurred on Mill Common, where dry vegetation was set alight. Those who recognise the man pictured should contact police online or call 101, quoting reference 35/61993/26. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk or newsdesk@huntspost.co.uk

metadata.title: Race Across Cambridge sells out all 54 team spots for charity event
metadata.contentSnippet: The second edition of Race Across Cambridge, which takes place on October 1, has sold out.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Race Across Cambridge sells out all 54 team spots for charity event
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A popular event is set to return to Cambridgeshire for a second year. Jenny Ballantyne, HR director at CB3 Consulting, created Race Across Cambridge from her home in Wimblington. She said: "It genuinely started as one of those ideas you have sitting at home. "I remember thinking how brilliant it would be to get people from across our industry out from behind their desks and bring them together for an afternoon completely removed from the pressures of everyday work. "I wanted it to be competitive, undoubtedly, because this is the construction industry. "But more importantly, I wanted to create something fun that would bring people together and have a real purpose behind it." Teams race around Cambridge solving clues, and the 2026 event filled all 54 places by August 27. The CB3 team after Race Across Cambridge last year. More than 200 people are expected to take part. This year, funds are being raised for The Phoenix Trust, a Cambridge charity that supports people with learning disabilities through work experience and skills development. Ms Ballantyne said: "Seeing it sell out at over 50 teams this year is quite overwhelming. "I may have come up with the original idea, but Race Across Cambridge has become a huge CB3 team effort. "So many people have put their time, enthusiasm and creativity into making it what it is. "I'm incredibly proud of what we've created together and incredibly grateful to all the businesses that have got behind it." The event will start at St John’s Innovation Centre on Thursday October 1. Donations can be made at justgiving.com/page/cb3phoenixtrust.

metadata.contentSnippet: A row has erupted between the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority and Huntingdonshire District Council over plans for free parking in Huntingdon, St Neots and St Ives.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Row over free parking plans in Huntingdonshire market towns
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A row has erupted between the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority and Huntingdonshire District Council over plans for free parking in Huntingdonshire's market towns. Mayor Paul Bristow accused the district council of delaying free parking, while its leader, Cllr Sarah Conboy, said he changed the proposal after councillors approved a different scheme. The dispute centres on a Combined Authority-funded parking initiative intended to support town centres in Huntingdon, St Neots and St Ives. Cambridgeshire Mayor has offered to fund free parking after 3pm in Huntingdonshire car parks like this one in St Neots. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) In a letter to Cllr Conboy dated September 24, the mayor said free parking had boosted high streets elsewhere and should do the same in the three towns. He wrote: "Free parking is a great way to do this. It's working in Peterborough and can work in the Huntingdonshire Towns." He said Combined Authority funding was still available and that free parking after 4pm was "a starting point for the offer, not the destination". The mayor said he wanted to see free parking introduced after 3pm and accused the authority of failing to bring forward a workable scheme. Cambridgeshire Mayor has offered to fund free parking after 3pm in Huntingdonshire car parks like the Cattle Market in St Ives. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) In the letter, he criticised what he described as "long periods of silence, punctuated by excuses, technical evasions and claims that no preparatory work can be done at all unless money is paid upfront". He also suggested the council had focused more effort on potential redevelopment of car parks than on implementing free parking. Mr Bristow said he had "lost faith" in the council and was seeking alternative providers if no deal could be reached. Huntingdonshire District Council strongly denied blocking the scheme. Cambridgeshire Mayor has offered to fund free parking after 3pm in Huntingdonshire car parks like Ingram Street in Huntingdon. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) In a statement, Cllr Conboy said cabinet members had approved a district-wide free-after-4pm parking scheme in July after officers worked with the Combined Authority to develop the proposal and provide modelling data. The council said this was the scheme formally offered by the mayor and subsequently approved by cabinet. She said the mayor then backed a different plan offering free parking after 3pm in selected car parks rather than across the district. "The council cannot implement a materially different scheme without following the appropriate decision-making process," Cllr Conboy said. She said the revised plan needed more analysis, approvals and implementation work, delaying its introduction. The council said each site needed assessing for operational, financial and delivery implications before the alternative scheme could proceed. The authority said the revised plan would have added to officers' existing statutory and operational workload. The council said it had explained the practical, financial and governance implications of both plans before the mayor withdrew the alternative proposal. "The council remains committed to working constructively with the Combined Authority on initiatives that support residents, businesses and town centres," Cllr Conboy said. The disagreement leaves uncertainty over whether a free parking scheme will be introduced in Huntingdonshire and what form it could take. Both sides say they want to help town centres but remain split over a district-wide free-after-4pm scheme or targeted free-after-3pm parking. The Combined Authority's budget set aside £1.5 million for a two-year free-parking trial in Peterborough and parts of Huntingdonshire, with schemes still required to pass local approval processes.

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire bus routes set for changes as new network plans approved
metadata.contentSnippet: Changes are on the way for bus routes in Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire bus routes set for changes as new network plans approved
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Changes are on the way for bus routes in Cambridgeshire. The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority Board approved new plans for the region's supported bus network on Wednesday, September 23. The plans follow a six-week public engagement, and include revised routes, new connections and improvements to existing services. Paul Bristow, Mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, said: "Thank you to everyone who told us what they need from their buses. "That feedback has made a difference to these plans, including where we’ve revised routes and retained connections that matter to communities. "Today’s decision allows us to move ahead with a network designed to make better connections and provide more reliable journeys across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. "It is another step towards getting our region moving." Some routes, including the 65 between St Neots, Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives, have been revised based on public feedback. The 62 will continue to serve the Werrington loop. The combined authority will now begin the tendering process, with the first changes expected in February 2027 and further updates planned for August 2027. A spokesperson for the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority said: "Residents, councillors, MPs and community groups told the Combined Authority they wanted reliable and frequent buses, suitable operating hours and better access to destinations including rail stations and healthcare. "Their feedback informed revisions to the proposals across the region, including changes to routes and timetables, replacement links where practical, and the use of Tiger on Demand where appropriate." The authority said it will clearly communicate confirmed routes, timetables and start dates once contracts are agreed. The review is part of the authority’s wider plans to improve the bus network, alongside its ambitions for bus franchising. Details of all proposed route changes can be found on the combined authority’s website.

metadata.title: Beyond the classroom: what makes Year 9 at Abbey College Cambridge different?

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: In partnership with Abbey College Cambridge For many families, choosing a school for Year 9 is about more than academics. It is about finding an environment where young people can build confidence, develop independence and prepare for the opportunities and challenges of the future. At Abbey College Cambridge, Year 9 offers an experience that goes beyond the traditional school model. Combining strong academic foundations with personalised support, international opportunities and unique access to the city of Cambridge, students are encouraged to see learning as something that extends far beyond the classroom. One of the most distinctive aspects of life at Abbey College Cambridge is their "Cambridge Is Our Classroom" philosophy. Through access to lectures, events and speakers from across the city, students engage with ideas and issues that are shaping the modern world. Topics such as politics, artificial intelligence, science and social justice become more meaningful when discussed by experts working at the forefront of their fields. As student Charles explains; “Being given access to a university-level of ideas as one of the youngest students has improved my academic maturity. Topics like politics, AI, science and social justice are easier to understand now because they have been explained using real examples from experts. This has also helped me understand difficult ideas in lessons and use real examples in discussions instead of just relying on me memorising information.” (Image: Abbey College Cambridge) The benefits extend beyond academic development. Students are encouraged to ask questions, engage in discussions and step outside their comfort zones. For many, this helps build the communication skills and self-belief that are essential for future success. Small class sizes also play a key role in the Year 9 experience. Students receive individual attention from teachers who know them well and can provide tailored support when needed. Students in Year 9 speak about the positive impact of this approach, noting how the personalised learning environment has helped them strengthen their understanding and make progress in subjects they previously found challenging. Alongside the National Curriculum, Year 9 students are immersed in a diverse international community that reflects the globalised world they will one day enter. Learning alongside peers from different countries and cultures gives students a broader perspective, enriching classroom discussions and exposing them to new ways of thinking. These daily interactions help build confidence, cultural intelligence and adaptability, ensuring students develop not only academically, but as globally minded young people ready to thrive in an interconnected future. Beyond the classroom, opportunities such as our exchange programme in Italy encourage students to step outside their comfort zones, experience different cultures first-hand and develop the independence and resilience that will serve them well throughout their education and future careers. (Image: Abbey College Cambridge) Learning beyond the classroom is further enhanced through the school’s extensive enrichment programme. Students can choose from a wide range of activities, including STEM, a wide range of sports, music, debating and animation. These experiences encourage students to explore new interests, develop practical skills and begin thinking about future career pathways. For local families seeking an education that offers more than a traditional school experience, Abbey College Cambridge provides a distinctive alternative. Year 9 students develop the confidence, curiosity and independence needed to thrive. Cambridge truly becomes the classroom, and students discover that their potential reaches far beyond the school gates. The school offers generous scholarships to local students for entry into Year 9. metadata.title: Bradley Walsh to replace Simon Cowell as judge on Britain's Got Talent
metadata.contentSnippet: Bradley Walsh is set to fill in for Simon Cowell during upcoming Britain’s Got Talent auditions while he has a back operation.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Bradley Walsh to replace Simon Cowell as judge on Britain's Got Talent
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Bradley Walsh is set to take Simon Cowell's seat on the judging panel of Britain’s Got Talent. The TV presenter, known for hosting The Chase and Gladiators, will fill in for Cowell during next month’s auditions. He will join regular judges Amanda Holden, Alesha Dixon, and KSI on the panel for the upcoming BGT auditions. Cowell is stepping down temporarily due to a back operation, following injuries sustained in a 2020 electric bike accident that led to long-term nerve damage and a metal rod being fitted in his spine. A source, speaking to The Sun, said: "Bradley will be a brilliant stand in for Simon and will offer an old school performer flavour, which will complement the rest of the cast nicely. "He's full of wise cracks and great one liners so should have the audience in stitches." Comedians Lee Mack and Greg Davies were also reportedly considered for the guest judging role. Huge TV star lined up to stand in for Simon Cowell in BGT auditions next month https://t.co/FBOnOwlzmc — The Sun TV (@TheSunTV) September 26, 2026 This is not the first time Cowell has missed part of the show due to injury; in 2020, Ashley Banjo stepped in as a guest judge during his absence. ITV has been contacted for comment. Britain’s Got Talent will return for its 20th series next year, though an exact start date has not yet been confirmed. This year’s series began in February, and a similar launch date is expected for 2027. Applications for BGT 2027 are now open and will close on Friday, October 16. ITV said: "Whether you can sing, dance, crack a joke or balance plates on your head while jumping on a trampoline, you could be our next winner! "So, don't hesitate, apply today." The Hawkstone Farmers' Choir, initially formed by Jeremy Clarkson to support farming and mental health awareness, won BGT 2026. The choir beat Celestial (drone art) and Anastasiia & Salsa (dog act) in the final, held on May 30. It was the first time a choir has won BGT. Have you applied for series 20 of Britain's Got Talent? metadata.title: World’s first Minecraft-themed hotel to open at huge UK theme park in 2027
metadata.contentSnippet: The world's first Minecraft-themed hotel is set to open in the UK, bringing the iconic video game experience to life.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: World’s first Minecraft-themed hotel to open at huge UK theme park in 2027
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The world's first Minecraft-themed hotel is set to open in the UK, bringing the iconic video game experience to life. Scheduled to launch in 2027, the hotel will be part of a new immersive land at Chessington World of Adventures in south-west London, called Minecraft World. The project is a collaboration between Merlin Entertainments and Mojang Studios, the company behind Minecraft. Daisy Mercedes, creative producer at Merlin Entertainments, said: "We promised something truly special when we announced Minecraft World earlier this year, and with Minecraft World Hotel we are offering even more. A new Minecraft ride will also open. (Image: Merlin Entertainments/Mojang Studios/PA Wire) "Not only will fans be able to experience the game imagined for real life, but they’ll be also able to sleep inside it, ensuring fans respawn exactly where they want to be." The four-storey hotel will feature 69 rooms, including 20 premium and 49 standard rooms, and will be fully themed around the game’s signature blocky design. Guests can expect to see biomes, mobs, and items brought to life in the décor, along with blocky trees, animals, and mine tunnel corridors. Amenities will include an underwater-themed restaurant and a bar inspired by the game’s Woodland Mansion. The new Minecraft World theme park land will feature the world’s first Minecraft rollercoaster, Escape The Nether. The ride promises a high-speed indoor adventure through dark mines before launching riders through a Nether portal into an Overworld-themed area. Ms Mercedes said: "Seeing the Minecraft World Hotel take shape alongside the attractions we are building at Chessington World of Adventures theme park is a Minecraft fans biggest dream. "Every room, corridor and detail has been crafted with immense love for this game, the stories made within it and its community." The hotel will be a world first. (Image: Merlin Entertainments/Mojang Studios/PA Wire) Filip Keatley Thoms, creative lead for Minecraft Parks and Experiences at Mojang Studios, said: "Bringing Minecraft into an entirely new medium has been a fascinating creative challenge. "We have thought about everything from the scale of the blocks to how mobs and biomes come to life in the real world. "Our goal is to create an experience that feels authentically Minecraft and gives guests the chance to experience the game in an entirely new way." The £50 million project is a collaboration between Merlin Entertainments, the owner of Legoland, Alton Towers and Thorpe Park, and Mojang Studios. Minecraft is the bestselling video game of all time, with millions of people playing every day. The block-building video game has previously been adapted into a film called A Minecraft Movie, which was the highest-grossing film at the box office in the UK and Ireland in 2025. Will you be booking the Minecraft hotel? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Crowdfunded dig to uncover more of Roman villa’s secrets in the Nene Valley
metadata.contentSnippet: A fresh dig is set to begin at a Roman villa in the Nene Valley, offering new insights into ancient life.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Crowdfunded dig to uncover more of Roman villa’s secrets in the Nene Valley
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A fresh dig is set to begin at a Roman villa in the Nene Valley, offering new insights into ancient life. The crowdfunded excavation at Sacrewell Farm is being led by DigVentures and marks the organisation’s first season of crowdfunded excavation in Cambridgeshire. It revisits a site first uncovered in the 1970s during water pipeline work, which revealed a Roman villa and evidence of industrial activity, including furnaces, tiled floors, painted walls, and metalworking. Participant with find (Image: Nene Valley) Harriet Tatton, Senior Project Officer for Project Development at DigVentures, said: "This area has such a rich history of industry and trade, and we’re excited to investigate this villa site to see what fresh discoveries we can uncover about Roman life here. "Archaeology is for everyone, and we’re so pleased to be able to help local people to engage with the history and heritage on their doorstep through these sponsored places and tours." The 1970s excavation did not reveal the full extent of the villa complex, leaving many questions about its residents and role in the wider Nene Valley. Pottery (Image: Nene Valley) The region was a major centre of Roman production, transport, and trade, with sites like Durobrivae (near modern-day Water Newton) forming part of an extensive network of villa estates, pottery kilns, and ironworking facilities. DigVentures will conduct a two-week excavation to help uncover more of the site’s layout, including the villa itself, nearby buildings, and other areas of activity. Samian Ware (Image: Nene Valley) The project aims to shed light on who may have lived there, and the role Sacrewell played in the wider Nene Valley economy. Free public tours of the site will take place on Saturday, October 3, and can be booked via Eventbrite. Education partner Nibble is funding a limited number of free places for people on low incomes, those facing social barriers, refugees, and members of migrant communities.

metadata.title: Royal Mint launches new 50p coin worth 39 times its value and it could win you £2,000
metadata.contentSnippet: Royal Mint launches collectable Cluedo 50p coins featuring iconic suspects, with a chance to win a gold coin worth over £2,000.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Royal Mint launches new 50p coin worth 39 times its value and it could win you £2,000
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Collectable Cluedo 50p coins are being launched, with a chance to win a gold 50p worth more than £2,000. The design features the iconic cast of suspects, including Miss Scarlett, Colonel Mustard, Professor Plum, Mrs Peacock, Reverend Green, and Mrs White. Some versions of the coin include colours associated with the board game. The coin was launched in collaboration with Hasbro to celebrate Cluedo’s enduring legacy and global popularity. Tim Mulhall, head of fandom at The Royal Mint, said: "Every coin we create tells a story, and the Cluedo 50p is no exception. Ellie Leach, who played Miss Scarlett in the stage production Cluedo 2 (Image: David Parry/PA Media Assignments) "Cluedo has captivated millions of players for decades, and we’ve channelled that spirit of mystery and intrigue into every detail of the design. "We hope members of the public enjoy cracking the case of 'the missing coin' as much as we’ve enjoyed bringing the coin to life. "There’s a real thrill to coin collecting, and we hope solving this case connects that same passion for collecting with the mystery and excitement of a game like Cluedo." The coin’s intricate design includes microtext naming the characters, locations and weapons from the game, encouraging collectors to use a magnifying glass to uncover its hidden details. To mark the launch, The Royal Mint is running a free-to-enter online competition called "the case of the missing coin," giving fans the chance to win a gold Cluedo 50p valued at more than £2,000. Marcia Lewis, daughter of Cluedo creator Anthony Pratt. (Image: David Parry/PA Media Assignments) Entrants must solve weekly clues released on The Royal Mint’s website and social channels, identifying the suspect, location, and coin type. A winner will be selected after the competition closes on October 19. Strictly Come Dancing champion Ellie Leach, who played Miss Scarlett in the stage production Cluedo 2, inspected the coins, alongside Marcia Lewis, daughter of Cluedo creator Anthony Pratt. Ms Lewis said: "My father invented the game at his home in Birmingham during the long nights under blackout in the Second World War, while my mother, Elva, designed the board. "Visiting The Royal Mint to strike my own coin and to see the range of skills, craftsmanship and minute attention to detail that went into its production was a moment I will always cherish and one I know my parents would have too. "Cluedo has brought entertainment, escapism and delight to hundreds of millions of people and I’m immensely proud to know my father’s legacy, so cleverly represented in this coin, will now be treasured by collectors and families for many years to come." Ms Leach said: "Playing Miss Scarlett on stage was one of my favourite roles, so getting to bring her back to life for The Royal Mint was such a fun challenge." Marianne James, senior vice president of global licensing at Hasbro, said: "Cluedo has brought generations together through mystery, strategy and play." Recommended Reading The Cluedo 50p is available to purchase from The Royal Mint’s website from 9am on Monday, with prices starting from £19.95. From October 6, visitors to The Royal Mint Experience in Llantrisant, South Wales, will also have the chance to strike their own Cluedo 50p. The edition available to strike will feature a more simplified design, depicting a magnifying glass set against a game board. Will you be buying the Cluedo 50p? Let us know in the comments.

metadata.title: Urgent appeal for adoptive families as 35 Cambridgeshire children wait for homes
metadata.contentSnippet: A campaign has been launched to find more adoptive families for children in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Urgent appeal for adoptive families as 35 Cambridgeshire children wait for homes
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A campaign has been launched to find more adoptive families for children in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Adoption Service is urging people to come forward and offer children a permanent, loving home. Thirty-five children across the region are waiting to be adopted, including 16 under two and 14 in sibling groups. Councillor Edna Murphy, chair of Cambridgeshire County Council’s children and young people’s committee, said: "Every child deserves the security, love and sense of belonging that comes from having a permanent family. "Unfortunately, there are still too many children waiting for adoptive families, and every extra day they wait is a day without the stability they need." The Every Day is Everything campaign highlights the need for more adoptive families and stresses that children need love, stability and commitment. Over the past year, children placed for adoption through the service were aged two years and six months on average and waited 17 months for a family. Cllr Murphy said: "We want people who may have considered adoption in the past to know that they do not need to have a perfect home, perfect finances, or all the answers. "What matters most is your ability to offer a child love, stability, and a lifelong commitment." The adoption service supports families from their first enquiry through approval, matching, placement and beyond. Throughout September, the service will share adoption information and adoptive families’ experiences on social media. People interested in adoption can email adoptionenquiries@cambridgeshire.gov.uk, call 0300 123 1093 or visit www.cpadoption.co.uk.

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire hospitals to introduce shared electronic patient record system
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridge University Hospitals (CUH) and Royal Papworth Hospital are joining forces to introduce a shared electronic patient record (EPR) system.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire hospitals to introduce shared electronic patient record system
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridge University Hospitals (CUH) and Royal Papworth Hospital are joining forces to introduce a shared electronic patient record (EPR) system. The system will improve care across the Cambridge Biomedical Campus and beyond by helping the two NHS trusts share information and avoid duplication. Harvey McEnroe, Royal Papworth Hospital’s chief operating officer and senior responsible officer for the EPR programme, said: "This is a huge step forward for our organisations and the patients we serve. The partnership aims to support more joined-up patient care (Image: Royal Papworth Hospital) "We are grateful to NHS England, our integrated care board and all our partners for their support and collaboration in helping make our ambitions to create a shared electronic patient record a reality." The EPR will use CUH’s Epic system, which has been in place since 2014, through the Epic Connect model. The model has already been used elsewhere in the UK to link neighbouring hospitals more closely. The rollout is expected to take just over a year and will involve both trusts and Epic Systems Corporation. Royal Papworth Hospital (Image: Royal Papworth Hospital) Harvey said: "This clinically led decision will transform the way we deliver care, strengthen collaboration between our hospitals, and enhance our research capabilities, benefiting patients and staff for years to come." Patients will get more joined-up care, with clinical teams able to see their complete information in one place. It should mean patients repeat themselves less and move more smoothly between services. Royal Papworth Hospital and Cambridge University Hospitals are working together (Image: Royal Papworth Hospital) Dr Sue Broster, chief medical officer at Cambridge University Hospitals, said: "This important development will improve the experience of patients receiving care across our two hospitals. "By bringing information together securely in one place, it will support smoother transitions, reduce duplication and help us achieve our aim of patients only having to tell their story once. "It will also help ensure that care remains consistent and is delivered at the right time." The partnership comes as GSK plans a £400 million global research and development centre on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, with around 1,000 scientists expected at the site by 2029.

metadata.title: Letter questions £1m Hunts housing spend as council considers 20-year parking plan

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Letter questions £1m Hunts housing spend as council considers 20-year parking plan
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A reader of the Hunts Post has sent a letter questioning parking and housing plans for Huntingdonshire Dear editor, I am beginning to wonder if I am on the same planet as Huntingdonshire District Council. On page 5 of your September 16, 2026 issue of the Hunts Post you report on the fiasco of the proposed housing developments by property developer Capital and Centric to be sited on car parks in Huntingdon, St Ives and St Neots. These ill-conceived concepts have been the subject of vociferous but entirely reasonable objections by residents of those townships and the surrounding villages for which they are hubs. HDC is now debating and examining the £1 million spent on these projects so far. And then what? Further into the paper on page 10, HDC cabinet is reported to be considering a new 20-year parking plan and strategy for the council’s 25 off-street car parks, which surely includes Huntingdon, St Ives and St Neots. This strategy has four aims, including supporting thriving town centres and linking parking to sustainable transport. As regular shoppers in St Ives, my wife and I consider that the town’s current car parking facilities largely satisfy those criteria. It is therefore both bemusing, and very concerning, that these two contradictory (and mutually exclusive, as you can only have one or the other, but not both) proposals have been arrived at by HDC. Time for a visit to HDC by the sanity inspector I think! Paul Faupel Somersham

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A hospice in Milton has been praised for its "exceptional care" by the High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire during a recent visit. Francis Burkitt DL, High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire, visited East Anglia’s Children’s Hospices (EACH) in Milton to present certificates of appreciation to long-serving staff and volunteers. He was joined by his wife Jo and Jonathan Jelley MBE JP during the visit, which included a tour of the care floor and meetings with children, families, and staff. Francis said: "I was delighted to be given the chance to celebrate and thank some of those who do so much to support EACH’s work. The High Sheriff of Cambridgeshire visited EACH’s hospice in Milton (Image: EACH) "EACH is widely known and highly regarded as one of the very best organisations in our county, doing so much for children and families across Cambridgeshire. "It’s the people who help deliver that exceptional care and support, and I can’t speak highly enough of the wonderful staff who work here." He also recognised the vital role of volunteers, adding: "Likewise, the amazing volunteers who selflessly give their time. "That’s why I was so thrilled to honour and recognise the contribution made by people like Mick and Graham here at Milton." High Sheriff’s Certificates of Appreciation were awarded to staff members Sandra Holmes, Helen Thrower and Sallyann Parkin, as well as volunteers Mick Housden and Graham Shipley. Awards were presented to staff and volunteers during the visit (Image: EACH) Additional certificates were left for housekeeper Ohla Hlukhodid and volunteers Elaine Hallworth and Lynn Saunders, who were unable to attend. Lucy Brumpton, head of care transformation and development at EACH, said: "We were delighted to welcome the High Sheriff, his wife, Jo, and Jonathan, and greatly appreciate them taking the time to visit us. "The interest they showed in our work and the positive conversations throughout were both encouraging and inspiring."

metadata.title: Millions of pensioners could be owed money after HMRC mistake
metadata.contentSnippet: Around 3.2 million pensioners are due HMRC refunds after a state pension tax calculation error. Find out who is affected and what happens next.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Millions of pensioners could be owed money after HMRC mistake
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of pensioners are set to receive tax refunds after an HMRC calculation error left them paying too much tax on their state pension. Around 3.2 million pensioners are affected, with repayments expected to total around £19.3 million. That works out at roughly £6 per person on average, although the amount each pensioner receives will vary. The error relates to the way HMRC calculated annual state pension income when working out how much tax was due. Tax specialist Andy Wood from Tax Barrister UK said the mistake could have been difficult for pensioners to spot - and warned that those affected need clear information about exactly which years have been checked. The problem concerns the pension income figure used in HMRC's tax calculations. Normally, where the state pension increases during the tax year, the annual figure should include one week at the previous pension rate and 51 weeks at the increased rate. However, some calculations instead used the higher pension rate for all 52 weeks. This meant the annual pension income figure was overstated, potentially resulting in too much tax being collected. Andy Wood said: “An error like this can be difficult for someone to spot because the pension figure used in their tax calculation may look perfectly plausible. “The difference between the two calculations might appear small, but accuracy matters. Pensioners should be able to trust that the income figure used to work out their tax is correct.” The HMRC correction exercise covers affected cases from the 2020/21 tax year onwards. Pensioners do not generally need to apply for the correction. Repayments will be dealt with automatically through PAYE adjustments, Self Assessment credits or other payment methods, where appropriate. Andy said automatic corrections should make the process easier for people who had no reason to realise something had gone wrong. He said: “Automatic corrections are welcome because they reduce the burden on people who may have had no reason to suspect an error. “However, the explanation accompanying a correction is just as important. People need to understand which tax years have been reviewed, how their repayment was calculated and whether anything remains outstanding. “The headline total should also be put into context. This is a correction of tax overpaid, so individuals should not assume they are all entitled to the same amount.” One important point is that the automatic correction does not cover tax years before 2020/21. HMRC does not hold sufficient data to correct those cases automatically. However, people who believe they may have been affected in an earlier year can request an individual review and provide supporting evidence. That means pensioners should not necessarily assume that an automatic repayment means every possible overpayment has been dealt with. Andy said: “The position for earlier years deserves particular clarity. Someone receiving an automatic correction could reasonably assume that every affected year has been addressed. “HMRC needs to make the boundaries of this exercise clear, including what evidence it would consider for an earlier period. That would help pensioners understand what has been resolved and where further questions may remain.”

metadata.title: UK drivers warned of £100 fines over common motorway mistake
metadata.contentSnippet: Red X signs are used to close lanes in the event of an obstruction, and ignoring them can result in a fine of up to £100 and three penalty points.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: UK drivers warned of £100 fines over common motorway mistake
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Thousands of motorway drivers risk a £100 fine and three penalty points by ignoring red X signs. Red X signs are used to close lanes in the event of an obstruction, and ignoring them can result in a fine of up to £100 and three penalty points. Nicholas Lyes, director of policy and standards at IAM RoadSmart, said: "Ignoring a red X sign on a smart motorway is dangerous because it risks a serious collision and, for this reason, we welcome police forces clamping down on those who break the law. "The majority of drivers have serious reservations about the safety of smart motorways where the hard shoulder has been removed, and these figures are unlikely to persuade them they are safe." National Highways staff activate the red X signs when a stopped vehicle is detected in a live lane, to prevent collisions and protect emergency responders. Mr Lyes added: "We know that no new all-lane running smart motorways will be built but it does beg the question of what we do with the existing stretches that are in operation? "This is something the new Government needs to give some serious thought to." A spokesperson for National Highways said: "A Red X signal is there to increase the safety of everyone using the road by highlighting an issue ahead. "Above 90% of drivers observe Red X signals, but ignoring Red X signals is an offence and puts themselves and others at risk." Speed cameras work using radar or road markings to monitor a vehicle’s speed and capture evidence of any offence. While older cameras used film, most modern devices are fully digital and can even track your average speed over many miles. These digital systems record: In some cases, they even capture a clear image of the driver and passenger. Contrary to common belief, there’s no universal “10% + 2mph” rule baked into law. Experts from BigWantsYourCar.com explained: ““The idea that you’re safe doing 35mph in a 30 zone is one of the biggest myths we hear. “Technically, you’re liable for a fine the moment you go even 1mph over the limit.” While the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) does recommend a “10% plus 2” margin to allow for officer discretion, this is not a legal threshold and can vary depending on the enforcement area or the officer reviewing the case. RAC advice adds: “The law states that you are liable for a speeding fine as soon as you exceed the limit, so if you’re doing 31mph in a 30 limit or 71mph on a motorway, you’re breaking the law and could receive a fine. “It is well worth remembering this is totally dependent on the officer who catches the speeder, and it is up to that officer whether to fine the offender or not. “The best advice is to not speed full stop.” Here are some other common speed camera myths: No. There are no laws about visibility, so nothing is stopping an officer from operating in the dark. But they don't often choose to do this and maintain that being visible acts as a deterrent in its own right. Go Safe Casualty Reduction Officer, Gareth Thomas said: "Legally, we don't have to be visible. I could camouflage myself if I wanted to - but it's all about being fair, education and preventing an accident. Even if I parked my van and went for a walk somewhere, it would deter people from speeding right away." If drivers choose to flash to warn others about a speed van, they could be in breach of the law. Under section 89 of the Police Act 1997 it is an offence to "wilfully obstruct a constable in the execution of his/her duty". However, Gareth says while it is an offence, it is very difficult to prove. He said: "It doesn't bother me that people flash to warn them of the speed van - I just want to educate people and the van to act as a speed deterrent." It all comes down to the circumstances within which you were caught speeding, and how much you were more than the limit. The minimum penalty for being caught speeding on the UK's roads is a £100 fine. But Gareth explained in some circumstances, police can offer the option of attending a speed awareness course - an alternative to a fine and penalty points. Gareth, said: "An accredited course is far more likely to improve driver behaviour and consequently make our roads safer. "Courses are available to drivers who respond quickly to the 'notices' and who were driving at no more than 10 per cent, plus 9 mph above the posted speed limit." So for example, anyone travelling over 86mph on a motorway would not be offered the awareness course. Those who don't have a clean licence at the time of the office, or if you have been on the course in the last three years, it is unlikely you will be offered the awareness course as an option.

metadata.title: St Neots Dragon Boat Team wins three national podium places and men's league title
metadata.contentSnippet: St Neots Dragon Boat Team Triumph at National Finals with Three Podium Finishes and an Award

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots Dragon Boat Team wins three national podium places and men's league title
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: St Neots Dragon Boat Team competed at the British Dragon Boat Racing Association National Finals, held at the National Watersports Centre in Nottingham on Saturday September 19 and Sunday September 20, racing against crews from across the UK. The club enjoyed a highly successful weekend, taking home three trophies. The team was recognised for its achievements throughout the season (Image: Matthew Power and Alex Eeles) On Saturday, the crew claimed 1st place in the Men's Grand Final over 200m and 3rd place in the Open Grand Final. The Ladies crew narrowly missed out on third place by just 0.01 of a second, in a nail-bitingly close finish. Sunday brought further strong performances across a full day of 500m racing. The men's crew claimed 2nd place in the Men's 500m Grand Final, and the Seniors came within 0.14 of a second of a podium finish. The club's junior paddlers also competed, gaining valuable racing experience. In addition to their on-water results, St Neots Dragon Boat Team was awarded a trophy for National Men's League winners across the whole season - recognising the squad's consistent performance and standing throughout the year, not just at the Finals. The club secured multiple podium finishes at the championship event (Image: Matthew Power and Alex Eeles) Speaking after the weekend, Adele Gilpin, Captain of St Neots Dragon Boat Team, said: "It's been a highly successful season and I couldn't be prouder of everything we've achieved. "This is such an accessible sport - our men's and ladies crews were strong all year, and it was great to see our juniors and seniors represented on the national stage. Every single paddler put in the hours this season, and it really shows." St Neots Dragon Boat Team enjoyed success at the national finals (Image: Matthew Power and Alex Eeles) The club would like to thank STS for their support in transporting the boats to and from the event, without whom the weekend would not have been possible. The National Finals mark the end of the competitive season for St Neots Dragon Boat Team, who now move into pre-season training ahead of a landmark year as the club celebrates its 30th anniversary in 2027.

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire firefighting family responds together to major Holme Fen wildfire

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire firefighting family responds together to major Holme Fen wildfire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Firefighting runs in the family for a Cambridgeshire crew. Alex Gould recently became an on-call firefighter at Thorney Fire Station, where she works alongside her long-serving father, Phil. She said: "Responding alongside my dad at Thorney has been so much fun. "Growing up, Dad had always been in the fire service, so being able to experience my first shout alongside him was a unique experience. "I'm very lucky to be able to learn from him and the others at Thorney who have been incredibly welcoming. "My first working job was made even better by the fact that Emily was the one to mobilise us." Emily is Alex’s sister, but they are not the only Goulds serving the fire service. Phil’s brother, Anthony Gould, is chief fire officer at Peterborough Volunteer Fire Brigade, while Anthony’s son, Jacob, is a wholetime firefighter with the service. The family showed that dedication by helping tackle the Holme Fen wildfire, one of the county’s biggest incidents in years. Every Gould currently serving with the service helped respond to the major incident, either on the frontline or behind the scenes in control. The service hopes the Goulds’ story will inspire others to become firefighters. Inspired to become the first firefighter in your family—or join relatives already in the role? Visit our careers section to find out how you can help your community. The blaze, which broke out on August 8, was described as "unprecedented" by Cambridgeshire's chief fire officer, with the fire burning up to six metres below the surface in the peat.

metadata.title: Deaf rescue dog Eddie wins hearts as RSPCA seeks him a caring home
metadata.contentSnippet: A deaf rescue dog is capturing hearts at Block Fen Animal Centre in Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Deaf rescue dog Eddie wins hearts as RSPCA seeks him a caring home
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A deaf rescue dog is capturing hearts at Block Fen Animal Centre in Cambridgeshire. Six-year-old Eddie, a bull breed, was rescued by RSPCA officers and police from unsuitable living conditions having been left behind in a property, in County Durham, when his owners moved out. He was taken in by the RSPCA’s Block Fen Animal Centre earlier this summer, where staff soon discovered he was deaf. Tiffany Fowler, kennel supervisor at Block Fen, said: "We believe Eddie was born deaf and he copes very well without his hearing. "In fact, we often forget that he’s deaf. "We all chat away to him and if he’s looking at us he’ll wag his tail and get excited; it’s like he can lip-read and knows we’re speaking to him." Deaf dog Eddie (Image: RSPCA) Staff believe Eddie could learn sign language and respond well to visual commands. Despite his hearing loss, Eddie has settled comfortably into kennel life. Ms Fowler said: "When we arrive in the mornings and go to say ‘good morning’ to all of the dogs, who are all barking and wagging their tails at their doors, Eddie is usually fast asleep, snoring in his bed. "He doesn’t get stressed by the noise and the other dogs, and this can be tough for some dogs. "We go into his kennel and give him a gentle stroke to wake him up and let him know that we’re there, so we don’t startle him and make him jump." Eddie has been enjoying spending time with the reception team at the animal centre, welcoming visitors to Block Fen. Ms Fowler said: "Eddie is one of those dogs who has a gift for making people smile. "He is incredibly friendly, affectionate and adores being around people." The RSPCA hopes to find Eddie a patient and caring home with someone who can continue his training and help him adjust to a new life.

"Working alongside our partners is a vital part of the everyday work carried out by our neighbourhood teams in response to issues raised by the public." The operation is part of ongoing efforts across Cambridgeshire to tackle the sale and distribution of illegal tobacco and nicotine products. Residents are encouraged to report any information or suspicions about the sale of illicit products. metadata.title: Red Arrows and Cold War spy plane facility star at Alconbury Weald heritage day
metadata.contentSnippet: The Red Arrows and a glimpse of Cold War espionage took centre stage at Alconbury Weald’s Heritage Open Day.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Red Arrows and Cold War spy plane facility star at Alconbury Weald heritage day
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Red Arrows and a glimpse of Cold War espionage took centre stage at Alconbury Weald’s Heritage Open Day. The packed programme celebrated the site’s military history, from its role in the Second World War to the Cold War. Crowds watched the Red Arrows and a Battle of Britain Memorial Flight Hawker Hurricane fly over the United States Air Force Honour Guard. Families enjoyed a programme of heritage activities and entertainment (Image: TIM GEORGE) Visitors toured the Avionics Building, a rare Cold War facility once used to service the TR-1 Dragon Lady spy plane. A future Alconbury Weald resident said: "I think what makes this event so lovely is that it isn’t just about looking back at history. "It’s about celebrating the story of the airfield, the people connected to it and the community that has grown around it today." The event celebrated the area's military and aviation heritage (Image: TIM GEORGE) Airfield Research Group chair Jeff Hawley presented a recorded interview with USAF veterans Greg Spark and Bob Shaeffer, who served at Alconbury during the Cold War. The Royal British Legion’s Brampton & District branch shared stories about Alconbury’s squadrons and met local residents. The Alconbury Weald Community Association ran a family fun day alongside the heritage event, with food, entertainment and live music. Heritage Open Day attracted residents and visitors to Alconbury Weald (Image: TIM GEORGE) Natalie Leigh-Brown, community development lead for Alconbury Weald, said: "The Heritage Open Day is a highlight of the Alconbury Weald event calendar, and we’d like to thank everyone who came along to find out more about the former airfield’s fascinating past and how it is helping shape the future development. "Special thanks go to the Red Arrows and Battle of Britain Memorial Flight for this year’s fantastic flypasts, a real treat for all ages."

metadata.title: New crematorium evacuated after 'increased level of smoke' during testing
metadata.contentSnippet: Further details have emerged after a new crematorium in Cambridgeshire was evacuated just weeks after it first opened to the public.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New crematorium evacuated after 'increased level of smoke' during testing
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council has revealed why a crematorium in Cambridgeshire was evacuated just weeks after it first opened to the public. Firefighters from Ely and March were called to Lake View Bereavement Centre on Chatteris Road, in Mepal, at 9.52am on Friday (September 25). Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service confirmed crews arrived "to find smoke issuing from a building". "They cleared the smoke using a positive pressure ventilation fan and left the building with the site management team," a spokesperson said. East Cambridgeshire District Council has since confirmed the electric cremator is undergoing a "period of testing during the commissioning process". The spokesperson added: "On Friday morning, one of these tests caused an increased level of smoke to be emitted," the local authority said in a statement. "Two fire crews attended as a precaution. "There was no fire or any damage caused, and the matter was resolved within an hour with no further actions to be taken." They added: "We would like to assure residents that no public services were impacted during this testing process, and other services will continue as normal." The county's newest crematorium opened its doors with a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by nearly 200 guests on September 10. The £13million facility stands on the former Mepal Outdoor Centre, which lay derelict for years. The project was funded by developer contributions, including Community Infrastructure Levy, rather than taxpayers. Have you got a story you want to share?
