metadata.title: Fast food chain given permission to extend opening hours
metadata.contentSnippet: KFC in St Neots has been given permission to extend its opening hours despite fears it may increase littering.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fast food chain given permission to extend opening hours
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A popular fast food chain has been given permission to extend its opening hours despite fears it may increase littering. KFC in St Neots applied to increase its closing time from 2am until 5am and to open an hour earlier from 9am instead of 10am. A resident objected to the longer opening hours for the chicken shop on Great North Road as they were “fearful that this may lead to a rise in anti-social behaviour”. They also raised concerns about littering which they said was “often quite evident” along the road heading into Eaton Socon. They said customers “may not bother taking their rubbish home with them and either dump it on the path, or, worse, simply dispose of it into people’s properties”. KFC had agreed to pick up litter within a 100m radius of the fast food shop but the objector said this “may not be enough” and asked for it to be extended further up the road. Huntingdonshire District Council’s licensing officer said that KFC didn’t consider this to be “reasonable or proportionate” and could lead to safety risks. They said patrols during the late evening and early morning “would require staff to leave the immediate vicinity” of the store and raise “welfare and safety considerations”. The officer added that there “is a limit to the level of control that any business can reasonably exercise over customers once they have left the premises”. The council’s licensing sub-committee granted KFC the extended licence with conditions to prevent noise and disturbance to neighbours. Customers won’t be allowed to use the outside seating areas after 11pm and four bins will be provided in the car park and regularly emptied.

metadata.title: Lorry driver killed 'loving family man' in horror motorway crash
metadata.contentSnippet: A lorry driver who killed a "loving family man" after ploughing into the back of his van on the M11 near Duxford, Cambridgeshire, has been jailed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Lorry driver killed 'loving family man' in horror motorway crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A lorry driver who killed a "loving family man" after ploughing into the back of his van on a busy Cambridgeshire motorway has been jailed. Misroslaw Muszynski, 69, failed to notice Gary Porritt, 43, had slowed for traffic in his Ford Transit Van. The horror crash occurred on the southbound carriageway of the M11, near junction 10 for Duxford, at about 12.15pm on June 12. Muszynski's HGV pushed the van into the back of another HGV, causing fatal injuries to Mr Porritt. Mr Porritt, of Exchange Square, Stockton-On-Tees, Teesside, who had been driving to a fishing trip with friends, was pronounced dead at the scene. Muszynski remained at the scene and passed breath, drugs, field impairment, and eyesight tests before being arrested. On Tuesday (September 22), at Huntingdon Law Courts, Muszynski, of Priory Road, Dartford, Kent, was jailed for three years and four months. He pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving. He was also banned from driving for six years and eight months. In a tribute, Gary's family described him as a "loving family man" (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) DC Kevin Drury said: "Gary Porritt should have been enjoying a fishing trip, but Musyznski's driving meant his life was tragically cut short. "The sentence reflects the seriousness of the offence and the devastating impact it has had on those who knew and loved Gary. "No prison sentence can undo the harm that has been caused, but we hope the outcome of these proceedings provides some measure of closure for his family. "We would urge all drivers, particularly those operating large vehicles, to recognise the immense responsibility they bear every time they get behind the wheel. "Preventable collisions continue to cost lives and cause lasting heartbreak." In a tribute, Mr Porritt’s family said: "Gary was a loving family man, a devoted partner to Claire and a great friend to many. "He was always willing to help others, loved fishing, and will be remembered for his kindness, generosity and love. "He has left a void in our family that will never be filled." metadata.title: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue wins national Menopause Friendly Employer award
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service won the Menopause Friendly Employer of the Year Award (Public Sector) at the Menopause and Menstruation Friendly Employer Awards.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue wins national Menopause Friendly Employer award
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service has won a national award for supporting staff wellbeing. Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service won the Menopause Friendly Employer of the Year Award (Public Sector) at the Menopause and Menstruation Friendly Employer Awards on September 16. The award recognises public sector organisations that build menopause awareness, education and support into workplace culture. Hayley Douglas, assistant director of communication and engagement at Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service and its menopause champion, said: "We were filled with pride just to be listed as a finalist in this category so to hear us announced as the winners of this award was an incredible moment! Feedback we receive from across the Service evidences the impact our work to ensure we are a menopause friendly employer is having. "Knowing that colleagues have all received awareness training about menopause, symptoms and their impact in the workplace - and at home – means that colleagues feel more comfortable having open conversations about what they are going through, knowing they will be supported. "To have our work recognised at a national level and to win Accredited Employer of the Year from all the organisations doing fantastic work to improve menopause support in the workplace was quite a feeling!" Now in their fifth year, the awards celebrate organisations across the UK improving workplace culture around menopause and menstruation. An independent panel of industry experts chose this year’s winners from a record number of entries. Deborah Garlick, CEO and founder of Henpicked: Menopause in the Workplace, said: "Together, the impact of their menopause and menstruation friendly work is shifting workplace culture, bringing meaningful and measurable change and creating environments where people feel understood, supported and able to thrive." The service has introduced mandatory menopause awareness training, updated guidance, workplace-adjustment risk assessments and improved toilet and welfare provisions for firefighters at incidents.

metadata.title: New dig to start at Cambridgeshire Bronze Age site with £700,000 of funding
metadata.contentSnippet: Archaeologists will begin a new dig at one of Britain’s most important Bronze Age sites next year, Flag Fen near Peterborough.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New dig to start at Cambridgeshire Bronze Age site with £700,000 of funding
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Archaeologists will begin a new dig at one of Britain’s most important Bronze Age sites in Cambridgeshire next year. The dig, at Flag Fen near Peterborough, must begin before information preserved in peat is lost as the ground dries out amid climate change. The timber causeway at the site was 1.1 km long, about 20 metres wide, and had about 22,000 posts, Mark Knight of Cambridge Archaeological Unit said. It was thought to have played a role in communication and trade, connecting two pieces of dry land over an area that got wet around 3,300 years ago, he said. Mr Knight, who will be excavation director on the new dig, said information was preserved in wet peat without oxygen for thousands of years but the hotter climate is drying the peat out. He said that a section of the causeway that was “a bit closer to the surface” is “drying out a little bit quicker”. “If we don’t excavate it in the next couple of years it will be gone forever so we will lose all of that information,” he said. Jacqui Mooney, general manager at Flag Fen Archaeology Park, said she was also concerned by a peatland fire that broke out at Holme Fen, around 11 miles from Flag Fen, during drought conditions last month. A blaze broke out at Holme Fen this summer (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue) “We’re on the peat, peat will burn and it will take a lot to put the peat out,” she said. “We absolutely don’t want that to happen here on such a significant landscape.” The area of destruction at Holme Fen covered 60 football pitches in total (Image: Emily Stevens) The six-month dig at Flag Fen, to begin next year, has received £700,000 in grant funding through the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service, Defra’s partnership with Historic England. Mr Knight said the excavation would be the “biggest area that’s ever been opened over the monument”. “We’re doing that because we want to gain pattern, we want to see it for what it is,” he said. “There’s been 40 years of investigation on this site but it tends to be keyhole, it tends to be small holes looking at small parts. “We think the way to really understand it is to see it on a scale that’s commensurate with the feature itself.” He said past interpretations of the causeway included that it was a “ritual monument, a place where you go and deposit metalwork or the dead”. “It’s also about communication, about trade, movement of people and animals, and it’s about a route that was once there back in the day before water levels rose and now, with water levels rising, they’ve been cut off so it’s about re-establishing that,” he said. “What’s really impressive is that our monument has at least 400 years of different iterations or different repairs and builds. “It’s got duration and longevity.” Flag Fen has been on Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register since 2012. Few Bronze Age platform structures survive anywhere in the world, and Flag Fen’s scale, complexity and completeness make it nationally significant. Farming Minister Stephen Morgan said: “Flag Fen has survived for thousands of years and it really demonstrates an extraordinary window into Bronze Age Britain. “We’re so pleased to be investing in this important community project.” The excavation project will offer volunteering opportunities, with volunteers being given training to become supervisors and tour leaders.

World of Sweets is recalling Dubai Style Crunchy Knafeh and Pistachio Milk Chocolate and Alyan Dubai Style Chocolate Truffles because Salmonella has been found in the products. A spokesman for the Food Standards Agency warned: “The presence of salmonella in the products listed above. “Symptoms caused by salmonella usually include fever, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps. Thursday 24 September. World of Sweets recalls Alyan Dubai Style Crunchy Knafeh and Alyan Dubai Style Chocolate Truffles due to Salmonella #FoodAlert https://t.co/33mYrJ39WO pic.twitter.com/tMepY2BHD5 — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) September 24, 2026 “If you are experiencing these symptoms, you should stay away from work, school or nursery until you have stopped having symptoms for at least 48 hours to avoid passing it on to others. “World of Sweets is recalling the above products. The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. metadata.title: Cambridgeshire fire service warns damaged or propped-open doors put lives at risk
metadata.contentSnippet: Damaged or propped-open fire doors could put lives at risk, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service has warned.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire fire service warns damaged or propped-open doors put lives at risk
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Damaged or propped-open fire doors could put lives at risk, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service has warned. The service is urging businesses and building managers across Cambridgeshire to check their fire doors during Fire Door Safety Week and ensure they are correctly installed, maintained and used. Station Commander Vinnie Crook, one of the service’s fire protection managers, said: "Having effective fire doors and checking them regularly are vital for business premises. "The difference it can make in an emergency cannot be underestimated. "Yet we often find that they are neglected and not maintained properly, putting premises and staff at risk." Fire door breaches remain one of the most common reasons for fines under the Fire Safety Order, with problems including wedged-open, missing or damaged doors and non-fire doors installed in their place. The fire service has launched an animated video showing building users what to check and how to record it. Mr Crook said: "Our new animation gives business owners a short guide to what to check and how to record it, as these records will be requested during a fire safety audit." He stressed that fire doors compartmentalise buildings and slow the spread of fire and smoke, giving people more time to escape and firefighters more time to act. The service recommends checking for certification labels, gaps of less than 4mm, damaged seals or hinges, and a door that closes properly onto the latch. Anyone who notices a damaged fire door, or a flat entrance door that hasn’t been checked for fire performance, is advised to report it to the building manager or landlord immediately. More guidance and resources are available from Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service.

metadata.title: New St Neots feature uses stone believed to be from original Priory Abbey
metadata.contentSnippet: The Saint Anselm feature has been installed in St Neots.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New St Neots feature uses stone believed to be from original Priory Abbey
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Saint Anselm feature has been installed in St Neots. Designed to resemble a well, it recalls a miracle attributed to Saint Neot involving fish and a well. The capstone bears an image of Saint Anselm, the former Archbishop of Canterbury who was born in Aosta, Italy. The saint is shown with enlarged hands, a Greek tradition intended to convey symbolic meaning when few people could read. His right hand represents benediction, while the book in his left signifies scholasticism and piety. The capstone is made from Welsh granite, similar to stone used in early medieval churches in the Fawton area of Cornwall and at Glastonbury Abbey, where Neot served as sacristan. The artwork is located where there was once a river inlet to the Priory of Saint Neot (Image: Priory of Saint Neot) The circular well is clad in Barnack Ragstone, quarried near Peterborough. The ragstone cladding, believed to have been part of the original Priory Abbey of Saint Neot, was retrieved from an archaeological dig in St Neots. The feature stands on a green where a river inlet and boathouse may once have stood in the Priory grounds. Saint Anselm’s endorsement helped establish St Neots as a major centre of pilgrimage and royal patronage for the next 500 years. An archaeological evaluation beneath the Priory Centre found medieval pottery and charcoal suggesting the site may have been an open ditch or watercourse, alongside evidence of human activity possibly associated with the priory.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Huntingdon Boat Club secured seven wins at Milton Keynes Regatta to end its regatta season. Huntingdon Boat Club recorded seven wins at Milton Keynes Regatta (Image: Huntingdon Boat Club) Mark Smith and Alice Ray each won twice. Ray then won the Women's Open sculls, beating fellow Huntingdon rower Isabella Dovey in the semi-final before defeating Milton Keynes in the final. Mark later joined Edward Adams, Daniel Grant and Tom Starling in the Open coxless four. Huntingdon made a quick start and held its lead to the finish, securing another win over Milton Keynes. They beat Warwick in the quarter-final and Milton Keynes in the semi-final. Huntingdon then faced Peterborough in the final and won. James Johnston-Keay won both his events. He beat Bedford Star in the Junior16 single sculls semi-final before beating Northampton in the final. He then partnered Seth Dovey in the Junior16 double sculls, beating West Norfolk in the final. Beau Jeffery and James Wilkin also raced in the Junior16 doubles. Racing together for only the second time, they performed well against West Norfolk but missed the final. Huntingdon finished the regatta season with a strong performance (Image: Huntingdon Boat Club) Hetty Weston-Leach and Jasmine Yallop also competed in the Women's Junior16 single sculls. Oli Burgess stepped up a year for the Junior18 double sculls with Nathan Duncanson-Hunter, who moved up two years. The pair narrowly missed victory against Warwick. The result gave Huntingdon seven wins at the final regatta, despite testing conditions across the lake and conditions at season's end.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new leisure venue is set to open as part of a major investment in a Cambridgeshire city centre. metadata.contentSnippet: Care Network Cambridgeshire is marking 40 years of helping people across the county.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Care Network Cambridgeshire is marking 40 years of helping people across the county. The charity helps people rebuild confidence and independence while staying connected to their communities. Lynda Phillips, chief executive of Care Network Cambridgeshire, said: "As we celebrate 40 years, we are incredibly proud of the difference our staff, volunteers and partners make every day. "This anniversary celebration is an opportunity to recognise everyone who has been part of our journey, while looking ahead to the future and the growing need for community support across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough." The charity supports people through three services: Help at Home, RISE (Resilience, Intervention, Support and Empowerment) and Community Support. Its work tackles social isolation, builds confidence and connects people to services and transport. Care Network supported 2,479 people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough in 2025, many facing loneliness, poor mental health or other challenges. One client said: "This phone call has been the most I have smiled and laughed in around three years." Another said: "You have made my day. "You are the first person who has called me to ask if I am OK… I live alone." The charity’s results show its impact: 90 per cent of clients reported greater independence and 94 per cent felt less isolated. A further 89 per cent said they felt less lonely, while up to 62 per cent said the support helped them avoid NHS services. Referrals to the RISE wellbeing service rose 21 per cent in 2025. The charity’s 40th-anniversary event will take place on Tuesday, October 6, from 1.30pm to 3.30pm at the William Collyn Community Centre in Girton. To attend, email admin@care-network.org.uk or call 01954 211919.

metadata.title: 28 per cent of Year 6 children in Cambridgeshire's poorest areas have obesity
metadata.contentSnippet: Obesity rates remain a major health challenge despite ongoing efforts to improve public health across Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 28 per cent of Year 6 children in Cambridgeshire's poorest areas have obesity
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Obesity rates remain a major health challenge despite ongoing efforts to improve public health across Cambridgeshire. Members of the Adults and Health Committee at Cambridgeshire County Council met on Thursday, September 17, to review progress on reducing obesity and creating healthier environments for residents. Councillor Luis Navarro, vice chair of the committee, said: "Obesity remains one of the most significant public health challenges facing our communities, affecting people's health, wellbeing and quality of life. "While progress is being made, there is still much more to do, particularly to address the inequalities that mean some communities experience poorer health outcomes than others. "By working together through the Strategic Obesity Framework and Obesity Charter, we can help more people eat well, stay active and live independently, supporting our ambition to enable full, healthy lives for all in Cambridgeshire." The committee heard that childhood obesity rates, which rose during the pandemic, have now returned to pre-pandemic levels but remain high and have since stagnated. Data from the 2024/25 National Child Measurement Programme shows that 7.7 per cent of children in Reception and 17.2 per cent of children in Year 6 in Cambridgeshire are living with obesity. Rates are higher in areas of deprivation, with 28 per cent of Year 6 children in the most deprived areas affected compared to just 13.2 per cent in the least deprived. Obesity rates also remain above average in Fenland. The council is delivering its Strategic Obesity Framework in partnership with NHS organisations, schools, district councils and community groups. Efforts focus on improving access to healthy food, increasing physical activity, and addressing broader social and economic factors that contribute to obesity. The Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Obesity Charter brings organisations together with a shared goal of making healthy weight the norm across the region.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A £1.75 million funding boost will tackle rough sleeping across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. Approved by Mayor Paul Bristow, the funding will support emergency help, prevention work and long-term accommodation, aiming to get people off the streets by Christmas. The funding is part of the Government’s Rough Sleeping Programme, announced in August, which will give the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority more than £7.3 million by 2029. Paul Bristow, mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, said: "This funding will not only help change the lives of those being given somewhere to sleep but will also address key regional issues that lead to someone ending up in this position. "As Mayor, I will be making sure we use this money where it will have the greatest impact across our region. "The Government is right to back Mayors, councils and voluntary organisations to do this place-by-place, and I look forward to working with local leaders to shape and support schemes that focus on the people and communities that need it most." Funding allocations are based on rough-sleeping data from key areas across the region. Previous local work has included an outreach service run with South and East Cambridgeshire councils and P3, alongside early-warning systems designed to prevent homelessness.

metadata.title: Cambs Chamber of Commerce urges Chancellor to tackle barriers to business growth
metadata.contentSnippet: The Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce has urged the Chancellor to act ahead of the Autumn Budget.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs Chamber of Commerce urges Chancellor to tackle barriers to business growth
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Connor Butler, engagement manager for the Cambridgeshire Chamber of Commerce, writes his first column Across the region, businesses are not short of ambition. They want to recruit, invest, innovate, expand and trade. But too often, that ambition is being held back by things outside their control: infrastructure constraints, skills shortages, rising employment costs and an increasingly difficult investment environment. That is the message we have taken to the Chancellor ahead of the Autumn Budget. Our region has an extraordinary economic opportunity. We sit between the science and innovation strengths of the Oxford-Cambridge corridor and the manufacturing, energy, agri-food, logistics and international trade strengths of the wider East of England. But potential alone does not deliver growth. We need action. That means progressing Ely-Haughley and the transport links that connect businesses to people and markets. It means ensuring skills funding responds to what employers actually need. It means securing the water, power and wider infrastructure required for businesses to invest and expand. And it means recognising that higher National Insurance, energy bills and business rates all influence decisions about recruitment and investment. We also need to make Britain a place where entrepreneurs want to start, scale and keep their businesses, and where more SMEs have the confidence and support to trade internationally. This is not about asking Government to create growth itself. It is about making targeted decisions that unlock far greater private investment. The question I hope the Chancellor asks of every Budget measure is simple: will this make it easier for businesses to employ, invest, scale and trade?

metadata.contentSnippet: A solar farm has been approved for land off Vicarage Lane in Diddington, Huntingdonshire, near the A1.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Solar farm approved next to small Hunts village
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A solar farm has been approved on farmland next to a small village. Huntingdonshire District Council’s development management committee met to decide on the application for land off Vicarage Lane in Diddington, just west of the A1. Buckden Parish Council and Southoe and Midloe Parish Council had objected to the plans as they said “there should be no more solar farms on greenfield sites until all residential and commercial roof spaces and brownfield sites have been fully utilised”. Edmund Thornhill spoke in favour of the application and said the solar panels, expected to generate 35MW of electricity, are proposed on the “poorest performing” fields. He said: “There needs to be careful consideration around best use of land even if that use is for a finite period – the farm already provides food, housing and space for nature. “We want to support energy production as well over the poorest land. “This scheme would provide diversified income to help fund moving to more regenerative agriculture on the rest of the farm.” Around 45 hectares of land will be covered and the solar farm is expected to operate for 45 years, which Mr Thornhill said would allow the soil fertility to improve. The company behind the plans, Cell Energy Limited, said it has an agreement with Anglian Water to provide the company with energy. An underground cable will be built to their facility at Grafham Water which the planning application said was a “very significant energy user”. Cllr Jon Neish, of Holywell-cum-Needingworth, said he couldn’t see a reason to object to the plans aside from the parish council’s objection. The Conservative councillor said: “Unfortunately they haven’t come to explain a bit more in detail their views so at the moment I would struggle anywhere to say why we shouldn’t agree with it.” Cllr Lara Davenport-Ray, of St Neots East, said renewable energy projects are “really important” as natural gas is still used to generate much of the electricity in the area. The Green councillor said: “If we don’t stop creating carbon emissions then our planet will continue to warm and it will make the growing of any crops impossible. “I am disappointed to see no battery storage included but because of the overall direction that we need to go in I will suggest that we approve this application.” The plans were approved with 12 voting in favour and one against.

metadata.title: 7O homes approved despite fears it will overwhelm ‘very poor’ sewage network
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdonshire District Council has approved plans for up to 70 homes on land south of Blenheim Grove in Offord D’Arcy despite fears from residents of increased sewage spills.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 7O homes approved despite fears it will overwhelm ‘very poor’ sewage network
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A council has approved plans for new homes despite fears from residents of increased sewage spills in a village already suffering from the worst spills in the area. Huntingdonshire District Council’s development management committee met to decide an outline plan for up to 70 homes on land south of Blenheim Grove in Offord D’Arcy. Offord Cluny and Offord Darcy Parish Council had objected to the plans as they said wastewater treatment plants were already suffering from “capacity problems”. Simon Young, a parish councillor, said figures from the Environment Agency show that Buckden has an average of 116 raw sewage discharges per year. He said this is 66 per cent higher than the second on the list – Kimbolton at 70 – and four times higher than the average across Huntingdonshire. He said the villages have “long-been a supporter” of “appropriate developments” but that Anglian Water’s infrastructure is “not fit for purpose”. Anglian Water originally objected to the application in 2025, but this was because the applicant had not identified a suitable connection point to their network. After two connection points were suggested, they removed their objection. They had always said there was “sufficient capacity” at the nearby Buckden Water Recycling Centre to accommodate the new homes after assessing dry weather flow. Cllr Young said: “The Buckden Works was discharging raw sewage on August 13, when we all know there’d been no rain for weeks. And the ten hours of discharges in June came after recent light rain – or almost no rain for days. As far as I’m aware, Buckden and the Offords do not have their own microclimate such that it rains more here.” Cllr Julie Kerr, of St Ives West, said she was “very concerned” by the “high numbers of spillages”. The independent councillor said: “There really shouldn’t have been any and you have a very poor network by the sounds of it in a village that’s already struggling.” Council officers advised that it would be “very difficult” to go against the advice of Anglian Water as they do not have the “technical expertise” to be able to defend their decision on appeal. Cllr Tom Sanderson, of The Stukeleys, said they would not be able to use their decision to “deal with an existing issue”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “Particularly as Anglian Water haven’t raised an objection now, they withdrew the objection they did have, I think it would be very difficult for us to object on that basis.” Cllr Lara Davenport-Ray said she felt the benefits of the scheme did not outweigh the harms. The Green councillor said: “If Anglian Water is saying that they have capacity and that there is no problem, then there is no condition that we can word to mitigate a problem that on paper doesn’t exist. Our officers cannot identify harm because they haven’t been shown that there is any harm that’s been created because their experts have failed to do so, but we can.” The committee first reached an impasse with five votes for and against the application and three abstentions – but it was approved on the second attempt with six for, four against and three abstentions.

metadata.title: Huntingdonshire Council approves plans for six homes on village bungalow site
metadata.contentSnippet: The plans by Meadowbarn Developments Ltd will demolish the bungalow and outbuildings at Kia Ora, Somersham Road, Colne, and build six detached homes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdonshire Council approves plans for six homes on village bungalow site
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Huntingdonshire District Council has approved plans for six new homes on the edge of a village. The plans by Meadowbarn Developments Ltd will demolish the bungalow and outbuildings at Kia Ora, Somersham Road, Colne, and build six detached homes. Permission was formally granted on September 15 for the development, which will provide five three-bedroom homes and one four-bedroom home on the 0.4-hectare site. The application originally sought permission for seven dwellings, but the scheme was amended during the planning process and reduced to six homes following discussions with council officers. The site on the village’s western edge contains a bungalow, an access track and outbuildings in varying states of repair. Officers said the homes would boost supply while the council lacks a five-year supply of deliverable sites. Although the site is in the countryside outside Colne’s built-up area, officers said national planning policy allowed the scheme because it was close to the village and would help meet housing needs. The report stated: "The proposal would deliver six additional dwellings and contribute towards the council's housing supply at a time when a five-year housing land supply cannot be demonstrated." Planning officers also concluded that the development would not cause significant harm to the character of the area, highway safety, biodiversity, neighbouring properties or flood risk, subject to conditions. The scheme will include six 1.5-storey chalet-style bungalows. Two will face Somersham Road and four will be reached by a private road into the site. Colne Parish Council backed the plans but raised concerns about surface-water drainage. Councillors said larger drainage pipes may be required and highlighted previous flooding issues in the area, as well as wider concerns about pressure on local infrastructure. Cambridgeshire County Council highways officers raised no objections, saying the access and visibility splays were acceptable. More than 20 conditions include detailed drainage plans, landscaping, biodiversity improvements, contamination checks, tree protection and at least a 10 per cent biodiversity net gain. In recommending approval, officers concluded that any limited policy conflicts were outweighed by the benefits of providing new housing and the associated economic benefits generated by the development.

news.title: Ramsey Builder Praised for Helping at Crash Scene Near Chatteris
news.summary: Matt from Ramsey-based All Day Building has been praised by police for his exceptional help at a two-vehicle crash scene near Chatteris, where he assisted with traffic, lent his jacket, and helped clear the road after an iPhone alert detected the collision.
news.content: Huntingdonshire builder praised after iPhone alert detects crash near Chatteris A builder has been praised for his help at the scene of a crash after an iPhone alert notified police of the incident. The crash happened on Friday evening at the junction of Forty Foot Bank and Doddington Road near Chatteris. Two vehicles were involved and one overturned. Police said nobody was injured, although two people went to hospital as a precaution. An iPhone automatic crash alert detected the collision and gave emergency services its location. Officers gave special thanks to Matt from Ramsey-based All Day Building. Not only did he help officers with the traffic and lend his jacket to one of those involved, but he also went the extra mile by helping to put the car back upright and move both vehicles to a safe location so the road was clear. The police spokesperson said: "All of your help is very much appreciated."

metadata.title: REVEALED: Number of Cambs students suspended for physical assault in last five years
metadata.contentSnippet: Nearly 3,000 students were suspended from schools in Cambridgeshire for physically assaulting teachers and other pupils over the last five years, data has revealed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: REVEALED: Number of Cambs students suspended for physical assault in last five years
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Nearly 3000 students were suspended from schools in Cambridgeshire for physically assaulting teachers and other pupils over the last five years, data has revealed. A total of 2,990 pupils faced suspensions or exclusions from state-maintained schools in the county, according to a Freedom of Information Act request. In the 2025/26 academic year there were 635 students suspended or excluded for physical assault against other students or teachers. The majority of these were primary school students at 510, with 118 incidents in secondary schools and six in special educational needs, or SEND, schools. Cambridgeshire County Council said they do not hold data on whether these were cases of physical assault towards other students or towards teachers. They also said they don’t record how many of these incidents were referred to the police or reported severe injuries needing medical attention. The number of suspensions or exclusions peaked at 797 during the 2024/25 academic year including 635 at primary schools, 152 at secondary schools and 11 at SEND schools. It had been steadily increasing from 2021/22 when there were 291 suspensions and exclusions – 223 in primary schools, 68 at secondary schools and none in SEND schools. Physical assault incidents – exclusions: Year Primary Secondary Special 2021/22 223 68 0 2022/23 436 103 4 2023/24 590 134 0 2024/25 635 152 11 2025/26 510 118 6 The council added the data is only what has been reported by the schools themselves and only as accurate as what they have reported to the council. They said that moving forward all schools have agreed that the council’s early years and education system (EYES) will capture this data straight from the school. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: “Our teams work closely with school staff and families to keep pupils in school. “It is always disappointing when pupils are excluded and it is always a last resort. “Schools have to follow statutory guidelines and will always look at potential suspensions and exclusions on a case by case basis. “We work closely with teaching staff and families to help manage challenging and difficult behaviour and keep pupils in school.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdon parent has launched a petition calling for action to improve road safety around schools in Ambury Road. Resident and parent Andrada Ioana Grab says she and her neighbours are increasingly worried about traffic, parking and safety around the schools. She says the area is regularly gridlocked during morning drop-off and afternoon pick-up. The petition highlights limited parking, vehicles stopping on double yellow lines and difficulty for buses and other road users to pass. A petition has been launched calling on Cambridgeshire County Council to take action to tackle congestion and improve road safety in Ambury Road Huntingdon during school drop-off and pick-up times. (Image: Andrada Ionana Grab) It says parents have few safe, practical places to stop when dropping off or collecting their children. The petition asks Cambridgeshire County Council to review parking, drop-offs, traffic and road safety around the schools. It calls on the authority to improve safety, cut congestion and protect children, parents, pedestrians, bus users and other road users at school times. Suggestions include extra parking, a redesigned layout, angled bays where feasible and other traffic-management measures. A petition has been launched calling on Cambridgeshire County Council to take action to tackle congestion and improve road safety in Ambury Road Huntingdon during school drop-off and pick-up times. (Image: Andrada Ionana Grab) Andrada says the issue is not just convenience but congestion, road safety and access for everyone using Ambury Road. The concerns affect parents, residents, school staff, pedestrians and everyone using the road each day. Parents, residents and regular Ambury Road users can sign the petition if they are concerned about the situation. It will be open for signatures until November 16. Cars regularly park on double yellow lines causing problems for residents and other road users. (Image: Andrada Ionana Grab) The campaign says every signature will show the issue affects the wider school community. The proposed review would cover parking, drop-offs, traffic and road safety around the schools on Ambury Road. It would identify practical changes for school arrival and departure times while considering people travelling by bus, on foot or by car. The petition says congestion is worst during morning drop-off and afternoon pick-up. A petition has been launched calling on Cambridgeshire County Council to take action to tackle congestion and improve road safety in Ambury Road Huntingdon during school drop-off and pick-up times. (Image: Andrada Ionana Grab) It says vehicles stop on double yellow lines, making it difficult for buses and other road users to pass. The request also stresses that Ambury Road is used by more than school families. School staff, residents, pedestrians, bus passengers, drivers and other road users may all be affected at the start and end of the school day. A petition has been launched calling on Cambridgeshire County Council to take action to tackle congestion and improve road safety in Ambury Road Huntingdon during school drop-off and pick-up times. (Image: Andrada Ionana Grab) Huntingdon Nursery School is one of the schools on Ambury Road and caters for up to 135 pupils.

metadata.title: Awards will celebrate the sustainability leaders of today and tomorrow
metadata.contentSnippet: Find out what the Net Zero Award and One to Watch Award judges will be looking for at the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Awards will celebrate the sustainability leaders of today and tomorrow
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027 will celebrate the organisations and individuals helping to create a more sustainable future across the region. This week, we spotlight the Net Zero Award and One to Watch Award. The judges for these two categories explain why they are important and the opportunities they provide to recognise success, innovation and environmental progress. Sophie Lewis, commercial director, Hornsea 3 at Ørsted, which sponsors the Net Zero Award (Image: Ørsted) Sponsored by Ørsted Sponsor judge: Sophie Lewis, commercial director, Hornsea 3, Ørsted Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? I have worked in offshore wind for 13 years, eight with Ørsted, having started my career in the industry as a business analyst for Norfolk-based Seajacks. I then continued within the financial and commercial areas of the sector at the UK Green Investment Bank, before moving to Ørsted. Why were you keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards? I spent the first 20 years of my life in Great Yarmouth, and nearly all my family and many of my close friends in the area are now involved in the renewable industry. I’ve witnessed the region transition from oil and gas to becoming a leader in renewables, and I am passionate about championing this continued path. What do you bring to the judging process? Passion for positive change, both for a cleaner environment and stronger local communities, is something I bring to every judging process. Alongside an open-minded and balanced approach, I’ll be looking at how projects deliver environmental outcomes while contributing to long-term community wellbeing, collaboration and inspiration for others. Have you ever been judged for an award yourself? Yes, I have been judged for awards in the past. Having been on the other side, I understand how much effort, pride and sometimes vulnerability goes into an application. I’ll use that experience to approach judging with empathy, fairness and respect. What will you be looking for in the winner? Ideally the winner would deliver a mix of tangible short-term outcomes with measurable results, but at the same time it’s important to see evidence of sustained and scalable improvements. The strongest entries will be those that break new ground, inspire others and bring people together through collaboration, while demonstrating a clear commitment to positive change. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? Don’t just focus on the numbers – also share your passion and purpose behind your drive towards net zero. This is your moment to shine! Why is ‘scalability’ an important consideration for the Net Zero Award? Cutting emissions at the scale needed to meet national or global net zero targets can’t be achieved by isolated organisations or one-off projects. Solutions must be able to spread across industries, regions and communities. Amy Bendall, managing director of Pier, which sponsors the One To Watch Award (Image: Pier Marketing Limited) Sponsored by Pier Sponsor judge: Amy Bendall, managing director, Pier Can you tell us a bit about your career to date? I’ve worked in PR and communications my whole career, across various industries. The golden thread running through everything has been a motivation to do good. At Pier we specialise in renewables and sustainability for exactly that reason – and that’s why Pier has been my home for almost half my career. What do you bring to the judging process? I’ve judged awards before, so this isn’t my first rodeo. The diversity of my 20-year career helps, including delivering campaigns at the fantastic environment charity, Friends of the Earth. I’d like to think I know what good looks like – and I won’t be sucked in by greenwashing. Have you ever been judged for an award yourself? Many times! Pier has been lucky enough to scoop several accolades over the years, including the prestigious PR Consultancy of the Year. We also draft award entries for our clients, so it’s a well-honed skill. How will you use that experience when judging this award? While a well-written entry certainly makes judging easier, ultimately what matters are the hard facts and the drive to do the right thing. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? Just go for it! The Clean & Green Awards are genuinely meaningful – not all awards give such due diligence to judging the entries. It means that even making the final is a well-deserved achievement that can and should be celebrated. What will you be looking for in the winner? I’d love to see passion and long-term thinking for a clean and green future. Why is ‘innovation’ an important judging consideration for this award? Innovation is essential to ensure we remain progressive – but I don’t think entrants should feel constrained by the size of their innovation. The small wins matter just as much as the big ones. The deadline for entries to the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards is Sunday, November 8 at midnight. For more information or to enter, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk

metadata.title: ‘Popular pub’ to be turned into shop after appeal granted
metadata.contentSnippet: Plans to turn The Bulls Head pub in St Neots into a corner shop have been approved on appeal after an inspector found its loss was “sufficiently justified”.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: ‘Popular pub’ to be turned into shop after appeal granted
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans to turn a pub into a corner shop have been approved on appeal after an inspector found its loss was “sufficiently justified”. The Bulls Head in St Neots shut in August 2023 before being put on market by brewery Greene King as they failed to find a new landlord. Huntingdonshire District Council refused plans from Noble Trading (UK) Ltd to re-open the Cambridge Street building as a “modern convenience store”. The Campaign for Pubs organisation objected as they said it had been a “popular pub which was well supported until its closure”. A licence application for the proposed shop was granted to allow them to sell alcohol, but planning permission was needed for the conversion to go ahead. The council rejected this as it would result in the loss of a pub and community space and they said there wasn’t enough evidence it had been marketed for continued use as a pub. Inspector David Reed of the Planning Inspectorate said the property was marketed over 15 months with a total of 38 enquiries, 16 viewings and one offer “which was withdrawn after a serious water damage incident occurred”. He said that feedback from the viewings “was poor” with potential buyers saying the kitchen was too small, there was no parking and the building was in “poor condition” with “too much work needed”. After the price was reduced it was bought by the current applicant, Mr Jeyaseelan Thambirajah. Mr Reed said that although there are no other pubs in the surrounding area, there are nine within one kilometre. He said: “These include Ye Old Sun, the Ale Taster, The Hyde Park and The Coach House. “This competition was also a likely contributing factor to the lack of interest in a public house use.” The council had said there was no proof certain websites listed in the marketing report were actually used but the inspector said this was “an unwarranted allegation”. They also said the premises were only actively marketed for eleven months and that “the asking price was unrealistic”. Mr Reed said that a gap while an offer proceeds “is standard practice” and the price was within the range of other “local comparable public houses”. He said: “It can be concluded that reasonable steps were taken to market the public house without success”. Permission was granted for the shop to open between 6.30am and 11pm from Monday to Saturday and 8am to 9pm on Sundays and Bank Holidays.

metadata.title: St Neots Town hit five as Histon suffer ninth defeat in 10 matches
metadata.contentSnippet: St Neots Town produced a commanding away performance, scoring five times as Histon struggled to create chances in a one-sided contest.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots Town hit five as Histon suffer ninth defeat in 10 matches
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: St Neots Town produced a commanding away performance, scoring five times as Histon struggled to create chances in a one-sided contest. The GCE Hire Fleet United Counties League South fixture was played at Histon. Harvey Henderson, Connor Furlong, Danny Baulk, James Stainsby and Connor Barnes were on target for the visitors. Henderson opened the scoring after four minutes, heading home at the far post from Lewis Burgess’s long throw. The forward movement and delivery gave the away side an early advantage, while Histon goalkeeper Tyler Key was left with little chance. Key then kept out Barnes, who was playing against his former club, after the striker had escaped the home defence. Histon were forced into an early change when Ryan Sharman suffered an injury, with Jake Coxall replacing him after 24 minutes. The hosts briefly threatened through Dan Brown, whose breakaway effort was blocked, but the visitors remained in control. St Neots doubled their lead after 31 minutes when Histon failed to clear a ball across the face of goal, allowing Furlong to finish. The home side missed an opportunity to reduce the deficit when Magloire Muyembe fired over, while Lil Francisco shot wide before half-time. Baulk added a third eight minutes after the interval, meeting a cross from Furlong with a powerful volley which gave Key no opportunity. Histon responded with attacking substitutions, but the changes failed to alter the pattern of the match. St Neots continued to defend comfortably, with their back line breaking up most attempts before they could develop into clear chances. Barnes struck the post with a header, and Histon’s problems deepened when Jonny Hall was sent off after 68 minutes. Stainsby made an immediate impact, scoring one minute after his introduction by chasing down the ball and finishing from a narrow angle. The away side continued to press despite making further substitutions, and Barnes completed the scoring five minutes from time after being set up by Joe Sutton. The result leaves Histon with nine defeats from ten matches, with their only victory coming against Brightlingsea in the FA Cup extra preliminary round.

metadata.title: Jail for uninsured driver who fled Cambs crash scene after killing pedestrian
metadata.contentSnippet: A uninsured driver from Cambridgeshire who fled the scene after hitting and killing a pedestrian has been jailed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Jail for uninsured driver who fled Cambs crash scene after killing pedestrian
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A uninsured driver from Cambridgeshire who fled the scene after hitting and killing a pedestrian has been jailed. Marcin Pilarski, 36, struck Sam Pope, 28, as he walked alongside Oil Mills Road, Ramsey Mereside, at just before 11pm on May 11, 2024. The crash was only reported when another driver called 999 after seeing Mr Pope, of Lincoln Road, Peterborough, laying in the road. Emergency services attended but despite their efforts, Mr Pope was declared dead at the scene. In a tribute, his family said: "Sam was a free spirit, who liked to live his life at 100mph and believed that rules were meant to be broken. "We shall miss his smile and crazy sense of humour that would always make you laugh, despite what mood you were in that day. "Sam was a rough diamond with a heart made of gold and will leave a big hole in our lives." Sam Pope was struck as he walked alongside Oil Mills Road (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Less than an hour after the collision, at 11.40pm, police were called by Pilarski’s partner who told them he had returned home in her Vauxhall Astra. She revealed the car was badly damaged, with a smashed windscreen and headlamp, and that there was also blood on the front of the vehicle. The woman said that they lived 15 minutes, about nine and a half miles, from the scene of the fatal crash. Police visited the house where they also noticed the damage to the car, and Pilarski, of Sorrell Avenue, Whittlesey, was arrested in relation to the fatal collision. In a statement, Pilarski’s partner said he had called her at 11pm to tell her he had “hit or killed somebody” who had been in the road, but she had to end the call due to him screaming. She said when he returned home in her damaged car she told him they needed to call the police and he answered, “I know”. In police interview Pilarski answered no comment to most questions. However, he later pleaded guilty to causing death by driving a car without a licence or insurance. He was sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on Thursday (September 17). He was handed one year and three months in prison. He was also disqualified from driving for four years and six months. The car was badly damaged, with a smashed windscreen and headlamp, and had blood on the front (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) In a victim impact statement, Mr Pope’s family said they had been left feeling angry that Pilarski didn’t seem remorseful and hadn’t apologised for his actions. The statement added: “We hope the memory of the night keeps him up at night like it does us. I don’t really know how as a family we will ever come to terms with this.” Detective Inspector Craig Wheeler, who investigated, said: “Pilarski made a conscious decision to drive his partner’s car without a licence or insurance. “He should never have put himself behind the wheel of a car and my thoughts and sympathies remain with the family and friends of Mr Pope, who needlessly lost his life at such a young age. “No sentence will ever ease the pain of their loss, but I hope the case acts as a stark reminder against getting behind the wheel while uninsured or without a licence. Just one journey could end in tragedy.” Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire girl, 16, suffered fatal head injury in river crash, inquest hears
metadata.contentSnippet: A 16-year-old girl died from a head injury after the car she was travelling in crashed into a river, an inquest heard today.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire girl, 16, suffered fatal head injury in river crash, inquest hears
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A 16-year-old Cambridgeshire girl died from a head injury after the car she was travelling in crashed into a river, an inquest heard today. Four members of Eden Bunn’s family attended the inquest into the horse-loving teenager’s death at Vantage House, Huntingdon. The inquest heard Eden, from Sutton Bridge, was sitting in the middle of the rear seat of a Volkswagen Polo driven by Declan Berry when it ended up in the River Nene at Wisbech on March 17. Eden Bunn loved her horses. (Image: Cambridgeshire Police) Ms Gray heard evidence from a collision report prepared by police accident investigators. The report said Mr Berry, 18, was driving the Polo at about 90mph on North Brink, Wisbech, at around 8.19pm when it hit a pothole, left the road, rolled several times and plunged into the fast-flowing river. Three other teenagers, all aged 18, were in the car with Eden and Mr Berry. Mr Berry also died, and his body was recovered from the river at Wisbech Marian nearly two weeks later. The many floral tributes that were left by the River Nene in Wisbech after the fatal crash that claimed the life of Eden Bunn. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Three of the passengers escaped the submerged car, but Eden did not get out. Her body was recovered the following day. A post-mortem found that Eden’s severe head injury was the primary cause of death. Ms Gray said there was no evidence of water in her lungs. The collision report blamed the car’s speed but said the road’s potholes, crumbling edges, undulating, and uneven surface also played a “less than minimal” part in the crash. Declan Berry had been driving the VW Polo in which Eden was a passenger. (Image: Cambridgeshire Constabulary) The three surviving passengers said Mr Berry was driving fast and that the front-seat passenger told him to slow down moments before the crash after noting he was doing 90mph. A female rear-seat passenger said Eden also shouted “Declan” just before Mr Berry lost control. The witnesses said Mr Berry shouted “oh shit” after the car hit a pothole and left the road. A nearby resident who witnessed the crash said he saw the headlights and rear lights “rotating through the air” but could not tell how they were rotating. He helped pull the survivors from the water, then searched the bank for the two missing occupants before emergency services arrived. Ms Gray said Cambridgeshire Highways had received 127 complaints about the road and that a survey four days before the crash found 98 potholes along North Brink. One near the crash site measured a quarter of the road’s width. The road was due to be repaired within 21 days, but the crash happened first. Highway workers filled the potholes the next day while the road was closed due to the incident. Ms Gray recorded a conclusion that Eden died in a road traffic accident, stating excessive speed was the main cause of the crash, and that the poor road surface had made more than a "minimal contribution" to the crash. She offered her condolences to Eden’s family members who were present: two aunts, an uncle and a cousin. Eden’s parents did not attend. An inquest into Declan Berry's death was heard yesterday.

metadata.title: Family describes horrific reality after teen's tragic death in Cambs river crash
metadata.contentSnippet: The family of a teenage girl killed in a river crash at Wisbech earlier this year have described the “horrific reality” they now face after an inquest into her death.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Family describes horrific reality after teen's tragic death in Cambs river crash
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The family of a teenage girl killed in a river crash at Wisbech earlier this year have described the “horrific reality” they now face after an inquest into her death. The hearing held today in Huntingdon heard that Eden Bunn, 16 and from Sutton Bridge, died as a result of a severe head injury suffered in the accident which happened on North Brink on March 17. Eden’s father Dean, mother Lisa, brother Jay and sister Shelby released the following statement after the inquest. “Eden was the kindest, most wonderful person and to have her snatched away from us so suddenly has left us heartbroken. "She was a beautiful soul and had such a love of life. No words can describe the devastation we feel and we will never get over losing her. "We don’t want to say anything about the lad who was driving. He has lost his life and his parents are going through the same living nightmare that we are. "Nothing will bring Eden back and her death is a horrific reality we will have to live with forever.” Sarah Townsend, a personal injury lawyer at Hodge Jones & Allen who represents the family, said: “Eden’s passing has understandably left her family inconsolable with grief and struggling to cope. "What is most tragic is that it was entirely avoidable and should serve as a warning to young drivers to not drive recklessly and put others at risk. "I hope that now the inquest process has concluded Eden’s family can slowly start to rebuild their lives.” The inquest heard that Eden was a rear seat passenger in a car driven by 18-year-old Declan Berry, from Wisbech, who also died in the accident, which was blamed on excessive speed, with potholes in the road a contributory factor. Another passenger in the car had told police the VW Polo had been going 90mph moments before the crash, which saw the vehicle leave the carriageway, roll down an embankment, before being fully submerged in the River Nene.

metadata.title: Six people complete 24-hour St Neots fitness challenge with 10,000 burpees
metadata.contentSnippet: Six people completed a gruelling 24-hour fitness challenge in St Neots.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Six people complete 24-hour St Neots fitness challenge with 10,000 burpees
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Six people completed a gruelling 24-hour fitness challenge in St Neots. The challenge, set by outdoor fitness group ABSolute Storm Fitness (Abstorm), included 25 back-to-back bootcamp sessions, 10,000 burpees, and a spin bike that ran non-stop for the full 24 hours. The event raised money for Ehlers-Danlos Support UK, Children’s Burns Camps and Parkinson’s UK. Abstorm founder and head coach Abi Black led all 25 sessions and oversaw the 10,000 burpees. Members of ABSolute Storm Fitness (Abstorm) who took part in the charity bootcamp (Image: Andy Clifton) Ms Black said: "We did it. "24 hours of bootcamps. "What a whirlwind of laughter and craziness, and so many memories. "I'm completely broken, but immensely proud. "This was our third year, our biggest year, and seeing six of our members pull off the full 24 hours non-stop is just unbelievable. "Abstorm isn't just a fitness group; we are a family and a core part of this community. "A massive thank you goes out to every single member who turned up to support, every person who jumped into a session, and everyone who has donated so far. "If you haven’t, please help us get to our total." Members of ABSolute Storm Fitness (Abstorm) who took part in the charity bootcamp (Image: Andy Clifton) The six participants, averaging 56, completed the entire challenge. The six were Ursula, 59, a Slimming World consultant; Ian, 57, a driving instructor; Nadine, 46, an environmental health officer; Sarah, 58, a geospatial analyst; Neil, 59, an aerospace and defence project manager; and Shaz, 58, a police force communications centre lead. They are the largest group to complete the full 24-hour challenge since the event began. Abstorm is aiming to raise a record £10,000 for the charities. Members of ABSolute Storm Fitness (Abstorm) who took part in the charity bootcamp (Image: Andy Clifton) The group promotes outdoor fitness in St Neots and nearby areas and welcomes members of all fitness levels. Sessions are held at Priory Park in St Neots and The Green in Brampton. The group's 2025 event raised more than £8,000—well above its £5,000 target—with support from more than 70 people who took part throughout the night.

metadata.title: Hospital redevelopment takes major step forward as land agreement reached
metadata.contentSnippet: Plans to redevelop a Hinchingbrooke Hospital have taken a major step forward.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hospital redevelopment takes major step forward as land agreement reached
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Plans to redevelop a hospital in Cambridgeshire have taken a major step forward. North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust has agreed in principle to acquire six hectares of land and associated highways. The acquisition of the former Cambridgeshire Police land marks a major step forward for the Hinchingbrooke Hospital redevelopment. Subject to planning consent, the land will allow for the creation of a new access road and 682 parking spaces. Environmental mitigation works and low-carbon energy infrastructure is also planned for the site. Hinchingbrooke Hospital was added to the New Hospital Programme in May 2023. The redevelopment programme is designed to address the challenges associated with ageing hospital infrastructure. Deborah Lee, senior responsible officer for Hinchingbrooke Hospital Redevelopment, said: "Reaching agreement on this land acquisition is a major milestone for the Hinchingbrooke Hospital Redevelopment Programme. "Securing this site will allow us to deliver the vital infrastructure needed to support our plans for a modern hospital that meets the needs of our patients, staff and communities for decades to come." Police and Crime Commissioner, Darryl Preston added: "As owner of the police estate in Cambridgeshire, I have a duty to ensure that land no longer needed for policing purposes is used in a way that delivers the greatest benefit to the public. "Once finalised, this sale will help improve access to local healthcare facilities, providing a positive outcome for residents and the wider community." Have you got a story you want to share? summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An investigation has been launched after two shops in the same Cambridgeshire village were burgled within the space of a day. The first burglary happened at around 3.50am on Monday September 21 at the Co-op on High Street in Willingham. A man smashed the front door panel but left empty-handed after a smoke security system was triggered. He was seen running towards Church Street and is described as wearing blue jeans, a black top, a baseball cap, and a snood covering his face. The second break-in took place at around 1am today (Tuesday September 22) at the One Stop on Church Street. Two men dressed in black and wearing balaclavas arrived in a black vehicle, smashed the front window. They stole a bag of cigarettes before fleeing towards Green Street. No arrests have been made and investigations are ongoing. Detective Sergeant Jonathan Lockwood said: "We appreciate these incidents will cause concern within the local community and would like to reassure residents that a thorough investigation is underway. "I would encourage residents and business owners to remain vigilant and to report any suspicious activity, no matter how minor it may seem.” Those with CCTV or dashcam footage should contact police online or by calling 101, quoting 35/73400/26. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A paedophile from Cambridgeshire who messaged people he believed were children and arranged to meet them has been jailed. Timothy Pavitt, 73, was brought to police attention after he uploaded indecent images of children to a Kik account in 2024. Officers were able to trace the IP address of the account, which led them to Pavitt’s home in Boxworth End, Swavesey. He was arrested on February 19, 2025, and claimed in interview to be “lonely” and using chat sites to speak to children and download images. A review of his devices found he had been speaking in a sexual manner with users he believed to be children and arranging to meet up with them. The devices also contained more than 350 indecent images. The identities of the people he was messaging have never been confirmed. Pavitt was jailed for four years and eight months at Peterborough Crown Court on Monday September 21. He had previously admitted to 18 counts, including communicating sexually with children and making indecent images. He was also handed an indefinite sexual harm prevention order (SHPO). Det Sgt Zip Lloyd said: "Pavitt knew what he was doing was wrong but continued to seek out users he believed were children, encourage sexual conversations and make indecent images. "He was also actively sharing those images for others to view, further fuelling the exploitation of children. I am pleased he is now behind bars. "Protecting young people from harm is one of our top priorities and we will continue to work tirelessly to keep children safe." Have you got a story you want to share?
