metadata.title: The hardest secondary schools to get into in Cambridgeshire revealed
metadata.contentSnippet: The hardest secondary schools to get into in Cambridgeshire have been revealed as parents and carers decide where their children will study next year.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The hardest secondary schools to get into in Cambridgeshire revealed
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The hardest secondary schools to get into have been revealed as parents and carers decide where their children will study next year. The window for applications for pupils starting year 7 in September 2027 opened earlier this month and will run until October 31. Last year, 7,050 students found out where they’d be heading with 96.7 per cent securing a place at one of their first, second or third preference schools. The hardest school to get into was Chesterton Community College, with enough places for just 60 per cent of children who put it down as their first preference. Earlier this year, the school was listed as the top performing school in the county – with 83.7 per cent of pupils achieving a Grade 5 or higher in their English and maths GCSEs. In its latest Ofsted report the school was also found to be outstanding in every category, with the inspector finding it has an “extremely high level of ambition for all pupils” which is matched by the pupils’ “own determination to succeed”. St Bede’s Inter-Church School in Cambridge was the second hardest to get into with 190 places for 301 first-place preferences – a success rate of 63 per cent. Soham Village College was ranked third with 78 per cent of pupils successfully admitted to 270 places from 247 first-place preferences. Parents and carers of children about to enter secondary school can submit their applications for places on the county council website. They have until the national closing date of October 31, after which late applications will be considered once all on-time applications are determined. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: “This year in Cambridgeshire 96.6 per cent of children were offered a place at either their first, second or third preference schools, this is above national benchmarks. Notably, both this year and last year, 5 per cent more children in Cambridgeshire received an offer from their first preference school than did nationally. “We’re committed to providing the best possible start in life for young people in our county and access to high quality education close to home is key. With population centres changing over time around our growing county, the council’s Education team work hard, in partnership with schools and with careful reference to pupil forecasting figures, to try and ensure we can offer the right numbers of school places, in the right areas, when they are needed.”

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire campaign could unlock £2m a year in unclaimed Pension Credit
metadata.contentSnippet: A campaign could put up to £2 million a year back in the pockets of older Cambridgeshire residents.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire campaign could unlock £2m a year in unclaimed Pension Credit
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A campaign could put up to £2 million a year back in the pockets of older Cambridgeshire residents. More than 700 households across Cambridgeshire will be contacted about unclaimed Pension Credit in a joint council campaign. The campaign is the county’s first targeted campaign to increase residents’ income since approval of the procurement of the Low-Income Family Tracker (LIFT) software platform at a meeting of the County Council’s Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee in February, funded through the UK Government’s Crisis and Resilience Fund via the DWP. Alison Whelan, chair of the Communities, Social Mobility and Inclusion Committee at Cambridgeshire County Council, said: "This new targeted campaign will boost financial security and quality of life for hundreds of families across our county. "I’m delighted to know that in Cambridgeshire we’re putting money, up to £2M, back in the pockets of the families that are most vulnerable to the cost-of-living pressures facing us nationally. "Please help us to spread the word about this excellent campaign so that families contacted by their district or city council will know they can trust the information they’ve been given – it’s good news!" Eligible residents will be contacted directly by their local council: Cambridge City, East Cambridgeshire, South Cambridgeshire, Huntingdonshire or Fenland. Councils will contact residents by letter, email or phone. Pension Credit comes in two parts: Guarantee Credit and Savings Credit. Some households may be eligible for both. The council estimates the 500 identified households could gain more than £2 million a year if they all claim Guarantee Credit, based on an average award of £4,300. No scams have been reported in connection with the campaign. The campaign follows a 2024 council motion calling for a proactive campaign to ensure eligible pensioners were informed about Pension Credit after changes to winter fuel payments.

metadata.title: Mayor backs Ely City FC with personal sponsorship and solar plans debated
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambs Mayor Paul Bristow answered questions from the public during a recent event held at Ely City Football Club.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Mayor backs Ely City FC with personal sponsorship and solar plans debated
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambs Mayor Paul Bristow answered questions from the public during a recent event held in Ely - here's what happened Last Thursday evening (September 17), keen football supporter and mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, Paul Bristow, was in his element when he held the third of his Question Time events at Ely City Football Club. And the charismatic chair of the football club, Alan Alsop, was a member of the audience, as host Paul Brackley, editor of the Cambridge Independent, asked the questions sent in prior that were all answered knowledgeably and in depth. He spoke about everything from the state of Fen roads to the siting of dropped kerbs, resolving water problems in south Cambridgeshire, to new building and proposed destruction of swathes of rural flora and fauna for a ‘busway’—a scheme with which he expressed his disapproval—to broader issues like the restructuring of councils. Paul Bristow answers many questions (Image: Cathy Gibb de Swarte) Mr Bristow also answered some lively questions from the floor—and mentioned he would be visiting Littleport this week, as well as his interest in the town’s history. Before leaving the club, which supports 33 teams, he discovered that both businesses and individuals can sponsor games for £80. This includes six guest tickets and refreshments in a hospitality framework. He then told chairman Alan that he was going to do just that personally. Alan then told the Mayor that he was going to look at the council grant scheme for installing solar panels on the roof of the club premises. Paul Bristow has served as the strategic authority mayor for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough since 2025. Prior to that he was the Member of Parliament for Peterborough, where he was brought up and still lives, from 2019 until 2024. In his introduction, he said: “Mayors have an increasingly important role in shaping the future of our communities, from improving transport and supporting local businesses to delivering new homes and creating opportunities for growth.”

metadata.title: Probe into care of man accused of throwing boy into crocodile pit continues
metadata.contentSnippet: Norfolk County Council has confirmed it continues to investigate the care given to a man accused of throwing a toddler into a crocodile pit.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Probe into care of man accused of throwing boy into crocodile pit continues
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council has confirmed it continues to probe the care given to a disabled man accused of throwing a toddler into a crocodile pit. Norfolk County Council opened a safeguarding inquiry after the three-year-old boy was injured at Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon, on June 18. He was rescued from the pit by staff members, including the zoo's owners Andy and Tracey Johnson, who are said to have leapt into the enclosure. It has was later revealed the toddler was attacked by one of the reptiles and he has since been discharged after spending more than a month in hospital. A 30-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and released on bail (Image: Newsquest) A 30-year-old man from Norfolk was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after the boy sustained serious injuries. He was released on bail until September 18 but has since been re-bailed by police until December 17. A source with knowledge of the situation claimed the man, believed to have learning difficulties, was visiting the zoo with two carers. It is alleged the carers left the crocodile enclosure with the suspect after the incident but were unable to leave the grounds after staff members intervened. Other witnesses claimed the carers were "on their phones" and "weren't paying him much attention". Police declared a critical incident after the toddler sustained serious injuries (Image: Joe Giddens/PA) Council officials confirmed it was investigating whether the man is being neglected or abused while in care. The county council revealed it had launched a Section 42 inquiry and stopped referrals to the care provider in the suspect's case. These require local authorities to investigate when they suspect an adult receiving care is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect. While the suspect is from the county, his care was not commissioned, provided or paid for by the council. In an update issued on Monday (September 21), Norfolk County Council said it continues to work with partner organisations. Norfolk County Council confirmed it was investigating whether the man is being neglected or abused while in care. (Image: Joe Giddens/PA) A spokesperson said: "This was a deeply distressing incident and our thoughts remain with the individual and their family. "While Norfolk County Council was not involved in providing, commissioning or funding the care concerned, we take our safeguarding responsibilities seriously and continue to work in collaboration with relevant partner organisations to ensure appropriate safeguarding processes are followed. "As enquiries remain ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment further on an individual case." The three-year-old boy has since been discharged from hospital (Image: SWNS) Johnsons of Old Hurst described the incident as "one of the most distressing" in its history. The zoo thanked visitors who "stepped forward to help," including off-duty paramedics and police officers. It was confirmed no safety concerns were indicated regarding the zoo's conditions at the time of the incident. Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire man sent racist messages to England footballer Djed Spence on X
metadata.contentSnippet: A Cambridgeshire man who sent abusive, degrading and racist messages to England and then Tottenham Hotspur player Djed Spence has avoided prison.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire man sent racist messages to England footballer Djed Spence on X
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire man who sent abusive, degrading and racist messages to an England international footballer has avoided prison. Brian Bealey, 69, posted multiple public comments on social media platform X between March 17 and 29. The messages were directed at England and then-Tottenham Hotspur player Djed Spence. Cambridgeshire Police's Football Policing Officer worked alongside the UK Football Policing Unit to identify Bealey. It follows a referral from the Football Association and Premier League after England’s fixture against Uruguay on March 27. Investigators linked the X account used to send the messages to Bealey, of Main Street, Witchford, Ely. The messages contained racially offensive language and slurs directed at Spence, who now plays for Inter Milan. They were also directed at other individuals, and were assessed as grossly offensive and racially aggravated. At Cambridge Magistrates’ Court on Thursday (September 17), Bealey pleaded guilty to sending by public communication offensive messages. He was fined £1,000. Detective Sergeant Dominic Carminati, who investigated, said: "There is absolutely no place for racism, either in football or in society as a whole. "Djed Spence was subjected to a series of offensive, degrading and racially aggravated messages that were intended to cause distress and spread hatred online. "People often believe they can hide behind anonymous social media accounts, but this case demonstrates that those who use online platforms to target others with racist abuse can and will be identified. "We would encourage anyone who experiences or witnesses racist abuse online to report it to the platform involved and to police." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have named a pedestrian who tragically died after being hit by a coach on the A14 in Cambridgeshire. A white Yutong coach was travelling eastbound on the A14 between Histon and Milton when it struck Nathan Price at around 1.35pm on Saturday September 12. The pedestrian, 33, and of King's Hedges Road, Cambridge, was pronounced dead at the scene. The driver of the coach, a 39-year-old man from Peterborough, was uninjured. In a tribute, Mr Price's family said: "In loving memory of Nathan Ellis Price, a very much-loved son, brother, father and uncle. The crash, near Cambridge, shut the eastbound carriageway for several hours, with motorists urged to avoid the area. metadata.title: Amazon warehouse plans could create more than 2,300 jobs
metadata.contentSnippet: Amazon's proposed Biggleswade warehouse could create 2,300 jobs, with plans for 166,000sqm at Stratton Business Park and A1 traffic changes in Bedfordshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Amazon warehouse plans could create more than 2,300 jobs
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. More than 2,300 jobs could be created through plans for an Amazon warehouse in Biggleswade, according to a councillor. A planning application has been submitted by the world’s largest online retailer to Central Bedfordshire Council for the premises on the town’s Stratton Business Park, said Conservative Biggleswade East councillor Grant Fage on social media. These employment opportunities would cover a range of roles, he posted on Facebook. “The warehouse would be accompanied by three extra units, while the site is expected to include 166,000sqm of floor space. “The company’s proposals include changes to the A1 south roundabout, including traffic lights on the approaches from both north and south. “This is a very complicated application and will have huge impacts on Biggleswade, positively in terms of job creation but negatively for our road network. “In the recent Central Bedfordshire Local Plan consultation, this site was referenced both in my response and that of Biggleswade Town Council, as being a site that could support commercial development in certain circumstances. “Having seen this application, I’ve no objection but would ask that the following commitments are honoured in full: “The reconfiguration of the A1 roundabout is needed, but it’s sub-optimal to have traffic signals.” Councillor Fage wondered if National Highways could be asked to confirm “whether traffic lights are absolutely necessary” on both the northern and southern approaches. “We need that independent view,” he explained. “If National Highways says traffic signals are required, I hope it highlights the desperate state of the A1 in Biggleswade. “We’d have the only traffic lights on the entire A1 stretch between South Mimms and Scotland. This didn’t work for the Black Cat roundabout and it feels like a step backwards. “The queues at Pegasus Drive are very challenging now for drivers exiting Stratton Business Park. Traffic lights east of the Lidl mini-roundabout makes sense, although further efforts are needed to remove bottle necks. “That would include as cars exit Lidl, while yellow lines are needed along both sides of Lancaster Way.” Reacting to his post, Biggleswade town councillor Mark Knight warned: “Installing (traffic) lights on the A1 roundabout is madness. “Planners are repeating the history of short-term thinking that was used for decades at the Black Cat roundabout.” Amazon made a shock announcement in January to close its Marston Gate centre at Ridgmont, opting for a new site in Northampton. Almost 600 employees were based at the company’s first UK site, and it was one of Central Bedfordshire’s biggest employers since opening in 1999. Central Bedfordshire Council’s development management committee is expected to consider the project in due course.

Cllr Nathan Hunt said he remains concerned about the plans to build a new Lidl supermarket in Hartford, Huntingdon, on land south of Main Street (B1514) and west of Huntingdon Road. metadata.title: 'Excessive speed' and potholes blamed for fatal Wisbech river crash inquest told
metadata.contentSnippet: Wisbech teenager Declan Berry drowned after his car hit a pothole at 90mph and plunged into the River Nene, an inquest heard. Sixteen-year-old Eden Bunn also died.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Excessive speed' and potholes blamed for fatal Wisbech river crash inquest told
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Wisbech teenager Declan Berry drowned after his car hit a pothole at 90mph and plunged into the River Nene, an inquest heard. The teenage driver was told to slow down moments before his car plunged into the water, killing him and sixteen-year-old rear passenger, Eden Bunn. Mr Berry, 18, was travelling at around 90mph when his Volkswagen Polo hit a pothole on North Brink, Wisbech, and rolled down an embankment into the river, the hearing heard. Declan Berry's family and friends laid tributes and waited for news as searches of the River Nene were carried out for his body. (Image: Sarah Cliss) None of his family was at the hearing at Vantage House in Huntingdon, which was conducted by written statements, and heard that Mr Berry drowned after the March 17 crash; his body was recovered from the river nearly two weeks later at the town’s marina. A police officer called to identify the body confirmed it was Mr Berry due to an unusual tattoo on the back of his neck and his clothing. Police investigator James Mills concluded that speed was the main factor in the crash, while the pothole-riddled road, with crumbling edges and an uneven surface, also contributed. Cambridgeshire area coroner Elizabeth Gray read the evidence from the various witnesses about the crash, which happened at around 8.19pm as Mr Berry drove four teenage friends along North Brink, away from the town centre. The front-seat passenger told police he had looked at the speedometer and that Mr Berry was driving at 90mph moments before the crash and he had asked him to slow down. Mr Berry replied, "It will be all right", before the car hit a pothole and he lost control. Eden Bunn, 16, died after the car she was travelling in entered the River Nene, near Wisbech (Image: Cambridgeshire) The unnamed 18-year-old witness said Mr Berry tried to control the car before shouting: "Oh shit" as the car left the road, rolled several times and plunged into the river. The witness said he met Mr Berry at McDonald’s, accepted an invitation to go for a drive and believed Mr Berry had "intended to show off". He escaped through the broken passenger window and described the water around him as dark, telling officers he did not know where the others were as he made his escape. Declan Berry's body was recovered from Wisbech Marina nearly two weeks after the fatal crash. (Image: Alan Berry) A female passenger sitting behind the front passenger, who was not wearing a seat belt, recalled a near miss on the same stretch of road a week earlier. The other unnamed second rear-seat passenger, who was sat behind Mr Berry, heard a thud beneath the car but did not know what it struck before it rolled into the water. She struggled to release her seat belt before escaping through a broken window and being rescued by members of the public. One of the women had also told police that she was used to Mr Berry driving at speed, and it was what she expected. Many floral tributes were left by the River Nene in Wisbech following the horrific crash. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Eden Bunn from Sutton Bridge was sitting in the middle and had reportedly called out "Declan" moments before the crash. Her inquest is due tomorrow. An eyewitness on his driveway at the time of the crash heard a vehicle approach at speed before a loud bang. He saw the headlights and rear lights "rotating through the air", then ran and found the vehicle completely submerged. He asked his partner to call emergency services before helping those involved, who had made it to the bank but needed help out of the water. A Cambridgeshire Search & Rescue team were at the scene for several days. (Image: Sarah Cliss) Mr Mills’ report found a steering defect and suspension modifications on the VW, but no evidence that either contributed to the crash. Investigators recovered a dashcam and black box from the Polo, but neither contained any data. Cambridgeshire County Council recorded 98 potholes during a survey just days before the accident and set a 21-day deadline for repairs, but the crash happened first. Repairs were carried out immediately after the crash, while the road was closed as a result of the incident. The accident report said speed was the main factor: it left the driver less time to react to potholes before he lost control. At a lower speed, the rollover would have been less severe. Ms Gray concluded that Mr Berry drowned after a single-vehicle crash. She concluded that "excessive speed", the road conditions, and the poor surface more than likely contributed to his death.

metadata.title: Cambs primary school praised for 'welcoming' environment in Ofsted report
metadata.contentSnippet: Earith Primary School has been praised for its "welcoming and nurturing" environment in its latest Ofsted report.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs primary school praised for 'welcoming' environment in Ofsted report
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire primary school has been praised for its "welcoming and nurturing" environment in its latest Ofsted report. Earith Primary School near Huntingdon, part of the Active Learning Trust, was inspected on July 14 and met the expected standard overall, with early years and personal development judged strong. Inspectors said pupils feel safe and well supported in a “welcoming and nurturing” school where they enjoy positive relationships with staff and each other. Ofsted also praised the school for tailoring parts of its curriculum to the local community. Because the school is surrounded by waterways, pupils receive extra water-safety lessons, while older children learn about healthy relationships, artificial intelligence, digital footprints and online misinformation. Duncan Low, Director of Learning at Active Learning Trust, said: “We are very pleased to see Ofsted inspectors recognise the strengths and achievements at Earith Primary School and the positive experience it provides for pupils and their families. The school is located near Huntingdon (Image: Earith Primary School) “We know that the school plays a hugely important role at the heart of the village community in Earith and would like to thank the staff for all the hard work and commitment that they bring every day." Inspectors said pupils build a strong understanding of different cultures, religions and beliefs through the school council, voting and debates about democracy. Every pupil has a responsibility in the school community, helping them build independence and leadership skills. The report also highlighted extra-curricular opportunities including sporting events, educational visits, music activities and residential trips. Inspectors noted that pupils develop a strong understanding of different cultures (Image: Earith Primary School) Pupils particularly value the on-site swimming pool, which inspectors said is important because of the school’s location. Most pupils achieved in line with national expectations, made appropriate progress and were well prepared for the next stage of education. Attendance was above the national average, including among disadvantaged pupils and those with special educational needs and/or disabilities. Headteacher Thomas Abbs said: “I am delighted that this Ofsted report recognises the warm, welcoming and inclusive environment we work so hard to achieve at our village school. Attendance rates were found to be above national averages (Image: Earith Primary School) “The report is a strong endorsement of the hard work of our staff and pupils, as well as the support of our families, and of the wonderful sense of community that makes our school such a special place. “We look forward to building on this excellent report as we continue to provide the very best opportunities for our children.” Ofsted said that leaders should continue to strengthen curriculum evaluation to ensure pupils consistently gain and apply intended knowledge and skills across all subjects. Inspectors also recommended further support to help pupils manage their emotions and behaviour more independently.

metadata.contentSnippet: A youth charity is appealing for urgent support as funding cuts threaten LGBTQ+ services across Cambridgeshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: LGBTQ+ youth services at risk as Cambridgeshire charity faces funding shortfall
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A youth charity is appealing for urgent support as funding cuts threaten LGBTQ+ services across Cambridgeshire. The Kite Trust says rising demand and funding shortfalls are putting its vital services for young LGBTQ+ people at risk across Cambridgeshire, Peterborough and nearby areas. Felix Turney, co-CEO of The Kite Trust, said: "The need for tailored youth services has never been greater as young LGBTQ+ people face more complex challenges. Kite Trust staff and volunteers "Where we operate, many LGBTQ+ young people have no access to other LGBTQ-specific support, and often do not feel comfortable or able to access mainstream services. "We provide vital space where LGBTQ+ young people can access accurate information, understand their own identity, and build community in a supportive and non-judgemental environment." The charity says young people, particularly those who are transgender, are facing more complex problems and need support in several areas of life. Felix said: "Even with the measures we’ve taken to cut our costs, we are urgently in need of further funding to ensure we can keep delivering life-affirming and life-saving youth work to LGBTQ+ young people for as long as they need it." Kite Trust team members Financial pressure has already forced the charity to cut support groups and suspend major community events, including its popular Queer Prom. The Kite Trust has joined easyfundraising, allowing supporters to raise money for the charity at no extra cost while shopping online. Supporters have already raised more than £1,150 through the platform. A Kite Trust spokesperson said easyfundraising lets people support the charity through everyday online purchases, helping fund vital services without a direct donation.

metadata.title: Huntingdon Scouts secure 30-year lease for permanent community centre
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdon Scouts could finally have a permanent home after years on the move.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon Scouts secure 30-year lease for permanent community centre
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Huntingdon Scouts could finally have a permanent home after years on the move. The group has secured a 30-year lease on a former maintenance building on St Peters Road, ending years of operating without a fixed base and regularly moving equipment between different borrowed spaces. They now plan to turn the industrial site into a dedicated scouting centre. Steve Harris, who is leading the project, said: "Having a permanent home means we can spend less time moving gear and more time providing life-changing adventures for our young people. This building represents a 30-year commitment to the youth and the people of Huntingdon." Huntingdon Scouts are part of the Scout Association, helping young people build life skills through camping, hiking, crafts and community service. The centre will include a main activity hall, modern meeting rooms, a kitchen, toilets and other amenities. The group also hopes the centre will become a community hub. The team wants other organisations to use the centre, helping tackle a shortage of quality community venues in the area. But turning the old building into a modern community hub will cost money. Several grants have been secured, but more money is needed to finish the project. Huntingdon Scouts are appealing to residents and businesses for donations, sponsorship, materials and labour. A group spokesperson said: "Every bit of help will go directly toward creating a lasting legacy for the town. The Scouts are inviting anyone who can offer money or professional services to get in touch." Anyone who can help should email info@hinchingbrookescouts.org or visit the Huntingdon Scout Centre Facebook page. The planned conversion is set to take place in three phases, starting with basic repairs before adding an accessible toilet and wet room, followed by enhancements for youth groups and other community users.

metadata.title: 75 attend sold-out Huntingdon talk on region's dark witch trial history
metadata.contentSnippet: More than 75 people flocked to a sold-out Huntingdon talk on the dark history of witch trials.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 75 attend sold-out Huntingdon talk on region's dark witch trial history
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: More than 75 people flocked to a sold-out Huntingdon talk on the dark history of witch trials. The event was part of this year’s Heritage Open Days in Huntingdonshire and was organised by Huntingdon Town Council and The Cromwell Museum. The talk, led by Cromwell Museum curator Stuart Orme, was moved from the Court Room to the larger Assembly Room, but extra tickets quickly sold out. Stuart said: "The Huntingdonshire Witch Trials are one of the most intriguing aspects of our local history, so it has been wonderful to see so many people wanting to learn more about the people and events behind the story. "Whilst Heritage Open Days shines a spotlight on our shared heritage, the Cromwell Museum is free to visit throughout the year, and I would encourage anyone with an interest in Huntingdon's past to come along and discover more of the remarkable stories our town has to tell." Guided Walk at Priory Road Cemetary (Image: Huntingdon Town Council) The talk covered the region’s witch-trial history, including the Witches of Warboys, the infamous Witchfinder General Matthew Hopkins and Huntingdon woman Mary Hicks, who may have been the last person executed for witchcraft in England, although both her existence and that claim are disputed. The witch-trials talk was part of a wider Heritage Open Days programme that included an open day at Priory Road Cemetery and Chapel, where visitors explored burial records and learned about former Huntingdon Burial Board members. The programme will conclude with two fully booked guided tours of Huntingdon Town Hall, giving attendees the chance to explore the town’s civic heritage. The Cromwell Museum and self-guided trails from the Discover Huntingdon Visitor Centre offer residents and visitors year-round ways to explore the town’s history. Huntingdon saw witchcraft trials in 1593, 1646 and 1716, with at least four people hanged at Mill Common after the 1646 proceedings.

metadata.title: Small changes urged as Zero Waste Week highlights how to rethink rubbish
metadata.contentSnippet: Martin Cooper, owner of The Refill Shop of Ikigai in St Ives, writes his latest column.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Small changes urged as Zero Waste Week highlights how to rethink rubbish
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Martin Cooper, owner of The Refill Shop of Ikigai in St Ives, writes his latest column It's time to rethink our rubbish. Do you know how much waste you produce on a weekly basis? With more bins being rolled out from the council, it’s hard to keep track of just how much we are throwing away, but Zero Waste Week is an opportunity to take notice. Zero Waste Week was held between September 7 and 11 and has become a regular in the calendar of environmental campaigns to help us reduce what we throw away. But why does it matter? Carry reusable items (Image: Martin Cooper) The scale of our waste problem is easy to overlook because most of it disappears the moment the bin lorry pulls away. We generate millions of tonnes of rubbish every year, most of which ends up in landfill rather than being reused or recycled. Landfill sites take up valuable land, can leach pollutants into soil and waterways and represent a huge waste of the energy and resources that went into making the products in the first place. Every takeaway container, unopened food packet or old appliance thrown away is a small loss multiplied by millions of households doing the same thing. Rather than demanding perfection – which we know will never be achieved, Zero Waste Week encourages us to pick one habit and try to improve it for seven days – then keep going until it sticks. And it’s not as hard as you might think: You can audit your bins – during Zero Waste Week, make note of what you throw away most – awareness alone often changes behaviour. Cut your food waste by planning meals, freezing leftovers and using up odds and ends before they spoil – food waste is one of the easiest and most impactful areas to tackle. Choose reusables – swap single-use bags, bottles and cutlery for versions you can use again and again. Repair, don’t replace – Huntingdonshire has a number of repair cafés throughout the year, that can fix clothes, electronics, and furniture that might otherwise be binned, and the Sew, Mend and Repair group, who meet in St Ives, help repair and alter clothes to keep them going. Buy loose and local – reducing packaging by shopping at markets or refill shops will cut your waste before it even reaches your home – and gives you an opportunity to reuse what you already have. Zero Waste Week won’t solve the waste crisis on its own, but small, collective changes add up. This September, it’s worth asking “what’s one thing I could throw away less of?”.

metadata.title: Young anglers catch and return 723 fish in confidence-building summer programme
metadata.contentSnippet: A summer fishing programme has helped young people in Huntingdonshire build confidence, improve their wellbeing and learn new skills.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Young anglers catch and return 723 fish in confidence-building summer programme
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A summer fishing programme has helped young people in Huntingdonshire build confidence, improve their wellbeing and learn new skills. The Dreamdrops Fishing Programme, run by children’s charity Dreamdrops in partnership with the Fly-Fishing Academy, took place every Tuesday in August at Rectory Farm in Great Addington, Northamptonshire. Up to eight young anglers attended each session, including graduates of an earlier life-skills angling course and two working towards the Angling Skills Activity Award. Roger Adams, an instructor from the Fly-Fishing Academy, said: "Where did August go? "It’s been tremendous fun, but my life has flashed before me – I have lost four weeks of it!" Richard Winser of the Fly-Fishing Academy said: "There have been some great sessions, they seemed to get incrementally better each time we ventured out; angling appeals on so many different levels and in so many personal ways, to different people. George Ward (Image: Dreamdrops Children's Charity) "It can enhance wellbeing and be very therapeutic just being outside and around water, in a safe and controlled environment." The young anglers caught and safely returned 723 fish during the programme. George Ward, a current participant, said: "I liked the way that the instructors had loads of time for you, and you didn’t feel rushed. "Everything was explained simply and they always told us what would be covered next. "The Zoom tutorials and Kahoot quizzes were serious fun. "It was great to have such a good course structure, and I learnt loads of new and different fishing techniques – amazing." Parent Michelle Quail praised the programme. She said: "For us personally, the fishing days have been such good fun and have stood out as a highlight of our summer, it has given us an opportunity to do things we would otherwise not have had a chance to do and to make some really lovely family memories along the way." Dreamdrops committee chair Christine Luckham congratulated the two young anglers who completed the course and will receive Gold Award Level certificates at a ceremony at Huntingdon Town Hall on September 12. She also thanked the Fly-Fishing Academy team, saying: "Once again, my thanks to the Fly-Fishing Academy team who have ploughed a new furrow and extended the boundaries further for our fishing programme and angling initiative." The Angling Skills Activity Award - Foundation (Gold) course includes three online tutorials and four additional fishing days, with participants required to demonstrate competency in 17 areas.

metadata.title: Hunts care home goes from 'requires improvement' to 'good' in latest inspection
metadata.contentSnippet: Montague House care home in Brampton has been rated good overall after previously requiring improvement by the Care Quality Commission (CQC).

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts care home goes from 'requires improvement' to 'good' in latest inspection
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Huntingdonshire care home has been rated good overall after previously being judged to require improvement by the Care Quality Commission (CQC). Montague House, in Keeling Lane, Brampton, was assessed between July 30 and August 19, with the report published September 8. The home provides accommodation, nursing and personal care for 52 residents, including people living with dementia. Montague House was awarded ‘Good’ ratings across four out of five criteria (Safe, Effective, Responsive and Well-led) and an 'Outstanding' rating for Caring. At the previous inspection in March 2023, inspectors found the provider breached regulations on safe care, treatment and governance. The CQC said the provider had made “sufficient improvements” and was no longer breaching the regulations. The care home no longer 'requires improvement' (Image: Montague House) Home Manager Paula Yorkston Toy said: “We are delighted with the CQC report and to have received an ‘Outstanding’ rating in ‘Caring’. “I want to thank every member of the team here for helping us to achieve this result and for their contribution to Montague House. “The residents and their wellbeing are at the heart of everything we do, and it’s terrific that the inspectors have recognised our dedication and care.” The latest inspection report reads: "People experienced personalised care from staff who understood them well and supported them to live meaningful and fulfilling lives. "Staff demonstrated a detailed understanding of people's individual needs, preferences and life histories. "There were many examples of compassionate, person-centred care, particularly for people living with dementia." Montague House in Brampton was rated 'good' in its latest inspection (Image: Montague House) Inspectors identified areas for further work, including safeguarding recognition and reporting, records showing repositioning had taken place as assessed, care planning and medicines oversight. There was no evidence of avoidable harm and the provider responded positively to feedback and took action. Residents took part in activities, therapies and community links, including exercise programmes, dementia activities and religious services. Inspectors found visible, approachable leaders and a positive culture at the home. Inspectors said residents had positive experiences, with staff acting calmly, patiently and respectfully and adapting to their emotional and wellbeing needs. A person told inspectors: "I like it here and I'm happy to be here."

metadata.title: 10 of the best independent restaurants in Cambridgeshire you need to try

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire's food scene is unrivalled, with hundreds of hidden gems and independent restaurants well worth a visit. Here are 10 of the best independent restaurants in the county that you need to try, with glowing reviews from previous visitors. The Cock is an award-winning country pub and restaurant. It has won the national dining pub title twice and serves seasonal British menus in a riverside village setting. It has more than 700 "excellent" reviews on TripAdvisor. This independent hotel restaurant in Huntingdon is known for modern British cooking, an excellent wine list and its riverside location. It has an overall rating of 4.5 out of five stars on TripAdvisor with more than 800 reviews. The Crown Inn is a highly regarded village gastropub. It is particularly noted for seasonal British food and is popular with local diners and food enthusiasts. One reviewer wrote: "We have just had our wedding at The Crown and we cannot praise the place and the team there highly enough. "They are attentive professional and diligent. The food is absolutely amazing." This independent Italian restaurant overlooking the river is one of the town’s best-rated restaurants and is suited to special occasions and date nights. One five-star review reads: "We dined on excellent pasta dishes which although not inexpensive turned out to be great value based on the high quality of the ingredients and lovely slightly old fashioned surroundings and atmosphere." The Old Fire Engine House in Ely is an independent restaurant and gallery established in 1968. It uses local and seasonal ingredients and is one of the city’s most iconic dining destinations. It has more than 600 "excellent" reviews on TripAdvisor. Eat Thai is a small independent restaurant in Ely, frequently cited among the town’s best eateries. One five-star review reads: "Everything was first class, fresh ingredients cooked perfectly with very friendly, helpful staff and very reasonable prices." The Lamb & Flag in Welney is among Fenland’s best-rated gastropubs. It is particularly renowned for Sunday lunches and has consistently strong customer reviews. On TripAdvisor, it is ranked first out of 96 restaurants in Wisbech. Oliver Twist Restaurant is an independent family-run restaurant in Guyhirn. It has an excellent local reputation and serves quality British cuisine. The country inn has more than 100 "excellent" reviews on TripAdvisor. The Red Lion in Wisbech is one of the best-rated independent restaurants in the town. It is popular for traditional British cooking and Sunday roasts. One five-star review reads: "Such a warm, welcoming atmosphere — I’ll definitely be back and only wish I’d found it sooner." Worzals in Wisbech St Mary is a landmark Fenland restaurant with a farm-to-fork focus. It is popular for celebratory meals and Sunday lunches. One visitor wrote on TripAdvisor: "Absolutely perfect roast dinner. I've been out for a lot of roast dinner in my time and this has got to be the best! "Lovely size meals perfect amount of meat for the roasts."

Anyone with information is asked to visit the police website, contact Crimestoppers or call 101, quoting Operation Stormwell.

metadata.contentSnippet: Passengers are facing rail disruption after an electricity supply failure which has reduced services between Stevenage and Finsbury Park.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Passengers warned of rail disruption after electricity fault
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Passengers are facing rail disruption after an electricity supply failure. The fault occurred in the Welwyn area and has reduced the number of services running between Stevenage and Finsbury Park. National Rail said services between Stevenage and London could be cancelled, changed or delayed by up to 20 minutes. Electricity suppliers and Network Rail are working to restore power, but disruption is expected until at least 3pm, National Rail said. The incident was first reported at 3.22am on Friday (September 18) and has affected several routes. Thameslink and Great Northern passengers are expected to face disruption throughout the morning. Customers have been advised to allow at least 45 extra minutes to travel and may need to catch a different train. Great Northern will run fewer trains between Cambridge and London. However, tickets will be accepted on Thameslink trains to London St Pancras International and Great Northern trains to London King's Cross. Passengers can also use Greater Anglia trains to London Liverpool Street at no extra cost, National Rail said. Great Northern will also run a reduced peak-time service between Peterborough and London King's Cross as well as Hertford North and Moorgate. LNER passengers can also use their tickets on Avanti West Coast, Great Northern and Thameslink trains. More information, including an alternative route map and details of ticket acceptance, is available on the operator's website. Have you got a story you want to share? Police were called to Chloe's Jewellers in March at 8.30am on Wednesday, September 16. The force arrived by 9am and a police spokesperson conformed a crime has been raised for business burglary. Investigations are ongoing. The family-owned jeweller has been trading for more than 100 years and has stores across East Anglia, including in St Ives, Wisbech and Royston. Police were called to the St Ives branch at just before 3.30am on April 30 to reports of the front window being smashed and thousands of pounds worth of jewellery being stolen. Joe Ross, of Hawkins Road, Cambridge, was jailed for 16 months at Peterborough Crown Court on August 26 after admitting smashing into a shop and stealing £29,000 worth of jewellery. The March branch will now be temporarily closed following the recent break-in.

The four Forest Live summer shows, organised by Forestry England and promoter Cuffe & Taylor, will take place in Delamere, Thetford, Cannock Chase and Westonbirt Arboretum in June 2027. Madness last headlined Forest Live in 2005 and will return to the stage in 2027. Madness, known for hits including Our House and Baggy Trousers, have had 15 Top 10 singles during a career spanning more than 40 years. Last year, they released Hit Parade, a 45-track anthology celebrating 45 years of music. Madness said: "From the early days to the latest tracks... we've packed up the lot and brought them all together in Hit Parade. "It's a proper nutty collection of our biggest and best. "Press play, turn it up, and enjoy the ride." The collection includes 27 Top 40 hits, including It Must Be Love, Lovestruck and chart-topper House of Fun. A new 4K restoration of their 1981 film Take It Or Leave It will be shown in cinemas in October. More than 2.5 million people have attended Forest Live concerts over the past 25 years. The series brings live music to outdoor settings while helping fund forestry work across the country. A spokesperson for Forestry England said: "We manage and care for the nation’s 1,500 woods and forests. "We use the money Forest Live raises to maintain these beautiful natural areas for everyone to enjoy, run important conservation projects and keep growing trees." Scouting For Girls will support Madness on the night. Formed in London in 2005, Scouting For Girls have sold more than two million albums and singles, earned four Brit Award nominations and scored a string of radio hits. They have also sold out shows at Wembley Arena and the Royal Albert Hall, plus two nights at the London Palladium. The Forest Live 2027 dates are: • Saturday, June 19, 2027 – Delamere Forest • Sunday, June 20, 2027 – High Lodge, Thetford Forest • Saturday, June 26, 2027 – Cannock Chase Forest • Sunday, June 27, 2027 – Westonbirt Arboretum Tickets for all shows go on general sale at 10am on Friday, September 25, through forestlive.com. Fans can also sign up through the website for updates, announcements and exclusive pre-sale access.

metadata.title: Pop icon Ronan Keating to headline Thetford Forest concert alongside Blue
metadata.contentSnippet: Pop icons Ronan Keating and Blue are set to perform at High Lodge in Thetford Forest, during Forestry England’s Forest Live concert series, next year.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Pop icon Ronan Keating to headline Thetford Forest concert alongside Blue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A pop icon will headline an outdoor concert next summer. Ronan Keating will perform at High Lodge in Thetford Forest, during Forestry England’s Forest Live concert series, on Tuesday June 15. The show is part of his Just Getting Started World Tour, which marks more than 30 years in music. Mr Keating said: "I’ve been incredibly lucky to have spent more than three decades doing what I love. "I’ve travelled the world, made records I’m enormously proud of and, most importantly, had audiences singing those songs back to me night after night. "I feel creatively energised, deeply grateful and more connected to what I do than ever, and I can’t wait to share that with people around the world." Blue (Image: Forest Live) He will be joined by Blue, who are also celebrating a milestone with more than 25 years in the music industry. The tour will feature a mix of Boyzone classics and solo hits, bringing together the songs and stories that have made Mr Keating a household name. He has sold more than 45 million records worldwide and holds a Guinness World Record for 30 consecutive UK Top 10 singles. His debut solo album, Ronan, went straight to No. 1 in the UK and achieved four-times platinum status, spending 63 weeks in the charts. Blue, known for their early 2000s hits and three consecutive UK No. 1 albums, continue to be regarded as one of the UK’s top pop acts. A spokesperson for Forestry England said: "Forestry England manage and care for the nation’s 1,500 woods and forests. "They use the money Forest Live raises to maintain these beautiful natural areas for everyone to enjoy, run important conservation projects and keep growing trees." Also performing on the night will be Australian pop trio Germein Sisters. Tickets go on general sale at 10am on Friday, September 25, via www.forestlive.com. Fans can sign up on the website for updates and exclusive pre-sale access.

metadata.title: 'Predator' raped woman in horrific late-night attack near filling station
metadata.contentSnippet: A "dangerous" predator who raped a woman in a late-night attack near the BP filling station on Lynn Road, in Wisbech, has been jailed.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Predator' raped woman in horrific late-night attack near filling station
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A "dangerous" predator who raped a woman in a late-night attack near a Cambridgeshire filling station has been jailed for seven years. Darius Andrulionis, 46, began speaking to the victim near the BP filling station, in Lynn Road, Wisbech, at around 3.45am on April 4. She had been on a night out with her sister, but the pair had become separated at the filling station. Andrulionis was part of a group that had stopped at the same location. Earlier, he had tried to dance with the victim at a nearby pub but she rejected his advances. Andrulionis approached the victim and sat on a wall next to her, near the filling station, before dragging her into nearby bushes. The victim begged him not to rape her, but he placed his hands on her mouth and neck to stop her from screaming, leaving the victim fearing for her life. She tried to reason with him, but he continued with the attack, and she only managed to get away once he had raped her. Police were called and Andrulionis was arrested the following day. On Tuesday (September 15), at Cambridge Crown Court, Andrulionis, of Balding Close, Wisbech, was jailed. He pleaded guilty to one count of rape before the case went to trial. He was also ordered to spend six years on extended licence, handed an indefinite restraining order against the victim. Andrulionis was placed on the sex offenders register for life and must pay a victim surcharge of £228. Sentencing, Judge Andrew Hurst described him as “dangerous”, that he was only “faintly familiar” with the concept of consent and a “substantial risk” to other women. DC Michael Childs, who investigated, said: "Andrulionis is a predator who preyed on a victim in a vulnerable state and the lengthy sentence handed down reflects this. "I would like to pay tribute to the victim; her bravery in coming forward and supporting us with a prosecution is admirable and has led to a dangerous man being jailed for a long time." metadata.title: Historic Gransden Show returns with livestock, vintage tractors and rural fun
metadata.contentSnippet: The Gransden Show is set to return for a day of countryside fun.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Historic Gransden Show returns with livestock, vintage tractors and rural fun
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Gransden Show returns for a day of countryside fun. The event will be held at the Show Field on Caxton Road, Great Gransden, on Saturday, September 26, celebrating farming and rural life. Organised by the Gransden and District Agricultural Society, the show dates back to 1891. Visitors can enjoy a range of agricultural show attractions The programme includes livestock and equestrian competitions, produce displays, homecraft and flower-arranging classes. Visitors can also see vintage tractors, exhibitors and attractions across the showground. The show brings farmers, rural businesses, competitors, exhibitors and the public together to celebrate countryside life. The annual event celebrates rural life and the local community Visitors of all ages can learn about farming, rural skills and traditions. The showground will be open from 9am to 5.30pm, with free parking available. Children under 11 accompanied by an adult can enter free. Online tickets cost £18 for adults and £9 for children aged 11 to 16. Tickets bought on the day cost £20 for adults and £10 for children aged 11 to 16. Livestock, equestrian and produce competitions will feature at the show The show is run by the Gransden and District Agricultural Society, a registered charity, with support from organisers, competitors, exhibitors, sponsors and volunteers. The Gransden Show brings traditional attractions, competitions, entertainment and community spirit to visitors from Cambridgeshire and beyond. The Gransden Show is supported by the Gransden and District Agricultural Society, a registered charity. The show has run every year since its establishment, apart from the war years between 1939 and 1945, when it was suspended.

metadata.title: The Cambs curry house named East Anglia finalist in top Asian restaurant awards
metadata.contentSnippet: A much-loved curry house in Cottenham, Cambridgeshire, is in the running for a top prize at this year’s Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA).

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The Cambs curry house named East Anglia finalist in top Asian restaurant awards
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A much-loved curry house in Cambridgeshire is in the running for a top prize at this year’s Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA). Cottenham’s Curry Palace is an East Anglia regional finalist in the awards, which celebrate the best of Pan-Asian cuisine across the UK. The awards, dubbed the “Oscars of the Curry Industry”, will be held on October 12, 2026, at the London Hilton on Park Lane. Curry Palace previously won the “Champion of Champions” title at the awards in 2018. Curry Palace in Cottenham has been named a regional finalist in the ARTA awards 2026. (Image: Google Maps/Street View) Mohammed Munim, founder member and CEO of ARTA, said: "Congratulations to every restaurant and takeaway named in the ARTA 2026 Regional Top 10. "Being shortlisted is a remarkable achievement and reflects the passion, resilience and dedication of the businesses shaping Asian hospitality across the UK. "At a time when rising employment costs, inflation and increasing overheads continue to challenge independent hospitality, Asian restaurants and takeaways remain vital to communities and the wider UK hospitality industry. "We look forward to welcoming our Regional Top 10 finalists to the Grand Finale on Monday 12 October 2026 at the London Hilton on Park Lane, where we will celebrate their achievements and crown this year’s national winners." More than 1,250 restaurants and takeaways were nominated by diners and food enthusiasts this year, many through ARTA partner ChefOnline, a platform connecting customers with Asian restaurants. Social-media activity and supporting data, including food hygiene ratings, also helped strengthen the nominations. Mr Kosru Miah founded Curry Palace in 1999 after entering the restaurant trade in 1992. His Bangladeshi upbringing and his mother’s cooking shaped his culinary style. He said he was proud to be nominated again, adding that it was his customers who have nominated the restaurant, which makes it all the more special. Mr Miah travelled the world to learn about spices and flavour combinations. He used that knowledge to create distinctive menus. The restaurant has built a loyal following and continues to grow with support from its customers and Mr Miah’s family. Curry Palace recently renovated and expanded to meet rising demand. Other East Anglia finalists are Jomidar Mahal in Littleport, Lalbagh Bangladeshi & Indian Diner in Bourn and Lowestoft Tandoori in Lowestoft. BBC journalist Samantha Simmonds and comedian Paul Sinha will host ARTA 2026. Leading restaurateurs, MPs, dignitaries and celebrities will gather to celebrate Asian cuisine. Regional winners will be announced at the ceremony, with one restaurant taking the national title. The nomination underlines Curry Palace’s standing in the region’s dining scene. The team hopes to add another trophy when the results are announced in October.

metadata.title: Family-run jewellers speaks out after second break-in in a year
metadata.contentSnippet: Chloe's Jewellers has spoken out after another break-in forced the business to close its March branch.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Family-run jewellers speaks out after second break-in in a year
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire jeweller has spoken out after another break-in forced the business to close one of its branches. Police were called to Chloe’s Jewellers in March on Wednesday, September 16, at 8.30am. The family-run business has opened branches across East Anglia during its 100-year history, including in St Ives, Wisbech and Royston. This marks the second break-in for the business within a year, after thousands of pounds worth of jewellery was stolen from the St Ives branch in April. Joe Ross, of Hawkins Road, Cambridge, was jailed for 16 months at Peterborough Crown Court on August 26 after admitting smashing into a shop and stealing £29,000 worth of jewellery. Chloe’s Jewellers said: "We want to inform our customers and local community that Chloe's Jewellers March branch will be temporarily closing its doors, due to another recent robbery, the second in less than a year. "Thankfully, we can reassure everyone that all customer belongings and jewellery left with us for repair are completely safe, secure and untouched. "Once we have more information about the future of our March branch, we will provide updates on our Facebook page and website. The March branch of Chloe's Jewellers suffered a break-in on September 16 "In the meantime, we are offering a cash reward for any information leading to the offender's arrest, you can get in touch with us at chloes.jewellery2014@gmail.com. "We’d like to thank you all for your continued support." The company’s Wisbech branch will handle customer repairs from March while the branch is closed. A police investigation is ongoing.

metadata.title: We visited new bakery with Indian street food that offers 'something different'
metadata.contentSnippet: The new SugaSpice Bakery & Kitchen, which offers freshly-made cakes and bakes with an Indian twist, has opened its doors on Moore's Walk in St Neots.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: We visited new bakery with Indian street food that offers 'something different'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A new bakery offering freshly made cakes and bakes with an Indian twist has opened its doors in St Neots - so I had to try it out. SugaSpice Bakery & Kitchen, on Moore's Walk just off the High Street opened its doors on August 8 and combines classic sweet treats with a little taste of India. Run by owner Raj Nandha and his wife, the bakery offers artisan cakes, freshly made doughnuts, and a hot counter with premium sausage rolls, pasties, and Indian snacks such as samosas and onion bhajis. They also have a takeaway service, with a menu featuring smash burgers and bold Indian street food like Samosa Chaat and Punjabi Paneer. Raj and his wife are both foodies, which was how the business was born. He said: "We both love food and sweet stuff. Raj Nandha and his wife are the brains behind SugaSpice (Image: Emily Stevens) "We have a history of that in our families as well so we decided to put our brains together and come up with SugaSpice Bakery and Kitchen. "My wife is the brains and the driving force behind the design and the cakes. "I kind of look after the kitchen, the recipes, the hot food and do a lot of the business management side of things." Raj told me that many of the recipes are from his mum, which he has adapted slightly for their customers. He said: "People can come in and try something traditional. "It's not your normal curry you would buy on the high street, it's very much what we would eat at home. SugaSpice Kitchen & Bakery has opened in St Neots (Image: Emily Stevens) "It's my mum's recipes which I've taken and enhanced slightly for the general public, so what I mean by that is they are not as spicy as what we would probably eat at home! "On the whole I think we have something different; I think it's something St Neots was looking for." It seems Raj is right about that. SugaSpice has more than 40 glowing Google reviews with countless five-star ratings and customers praising the friendliness of the staff. One visitor wrote: "Great little place, popped in for a sweet treat and greeted by lovely staff. SugaSpice combines sweet treats with Indian street food (Image: Emily Stevens) "A great addition to the high street!" Indeed, the welcoming staff was one of the first things I noticed when I paid SugaSpice a visit. The customers in front of me were chatting away to the server, who had recognised them as they had visited before. I decided to try one of their freshly-made doughnuts and went for the "cream & flake" filling, which did not disappoint. Cream and Flake doughnut (Image: Emily Stevens) Two great seaside snacks, a classic sugar doughnut and a 99 with a flake, merged into one was a match made in heaven! If you're just strolling down the High Street, it's easy to miss SugaSpice. But I would definitely recommend taking a look down Moore's Walk as they are well worth a visit.

metadata.title: Cambs campaign group renews calls for mesh compensation and healthcare transparency
metadata.contentSnippet: A Cambridgeshire-founded campaign group is urging the Government to take action on long-standing patient safety concerns.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs campaign group renews calls for mesh compensation and healthcare transparency
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire-founded campaign group is urging the Government to take action on long-standing patient safety concerns. Sling The Mesh has renewed calls for change on World Patient Safety Day, which was marked on September 17. The group is pushing for compensation and greater transparency following the First Do No Harm review, which exposed the harm caused by pelvic mesh and other treatments. Kath Sansom, founder of Sling The Mesh and a campaigner from March, said: "World Patient Safety Day is a moment to reflect on what happens when patients are not listened to, warning signs are ignored and vested interests are allowed to outweigh patient welfare. MP Sharon Hodgson with Kath (Image: Kath Sansom) "The greatest mistake would be to believe that the mesh scandal belongs to history. "It does not. If we fail to deliver accountability and transparency now, we create the conditions for the next patient safety scandal to emerge. "It may already be happening in plain sight." The group wants to see two key recommendations from the First Do No Harm review put into effect: compensation for women avoidably harmed by pelvic mesh, and ‘Sunshine legislation’ to improve transparency around industry payments in healthcare. They say these steps are vital to preventing future scandals and restoring public trust. Kath Sansom at Parliament (Image: Kath Sansom) Sharon Hodgson MP, co-chair of the First Do No Harm All Party Parliamentary Group, said: "The lack of progress sends a damaging message to patients that when healthcare systems fail, people can simply be left behind. "Women affected by the mesh and valproate scandals are still waiting for justice. "Those who suffered avoidable harm deserve accountability, proper support and fair redress. "Patient safety must be more than a slogan. "We must ensure that lessons are acted upon and that transparency and openness are placed at the heart of our healthcare system."

metadata.title: RSPCA seeks quiet home for loving Martha after 67 per cent rise in mass cat rescues
metadata.contentSnippet: The RSPCA’s Block Fen Animal Centre is seeking a new home for sweet, sensible Martha, rescued from a multi-cat household.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: RSPCA seeks quiet home for loving Martha after 67 per cent rise in mass cat rescues
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The RSPCA in Cambridgeshire is seeking a new home for sweet, sensible Martha, rescued from a multi-cat household. Martha has had a difficult start, but her loving personality still shines through. Three-year-old Martha is one of many cats at the RSPCA’s Block Fen Animal Centre seeking a loving forever home. A spokesperson for the centre said: “Martha is a loving and gentle girl who is looking for a quiet home where she can come out of her shell. “She can be a little cautious when meeting new people and may need a bit of time to settle into any new home. But once she feels comfortable, her loving personality really begins to shine. “Martha had previously lived in a household where cat flu was present. Due to this, she could be the only cat in the home. Martha could live with sensible secondary school-aged children depending on the introductions made at the centre.” Anyone who can offer Martha the right home can complete the RSPCA’s online application form. RSPCA centres are under mounting pressure as new figures show a 67 per cent rise in multi-cat rescues in one year. Figures released for the RSPCA’s Cruelty Hurts, Love Rescues campaign show it dealt with 1,752 mass-cat incidents last year, involving 10 or more cats in one property—almost five a day. That was a 67 per cent rise from 1,045 in 2024 and a 186 per cent increase from the 613 recorded in 2021. The charity said the incidents are placing unprecedented pressure on its resources in England and Wales. About 20,000 cats entered RSPCA care in 2025, and the charity fears that figure will be exceeded this year. Cat breeding peaks between May and September, bringing centres and branches unwanted kittens and pregnant mothers and putting further pressure on the charity’s limited space. Martha’s rehoming needs Martha needs access to the outdoors. Martha could live with secondary school-aged children. Martha would prefer to be the only pet in the home. Martha is quiet but full of love. The same centre has previously appealed for a home for a lurcher who spent 1,000 days in RSPCA care.

metadata.title: Metrion Biosciences staff take on 112-mile ride for Cambs youth charity
metadata.contentSnippet: Cyclists are taking on a 112-mile challenge to raise money for a youth charity which helps young people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough with mental health, housing and financial advice.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Metrion Biosciences staff take on 112-mile ride for Cambs youth charity
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Staff at a Cambridgeshire company are taking on a 112-mile cycling challenge to raise money for a youth charity. The team at Metrion Biosciences organised the event to support Centre 33, which helps young people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough with mental health, housing and financial advice. The ride began in Cambridge on Friday, September 11, and will take cyclists to all five of the charity’s support hubs, including those in Peterborough, Huntingdon, Ely and Wisbech. Gary Clark, director of ion channel screening at Metrion Biosciences, said: "We’re proud to support Centre 33 and the vital work it does for young people across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough. "Having a safe, non-judgemental place to turn to for support can make an enormous difference, and providing help early can strengthen wellbeing and prevent problems escalating to crisis. "Cycling 112 miles to pass every Centre 33 location felt like a fitting way to recognise the reach of the charity’s work. "It’s a real team effort for a cause that makes a meaningful difference in our local community." Centre 33’s drop-in hubs offer free support to 13-to-25-year-olds facing mental health challenges or practical problems such as financial, housing and employment issues. Last year, Centre 33 supported nearly 4,000 young people across Cambridgeshire; 70 per cent reported better mental health and 86 per cent made progress towards their personal goals. Harriet Millward, director of development at Centre 33, said: "The local need for young people’s support has been growing significantly, with long waits for mental health support and above-average numbers of young carers and people living homeless. "The team at Metrion Biosciences have been brilliant, and we’re incredibly thankful for all their efforts to raise much-needed funds for Centre 33." Centre 33 also received £500 from Hartford's annual King of the Beerfests charity festival in 2025.

Weekly Family Update –  10.07.26  
Please read, share, and encourage others to do the same.   
  
Headteacher’s Update: Keeping You Informed About What Matters Most 
Building Improvements Update 
The next phase of our school improvement programme will begin on Monday 13 July 2026 
and continue until September 2027. This work will include upgrades to the gym, changing 
rooms and student entrance areas. 
Student Arrival 
From September, the following arrangements will be in place: 
 Years 7 and 8: Enter through the green gate in the Maths Quad and go to year 
group areas. 
 Year 9: Go directly to the North Courts. 
 Year 10: Enter through the lower South Hall entrance. 
 The main student entrance will be closed. 
 Students should use the designated pathways and zebra crossings around the site. 
Please note the year group areas are not supervised by staff until 8.20am. 
Student departures at the end of the school day  
 Students whose final lesson is in Maths, Science, Creative Arts, Performing Arts or 
BITE will leave the site via the green gate in the Maths Quad. 
Thank you for your support and understanding as these important improvements take place. 
The completed works will further enhance our facilities for students. 
PE Lessons - next academic year 
Due to the building works, the school changing rooms will not be available during the 2026–
27 academic year. 

From 1 September 2026, students should come to school wearing their PE kit on any day they 
have a PE lesson.

you for your support and cooperation.

Thank you for your continued support throughout another successful year. We are proud of

Students will be taking their HuSH phone pouches home for the summer holidays. Please 
keep them safe over the break and ensure they are brought back ready for use at the start of 
the new school year. 
Safety First 
AI 
We are sharing an important online safety guide about how AI (Artificial Intelligence) can be 
used to change or misuse photos of children. While AI can be helpful, some people use it in 
harmful ways, including creating fake images from photos shared online. The guide explains 
the risks in simple terms and gives practical advice on how to: 
• Keep your child's photos safer online.  
• Check privacy settings on social media.

Morrisons Breakfast Club 
Morrisons and Kellogg’s have announced the return of their school holiday ‘Breakfast Clubs’, 
offering free meals to families across the UK to help ease the financial pressure over the 
summer holidays.  As schools close for the summer holidays, many parents face a financial 
pinch, with new research from Morrisons showing that more than half (54%) of parents feel 
the strain during the long summer period. In fact, week three of the school holidays is the 
critical tipping point where the financial impact is most acutely felt by households. 
Almost half (48%) of parents also confessed they have been forced to skip meals entirely just 
to make ends meet and ensure their child does not go without – with breakfast being the 
number one thing cut from the menu.  Families visiting their local Morrisons Café 
throughout the summer holidays can enjoy a free ‘Kellogg’s Breakfast’, which includes a 
bowl of cereal and a portion of fruit. The best part, it’s not just for kids, adults get to eat 
completely free too.  Both children and adults can choose from much-loved favourites Corn 
Flakes or Rice Krispies, topped with their choice of dairy or non-dairy milk and a free apple 
or banana.  The summer holiday offer will be available from 29th June to 6th September 
across all Morrisons Cafes nationwide.

cream as part of the attendance flash reward. 
• Remember:  As we approach the end of term, please ensure your child attends 
school every day and arrives on time to make the most of their learning. 
• How you can help: Please ensure sure your child leaves home with enough time. 
Every day in school makes a difference. Thank you for your support.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Police have made an arrest after a pedestrian was seriously injured in a crash involving three vehicles on the A1. Police were called to the collision at around 6pm on Thursday (September 17) on the A1 at Thornaugh near Peterborough. Emergency services attended and the pedestrian was taken to hospital with serious injuries, where they remain.
