metadata.title: Huntingdonshire Turkish restaurant staff accommodation plan refused by council
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdonshire District Council has refused a retrospective bid to turn part of a Turkish restaurant complex in St Ives into staff accommodation.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdonshire Turkish restaurant staff accommodation plan refused by council
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Huntingdonshire District Council has refused a retrospective bid to turn part of a Turkish restaurant complex in St Ives into staff accommodation. The application sought to turn a former storage building behind Vadi Kitchen, at 40 The Broadway, into a three-bedroom house in multiple occupation with a shared kitchen and bathroom. The accommodation had already been created and was being used as staff accommodation. Planning officers accepted residential use in St Ives town centre but recommended refusal over the building’s layout and poor living conditions. Planning officer Kevin Simpson said the scheme had a "contrived layout" that failed to provide an acceptable standard of living for future occupants. Officers said the shared kitchen had no natural light and doubled as the corridor to both bedrooms and the bathroom. Environmental Health officers warned that cooking facilities had been placed in the escape route. They feared residents could brush against hot pans or spill liquids while walking between the bedrooms and bathroom, risking burns and scalds. The council also warned that water from the bathroom could make the area near the cooking equipment slippery and force rescuers through an escape route containing cooking facilities. Planners also criticised the lack of communal living space, saying the three bedrooms were the only rooms residents could live in. Officers also raised concerns about the bedrooms facing directly on to George Yard. They said windows opening straight on to the pedestrian route could allow people to see inside and reduce residents’ privacy. Officers said revised plans failed to address the concerns. The report said the amendments made "very little change" and failed to resolve the fundamental issues raised by Environmental Health and planning officers. The council also refused the application because the applicant failed to agree to provide wheeled bins for the development. St Ives Town Council also objected, calling the scheme an overdevelopment and criticising the accommodation’s size, layout and location in Flood Zone 3. Despite those objections, officers found the scheme acceptable on flood risk, heritage, parking and highway safety. But they concluded the scheme breached local and national planning rules on living conditions and should be refused. Huntingdonshire District Council formally refused planning permission on September 16. In May, Vadi Kitchen operator Bora Demir also applied to vary the restaurant's premises licence to allow alcohol sales for consumption on site.

metadata.title: Care home manager defrauded residents out of £32k in 'breach of trust'
metadata.contentSnippet: A fraudster has avoided prison after scamming a supported living complex on Gaul Road, in March, out of £32,000.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Care home manager defrauded residents out of £32k in 'breach of trust'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A former manager at a supported living complex in Cambridgeshire who defrauded residents out of tens of thousands of pounds has avoided prison. Abigail Smith, of Hazelnut Close, in March, pleaded guilty to fraud by abuse of position at a hearing on April 9. The offence involved more than £32,000 and, according to court listings, occurred on January 28, 2019. Smith worked as service manager at Broad Oaks, on Gaul Road, in March, which is run by the learning disability charity Mencap. On August 26 at Cambridge Crown Court, the 38-year-old was sentenced to two years and eight months in prison, suspended for three years. A spokesperson for Mencap confirmed the charity had "reimbursed the people who were victims of this crime." "We remain hopeful that the stolen funds can be recovered so that they can be used to help change the lives of people with a learning disability," they said. "The actions of this individual were a serious breach of trust and go completely against our values. "We responded immediately when concerns were raised, dismissing the staff member and fully supporting the police investigation. "We have also been supporting those affected and helping them come to terms with what happened. "We welcome the outcome of the case. The safety, wellbeing and rights of the people we support remain our absolute priority." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An investigation launched after a woman was sexually assaulted in a Huntingdonshire village remains ongoing after three weeks. Police were called at around 10.30pm on August 27 with reports of a sexual assault on a woman an hour earlier on Mill Lane in Little Paxton. Cambridgeshire Constabulary confirmed patrols had been ramped up in the area but that no arrests have been made. In an update on Thursday (September 17), the force revealed still no arrests have been made and that an investigation is ongoing. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An investigation continues more than a week after a teenage boy was found on the tracks at a busy railway station. It comes after emergency services were called to reports of trespassers on the tracks between Peterborough and Stevenage. The British Transport Police revealed the boy was found at St Neots Railway Station at around 6.30pm on (September 8). A spokesperson said: "Officers attended and a teenage boy was located and taken to a place of safety." In an update on Thursday (September 17), the force confirmed officers continue to make enquiries to "understand the circumstances of this incident". The incident caused delays to a number of routes between Peterborough and London, including Hull Trains, LNER, Lumo, Thameslink and Great Northern services. Have you got a story you want to share? metadata.title: Major hotel brand adds Cambs to UK portfolio in 10-site deal
metadata.contentSnippet: Hilton has added Peterborough’s Milestone Hotel to its portfolio in a deal signed this week.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Major hotel brand adds Cambs to UK portfolio in 10-site deal
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A major hotel brand has added a Peterborough hotel to its brand in a deal agreed this week. The 99-room Spark by Hilton Peterborough Norman Cross will open just off the A1(M), one of 10 new sites covered by a deal between Hilton and AG Hotels Group. The other sites are in Cardiff, Coventry, Derby, Doncaster, Hull, Runcorn, Sunderland, Wakefield and Washington. Hilton says the Milestone Hotel at Norman Cross will serve the area’s growing logistics sector, visitors to Peterborough’s historic attractions and people attending events. Paul Blackmore, vice president of development, UK and Ireland at Hilton, said: "These signings underline the strength of demand for Spark by Hilton that we are seeing from owners across the UK. "With nearly 700 rooms in the pipeline, including the brand's first hotel in Wales, Spark continues to gain momentum as owners recognise the strength of its value proposition and its ability to meet the needs of today's travellers." AG Hotels Group owns and runs hotels across the UK. Girish Grover, founder and CEO of AG Hotels Group, said: "We are delighted to partner with Hilton to expand Spark by Hilton across the UK. "This landmark agreement is closely aligned with AG Hotels Group’s mission to create happy, thriving places nationwide and represents an important step in the next phase of our growth. "Our strategy is to build a scaled, high-quality hospitality platform by acquiring, repositioning and investing in well-located hotels across the UK, combining strong operational capability with leading global brands." The new hotels are due to open between late 2026 and 2028. The Hilton group also has its Hilton Garden Inn branding on a new 160-bedroom hotel currently under construction at Fletton Quays. Spark by Hilton allows existing hotels to be rebranded and repositioned under the Hilton name. Owners can then use Hilton’s global commercial platform and Hilton Honors loyalty programme. Launched in 2023, Spark by Hilton has expanded across Europe and the Middle East, with sites recently announced in Italy, Spain and Saudi Arabia. The brand currently has more than 275 open hotels worldwide and more than 200 in development. The 160-room Hilton Garden Inn was sold to Leisure & Co Hotel Ltd and is expected to open at Fletton Quays in summer 2027.

metadata.title: Gamlingay care home seeks 100 birthday cards for resident Dorothy Hinton
metadata.contentSnippet: A Gamlingay care home is asking for birthday cards for a resident turning 100.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Gamlingay care home seeks 100 birthday cards for resident Dorothy Hinton
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Gamlingay care home is asking for birthday cards for a resident turning 100. Potton View care home on Potton Road is asking people to send birthday cards to Dorothy Hinton, who turns 100 on October 11. Dorothy has lived in the area all her life, having been born in nearby Croydon on October 11, 1926. She started work in Hatley St George at 14 before becoming a hairdresser. Dorothy Hinton She married William “Bill” Hinton and had two daughters, Christine and Yvonne, two grandchildren, Lucy and Catherine, and two great-grandchildren, Anna and William. During the Second World War, Dorothy supported the war effort by writing to soldiers and knitting them socks. A keen cyclist, she often rode between villages to visit family and get to work. She also cycled regularly to RAF Tempsford to help at the NAAFI (Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes) canteen, a social hub for the base. After moving to Gamlingay in 1962, Dorothy threw herself into community life. At St Mary's Church, she taught Sunday School, helped launch a coffee morning, formed a fundraising sewing group and ran a marmalade stall. She even dressed as a St Trinian's schoolgirl on a gala float. Dorothy enjoying Elvis Dorothy's husband died in 2000, and she moved into Potton View in October 2024. Her family says Dorothy’s sense of humour remains intact and credits laughter as one key to her long life. Dorothy will celebrate her milestone birthday at the home with family, friends and fellow residents. People are invited to send cards and well wishes to Dorothy Hinton, c/o Potton View care home, Potton Road, Gamlingay, SG19 3LW. Potton View previously received nearly 200 cards for resident Joan Cosson's 100th birthday, including messages from Florida.

metadata.title: Huntingdon pupils raise funds to transform unused school grounds into sensory garden
metadata.contentSnippet: Huntingdon pupils are raising funds to build a sensory garden.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon pupils raise funds to transform unused school grounds into sensory garden
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Huntingdon pupils are raising funds to build a sensory garden. The 12-member gardening club at Stukeley Meadows Primary School is leading the project to transform an unused area of the grounds. Helen Billany, who is helping the children, said the project would give pupils practical lessons in gardening. "Most importantly, the children will be involved in creating and caring for it," she said. "They will learn practical gardening skills, responsibility and teamwork..." The sensory garden will feature colours, scents and textures for everyone to enjoy. More than £340 has been raised towards the £700 target. The money will pay for plants, soil, landscaping materials and seating. Helen said the garden would be for all pupils to enjoy. "Our gardening club is made up of 12 enthusiastic pupils and an adult volunteer, who meet together to learn about gardening, nature and the environment," she explained. "We now have an exciting project in mind: transforming an unused area of the school grounds into a beautiful, welcoming sensory garden that can be enjoyed by pupils across the school." "The garden will provide a space where children can explore, discover, grow and connect with nature." The garden will include welcoming areas where children can sit and relax. The club is also asking local businesses and community members for support. Helen said: "We would also love to involve local businesses and members of our wider community who may be able to donate materials, plants, soil or their time." The school hopes the garden will give all pupils a place to learn, explore and enjoy nature. Visit the fundraiser page to support the project or donate. A nearby sensory garden at Samuel Pepys School in St Neots was completed in April 2026 with £30,000 in grant funding.

metadata.title: Huntingdon Boat Club win races at Cambridge Autumn regatta
metadata.contentSnippet: Racing over a distance of 550 metres, Huntingdon Boat Club came away with an impressive six wins at the recent Cambridge 99 Autumn Regatta.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Huntingdon Boat Club win races at Cambridge Autumn regatta
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Racing over a distance of 550 metres, Huntingdon Boat Club came away with an impressive six wins, as well as securing the Victor Ludorum award for the most successful club on the day, at the recent Cambridge 99 Autumn Regatta. Finn Walsh got the club off to a winning start in the Junior 15 single sculls, progressing through to the final. Racing up a year, Finn pulled away from his opponent to take a convincing victory over Cantabrigian. Daniel Grant and Edward Adams also progressed to the final of the Open Double Sculls, where they faced a crew from 1st & 3rd Trinity. Huntingdon Boat Club crews competed at Cambridge Autumn Regatta (Image: Huntingdon Boat Club) The pair raced strongly to secure a comfortable victory. Grant then teamed up with Tom Hancock, Oli Burgess and Jack Bennett to compete in the Junior 18 coxless quads. In a straight final against Bedford Star Club, the crew took another win for the club. Adams continued his successful day by winning the Masters B/C single sculls against Peterborough. James Johnston-Keay and Seth Dovey progressed to the final of the Junior 17 Double Sculls against Sudbury. Racing up a year, the boys had already beaten Broxbourne in the quarter-final and West Norfolk in the semi-final before reaching the final. They went on to win against Sudbury. Rebecca Howard and Bianca Alvarez won their semi-final in the Women’s Open Double Sculls, racing another Huntingdon crew made up of Louise Hinkley and Holly Seabrook. In the final, Howard and Alvarez faced Rob Roy and produced another strong performance, winning by two lengths. Making their racing debut, Beau Jeffery and James Wilkin competed in the Junior 16 Double Sculls. Rowers secured multiple victories at the Cambridge event (Image: Huntingdon Boat Club) The pair defeated Leicester in the semi-final to progress to the final, where they narrowly missed out on victory to Broxbourne. Hannah Hooson was also racing for the first time, partnering Jasmine Yallop in the Women’s Junior Double Sculls. The girls faced Leicester in their semi-final before progressing to the final, where Globe took the win. Also competing on the day were Callum Sutton and Will Manchett in the Open Double Sculls, while Fiona Richardson and Isabella Dovey both raced in the Women’s Single Sculls.

metadata.title: Bull, Clark and Keys-Batson win at Grafham amid 20 capsizes and two mast failures
metadata.contentSnippet: Daniel Bull, Nathan Clark and Will Keys-Batson won their fleets at the UKLA East ILCA Grand Prix at Grafham Water Sailing Club.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Bull, Clark and Keys-Batson win at Grafham amid 20 capsizes and two mast failures
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Daniel Bull, Nathan Clark and Will Keys-Batson won their fleets at the UKLA East ILCA Grand Prix at Grafham Water Sailing Club. The event drew 38 entrants, with strong winds bringing three races and frequent capsizes. South-westerly winds reached 12 knots, with gusts up to 27 knots beneath broken cloud and sunny spells. Several sailors changed down a rig size before launching to stay in control. John Elder was second in the ILCA7 fleet at the UKLA East ILCA Grand Prix at Grafham Water Sailing Club Race officials staged three consecutive races on a trapezoid course. The first race lasted three laps, but officials cut the final two to two laps because of the wind. Will Keys-Batson of NBYC/WOBYC won all three ILCA 4 races to take the class title with 2.0 net points. He also won the overall handicap title, while Isobelle Johnson of WOBYC finished second on 4.0 points and Ella Bonnett of Orford Sailing Club third on 5.0. Nathan Clark of WOBYC won all three races in the 22-boat ILCA 6 fleet to finish first overall on 2.0 net points. Kieran Vanhoutte of Ely Sailing Club was third on 5.0, with local sailor William Swann fourth on 8.0. UKLA East ILCA Grand Prix at Grafham Water Sailing Club- Daniel Bull of Rollesby Broad Sailing Club won the ILCA 7 fleet with 2.0 net points after recovering from seventh in the first race to win the next two. Grafham sailor John Elder won the tie-break for second on 4.0 points ahead of clubmate David Gale, who also scored 4.0; Marcellus Pryor was fourth on 7.0. The gusts snapped two masts, while one competitor endured at least 20 capsizes before finishing. Competitors thanked the race officer, safety-boat crews and shore volunteers for handling the difficult conditions. Grafham Water Sailing Club invited ILCA sailors to its winter series, held every Sunday from November to March. Grafham Water Sailing Club, established in 1966 alongside the creation of Grafham Water reservoir, is also an RYA-recognised training centre.

metadata.title: Charity offers free training to break workplace barriers for neurodivergent staff
metadata.contentSnippet: A Cambridgeshire charity is offering businesses free training on supporting neurodivergent employees.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Charity offers free training to break workplace barriers for neurodivergent staff
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A Cambridgeshire charity is offering businesses free training on supporting neurodivergent employees. Red2Green will host the online session on Thursday, September 24, to help organisations identify and remove hidden workplace barriers. The session will examine how communication, workplace environments and established practices can affect neurodivergent staff. Liz Taylor, chief executive of Red2Green and neurodivergent herself, said: "Many workplace barriers are not created deliberately. "They are often found in the everyday things organisations have always done. "Small, thoughtful changes can make a significant difference. "They can help neurodivergent employees feel more confident and remain in work, while often making the workplace better for everyone." The charity’s Encompass programme turns awareness of neurodiversity into practical workplace change. It promotes changes that support autistic people and those with learning disabilities. Government research shows that only around three in ten working-age autistic people have jobs. That compares with five in ten disabled people and eight in ten non-disabled people. Liz said: "We are proud that Encompass has been developed by a local charity, based on our experience of supporting autistic people and those with learning disabilities. "We understand the barriers employees can face, but we also see the skills and potential that organisations can miss when their workplaces are not designed inclusively. "This free session is an opportunity for local organisations to begin looking at their own practices and identify changes they can make." Red2Green has supported autistic people and people with learning disabilities across Cambridgeshire for more than 25 years. The training is free, but places must be booked in advance. Register at https://fundraising.red2green.org/event/encompass-free-taster-training-session. Inclusive workplace policies should allow employees to discuss health needs openly and make reasonable adjustments where required, helping create a more supportive working environment.

metadata.title: Godmanchester Town Show attracts more than 400 entries as artwork takes top honour
metadata.contentSnippet: The Godmanchester Town Show attracted more than 400 entries this year.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Godmanchester Town Show attracts more than 400 entries as artwork takes top honour
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The Godmanchester Town Show attracted more than 400 entries this year. The annual show, held at the Community Plant Nursery on September 5, celebrated Godmanchester’s talent, creativity and community spirit. Sunny weather drew visitors to the show, which featured a wide range of judged categories. Categories included flowers, home-grown fruit and vegetables, cookery, handicrafts, children's classes, photography, and artwork. More than 400 entries were submitted across show categories (Image: Godmanchester Town Show) The mayor chose Margaret Greenhalgh’s artwork as Best in Show. Alexandra White won the flowers category, Kingsley Lawrence won fruit and vegetables, and Paula Williams took Floral Display. Sarah Jones won cookery, Jonathan Strong won jams and preserves, and Jill Sapsed won Handicraft. Simon Hailstone won photography, Ariadne Vane won the children’s section and Margaret Greenhalgh also won the art category. Caydence Wilson won the under-16 art section. The HuMS Big Band and Harmonia Singers provided live music throughout the afternoon, helping create a lively atmosphere. Stalls sold local crafts and other products, while children enjoyed games and activities. The miniature train carried passengers on more than 100 rides. Awards were presented to winners at the community event (Image: Godmanchester Town Show) Organisers thanked everyone who helped stage the event, including sponsors The College of Animal Welfare, The Godmanchester Co-op and Dura-ID Solutions. Organisers also thanked the Community Nursery for hosting the event. Organisers also thanked the raffle donors, programme sponsors and cup sponsors for their generous support. In a statement, the Town Show Committee said: "Above all, the Town Show Committee would like to thank the people of Godmanchester for turning out in such wonderful numbers and supporting the event. "Their enthusiasm, participation and community spirit ensured that the Godmanchester Town Show was once again a fantastic celebration of everything that makes the town such a special place." As the show drew to a close, raffle prizes were distributed and show cups were awarded to winners.

metadata.title: Hunts MP's rescue dog wins public vote at Westminster Dog of the Year competition
metadata.contentSnippet: A rescue dog owned by the MP for Huntingdon has captured the public’s heart in the 2026 Westminster Dog of the Year competition.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hunts MP's rescue dog wins public vote at Westminster Dog of the Year competition
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rescue dog owned by the MP for Huntingdon has captured the public’s heart in a national competition. Leto, a five-year-old mixed breed owned by Ben Obese-Jecty, won the "Sir David Amess Pawblic Vote" at the 2026 Westminster Dog of the Year competition, held on September 10. The win was announced following a strong social media campaign. Ben Obese-Jecty competes with Leto, mixed breed at the Westminster Dog of the Year competition, organised by Dogs Trust and The Royal Kennel Club, outside the Houses of Parliament, London. Picture date: Thursday September 10, 2026. PA Photo. The (Image: Doug Peters/PA Media Assignments) Mr Obese-Jecty said: "Absolutely wonderful to receive the public vote today, it means a lot. "It’s lovely to think that Leto has captured everyone’s imagination with her back story. "Fantastic to see how the public are really engaged in these stories of how we can adopt and rescue dogs who otherwise wouldn’t get this same chance at life." The competition, organised by The Royal Kennel Club and Dogs Trust, took place in Victoria Tower Gardens and featured 14 dogs. It aims to promote responsible dog ownership and raise awareness of key welfare issues. Leto, who was rescued as a puppy, has been with Mr Obese-Jecty for five years. Jannine Edgar, chief executive of The Royal Kennel Club, said: "Many congratulations to Ben Obese-Jecty and Leto for winning the hearts of the public and taking victory in the Sir David Amess Public Vote. "The bond between the pair has been so clear to see throughout the day, and it is wonderful to see them recognised by the public." The competition honours the late Sir David Amess MP, a long-time supporter of the event and a passionate advocate for animal welfare.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A 14-year-old has been charged with grievous bodily harm after another boy suffered a knife injury near a Cambridgeshire school. Emergency services were called to Orton Goldhay, Peterborough, at around 4pm on Monday, September 14, after reports that a 14-year-old boy had suffered a knife injury. Police put a cordon around playing fields beside Ormiston Bushfield Academy. Officers and paramedics attended before taking the injured boy to Peterborough City Hospital. Police confirmed on September 16 that the boy remains in hospital with serious but not life-threatening injuries. Two 14-year-old boys from Peterborough were arrested in connection with the incident. One boy has been charged with grievous bodily harm with intent, theft and possessing a knife in public. He is due to appear at Peterborough Magistrates Court today. The other 14-year-old boy, who was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm and assisting an offender, has been released on bail until December 14. Ormiston Bushfield Academy spoke out following the incident. A spokesperson for the school said: "The safety and wellbeing of our entire school community is always our top priority and as soon as we became aware of this matter we took immediate action in line with our safeguarding processes and procedures. "We are also working with the authorities and providing support to any students, staff and families, as appropriate. "As an investigation is now underway, we are not able to comment further at this stage."

metadata.title: Cambridgeshire Search and Rescue celebrates 20 years supporting emergency services
metadata.contentSnippet: Cambridgeshire Search and Rescue volunteers have celebrated 20 years of supporting emergency services.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire Search and Rescue celebrates 20 years supporting emergency services
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire Search and Rescue volunteers have celebrated 20 years of supporting emergency services. Cambridgeshire Search and Rescue marked its 20th anniversary with an open day in Ely, attended by assistant chief constable Leighton Hammett, volunteers, supporters, and partner agencies. Visitors saw the team’s specialist skills in action, including water searches, search dogs, medical support bikes and drones. Mr Hammett said: "On behalf of Cambridgeshire Constabulary, I would like to express our sincere gratitude for the extraordinary commitment, professionalism and compassion shown by your volunteers over the past two decades. "Your willingness to give your time freely, often at short notice and in challenging conditions, to help locate missing and vulnerable people provides invaluable support to policing and brings comfort and hope to families during some of the most difficult moments of their lives." The volunteer-led charity works with police and other emergency services to find high-risk missing people and provide specialist support across Cambridgeshire. Trained volunteers and specialist technology support emergency operations across Cambridgeshire. Cambridgeshire Search and Rescue was founded in 2006 after a high-profile missing-person case in the county highlighted the need for a dedicated search team. Its trained volunteers are available to respond around the clock, every day of the year, to callouts involving missing children, people living with dementia and those at risk of harming themselves. The charity is one of 35 Lowland Rescue member teams and provides nationally recognised, licensed search technician training for its volunteers.

metadata.title: Disgraced ex-Cambs police sergeant jailed over 'toxic' Whatsapp culture
metadata.contentSnippet: Disgraced former Cambridgeshire Police officer Paul Street who created a “toxic” WhatsApp culture has been jailed for four years at the Old Bailey.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Disgraced ex-Cambs police sergeant jailed over 'toxic' Whatsapp culture
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A disgraced former Cambridgeshire Police officer who created a “toxic” WhatsApp culture has been jailed for four years after asking for a female suspect’s sex video. Ex-Cambridgeshire Constabulary police sergeant Paul Street, 41, engaged in “salacious gossip” with former PC Josh Williams after he found intimate pictures and footage on the woman’s personal phone. On Wednesday, the woman told of her “overwhelming sense of shock, violation, anger and humiliation”. Street also encouraged colleagues to “bully” a teenage detainee in WhatsApp messages. Following an Old Bailey trial in June, Street, of Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office. He admitted two offences of unlawful disclosure of personal data relating to confidential information and screenshots he sent to his partner in 2020. In a televised sentencing at the Old Bailey, Street was jailed for four years. Williams, 38, also of Huntingdon, who had pleaded guilty to misconduct in public office, was handed 16 months in prison and waved to family in the public gallery as he was sent down. Judge Mark Lucraft KC said: “The public should expect to be able to trust police officers to act fairly in the execution of their powers to prevent, detect and solve crime – anything less does great harm to the public faith in police forces and individual police officers. “The public expects, and rightly so, the highest of standards from police officers. I am sure there will be many thousands of officers in police forces in this country and abroad utterly horrified by your actions and by the attitude you have each displayed here. It is both appalling and inexplicable.” The judge noted the “collateral impact” of Street’s offending with 67 cases he was connected with – or via the contents of his phone – being discontinued and a further 14 under review. Street found fame in television crime shows on the BBC and Channel 4 and was known for getting “impressive results” through his “robust” style. However, anti-corruption officers began investigating him and uncovered his two WhatsApp groups in 2021 after a new police officer reported him. The offences were committed while working at Cambridgeshire Constabulary leading a unit at Cambourne police station, mainly dealing with county lines drug supply and organised crime. During the trial, prosecutor Anne Whyte KC had described how Street created a “toxic culture” which led to investigations into 11 other officers. After a junior officer raised concern about WhatsApp use, Street messaged colleagues: “Just a shame we have snakes as we are all such good mates.” In April 2020, Street called on his team to “bully” 17-year-old detainee Robiul Islam, encouraging them to “please hit him” and “smash his head in”. In the autumn of 2020, Williams was tasked with examining the phone of a female suspect he told Street was “quite fit”. Street asked him if there were “any nudes”, and Williams replied there was a video of the woman committing a sexual act. Williams went on to send Street a photo from the woman’s phone depicting her in underwear. The following year, Street asked on WhatsApp if Williams still had the intimate private video because he wanted to show it to “the lads from footy”. Williams responded that he doubted he still had it and there was no evidence the video was shared. Reading her victim personal statement in court, the woman said: “The photographs and videos on my phone were deeply private and intimate. “They were never intended to be viewed or shared by anyone without my consent. Learning that people in positions of authority deliberately accessed and circulated these images has left me feeling exposed, degraded and powerless. “Something that was entirely personal to me was taken and treated as if it had no value or dignity. “Members of the public are taught to trust the police and believe that officers will act with integrity and respect for the law. “In my case these individuals entrusted to safeguard my property and uphold the law abused their position in order to invade my privacy in an extremely personal and humiliating way. “I feel violated by these individuals who were in a position of power over me at the time. The abuse of that power has and continues to make this experience particularly difficult to come to terms with.” Mitigating, Jennifer Dempster KC said Street “enormously regrets his behaviour”. Father-of-two Street made a significant contribution to disrupting the drug trade before his 17-year career came to a “crashing end”, she said. Ms Dempster said: “He recognises he has not only let the public down, he has let the police down and he has let his family down.” For Williams, Robert Morris said: “He recognises what he did was deeply inappropriate, driven by misguided and stupid desire to engage in salacious gossip.” Eleven other officers were investigated over their conduct arising from the culture Street had fostered. Of those, two resigned, one was dismissed for gross misconduct, one received a final warning, two received written warnings, and five others were dealt with for low-level performance issues. Senior specialist prosecutor Lisa Rose, from the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “This case exposed a sustained pattern of unacceptable conduct by a police officer who abused his position of trust. “Police officers are entrusted with significant powers and are expected to uphold the highest standards at all times. “Members of the public should have confidence that any personal material obtained during an investigation will be handled lawfully and appropriately. “The actions of Paul Street and Joshua Williams represented a serious breach of that trust.” Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) director of engagement Emily Barry said: “Paul Street’s behaviour was appalling and a complete abuse of his position as a police officer. “He fostered a toxic culture in his team and instead of leading by example, he encouraged others to join in exchanging inappropriate messages – creating an environment that junior officers would find very difficult to challenge. “However, this investigation shows that officers must be courageous and call out this sort of behaviour and forces must make sure that they support and protect those that do report. The officer who reported Street should be acknowledged for standing up for what is right. “The public would also be shocked at knowing officers shared intimate photos from a woman’s phone without any policing purpose and that Street made a video threatening a child who was detained in custody.”

metadata.title: Go potty for major celebration of ceramics at Melton Mowbray Potfest
metadata.contentSnippet: Potfest will return to Melton Mowbray Market and Livestock Auction, LE13 1JY from October 30, 31 and November 1

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Go potty for major celebration of ceramics at Melton Mowbray Potfest
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Brought to you by POTFEST Potfest will return to Melton Mowbray Market and Livestock Auction, LE13 1JY from October 30, 31 and November 1 Operating under the same ethos as the Cumbrian Potfest in the Pens events, 90 ceramics artists will congregate for a three-day artisan market in the heart of  Melton Mowbray - just in time for your Christmas shopping. See the work of the well-established alongside the up-and-coming, in an exciting mix of the sophisticated and the raw power of the next generation, combined in a bustling arts market marketplace. . (Image: Potfest) No art hype, no gallery glitz, just potters and public mixing in a down-to-earth setting. Held under cover to save everyone from the weather. From the South Coast of England to the centre of Scotland There are now ten Potfest events distributed through the year from April to November. Spanning the country from the south coast near Brighton, to Perth in Scotland, each show features the work of between 90 -110 potters who exhibit and sell their handmade ceramics. Potfest is a fantastic day out – a popular event among ceramic enthusiasts, collectors, and members of the general public who are interested in pottery and ceramics. In addition to the exhibits, visitors have the chance to meet and talk with the artists themselves, and at the spring Penrith event there are also demonstrations, talks, and workshops by renowned potters and ceramicists. . (Image: Potfest) “It’s very much a boom time for ceramics at the moment,” said organiser Matt Cox. “Post pandemic all of the shows in the last couple of years have absolutely exploded. I don’t know if that is partly to do with people becoming a little bit more craft focused over the pandemic or whether The Great Pottery Throwdown on TV has had an influence.” During the pandemic, Potfest was one of the few arts festivals able to continue, as it was classed as an outdoor event because the sides of the marquees are kept open. “The idea is that we hold the shows in beautiful places so it would seem an absolute waste to hold a show with such fantastic vistas but then put it inside a tent so you can’t see any of the surroundings,” said Matt. “We always open the sides of the tents up, which meant that during the pandemic they were judged to be outdoor events and we were able to run all the way through." . (Image: Potfest) POTTERS’ COMPETITION At each of the Potfest shows, the potters are invited to enter a piece of their work that responds to a theme. The theme for the potters’ competition at all of the 2026 Potfest events will be 'Famous quotes and sayings'. . (Image: Potfest) Vote for your favourite on the day for a chance to win a free entry to all of the Potfest events for life with a Potfest Passport. Potfest admission tickets will also be available to buy at the gate each day.

metadata.title: Winter Fuel Payment recipients soar by 9.6 million after major Government U-turn
metadata.contentSnippet: Winter Fuel Payment recipients soared by 9.6 million to 10.9 million in England and Wales last winter after the Government widened eligibility.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Winter Fuel Payment recipients soar by 9.6 million after major Government U-turn
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The number of pensioners receiving the Winter Fuel Payment has soared by 9.6 million in just one year, new figures reveal, after the Government dramatically widened eligibility for the cash. Some 10.9 million people in England and Wales received the payment in winter 2025 to 2026, according to new Department for Work and Pensions statistics. That is a huge increase from the 1.3 million who received the payment in the previous winter. The latest figure is also around 290,000 higher than the 10.6 million recipients recorded in winter 2023 to 2024, when the payment was universal for most pensioners. The dramatic rise follows a major change to the rules. In winter 2024 to 2025, the Government restricted the Winter Fuel Payment to pensioners receiving certain means-tested benefits. But for winter 2025 to 2026, most pensioners living in England and Wales once again became eligible, provided they met the qualifying criteria. Those born on or before September 21, 1959 were eligible, although pensioners with income above £35,000 had their payment recovered by HMRC through the tax system. The DWP figures do not include subsequent HMRC recoveries and exclude pensioners who opted out of receiving the payment before it was made. The number of beneficiaries was even higher once eligible pension-age partners were taken into account. There were 11 million Winter Fuel Payment beneficiaries in winter 2025 to 2026. The payment was worth between £100 and £300, depending on the recipient's circumstances. Of all recipients: The majority of recipients were under 80, with 7.7 million people – 70 per cent – falling into this age group. Despite the much wider eligibility, 53,000 pensioners opted out of receiving their Winter Fuel Payment last winter. The Government's income-based recovery system also meant that some higher-income pensioners could receive the payment before HMRC reclaimed it. An HMRC impact assessment estimated that 2.2 million pensioners, including those in Northern Ireland, would be affected by these recoveries. The DWP said its latest statistics only cover payments made by the department and do not include money subsequently recovered by HMRC. The new figures also reveal a stark regional breakdown. North Yorkshire had the highest number of Winter Fuel Payment recipients, with 150,000, followed by Birmingham and Cornwall, both with around 140,000. At the other end of the scale, the Isles of Scilly had just 500 recipients, followed by the City of London with 1,200 and Rutland with 10,100. Recommended reading: The figures cover people living in England and Wales. Winter Fuel Payment has now been devolved to Scotland, which operates its own Winter Heating Benefit. The Winter Fuel Payment was introduced in 1997 to help pension-age people with their heating bills. It is an annual tax-free payment designed to help with the cost of heating a home during the winter. The latest figures provide the clearest indication yet of the scale of the Government's decision to reverse the sharp restriction in eligibility introduced the previous year.

metadata.title: New petition calls on council to cancel car park regeneration plans
metadata.contentSnippet: A new petition addressed to Huntingdonshire District Council calls for car-park regeneration plans to be scrapped.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New petition calls on council to cancel car park regeneration plans
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A new petition calls for Huntingdonshire's car-park regeneration plans to be scrapped. The proposals by property developer Capital & Centric involve the redevelopment of council-owned car parks in St Ives, Huntingdon and St Neots. At a full council meeting on September 9, councillors unanimously backed a motion to examine spending on the project. No planning application has been submitted, yet more than £1 million has already been spent on consultation. David Keane, district councillor for Hemingford Grey & Houghton, launched the petition to end the regeneration plans. He said: "We further ask Cabinet to confirm that these Council-owned sites will not be progressed for redevelopment under the current Capital & Centric programme, and that any future proposals for their use should only be considered through a new transparent process supported by a clear business case and meaningful engagement with residents, businesses and other affected stakeholders." Cllr Alex Bulat, district councillor for St Ives South, also backs the petition. Cllr Keane said the same request was being submitted through Huntingdonshire District Council’s official petition process, which can take 90 days. Cllr Keane said: "If HDC accepts and opens the official petition, we will publish the link and encourage supporters to sign that petition too." Earlier consultation plans included turning Princes Street Car Park and Huntingdon Bus Station into a housing development in Huntingdon. The proposals have also previously led Green councillors to leave the Liberal Democrat-led coalition on Huntingdonshire District Council, citing the council's handling of the regeneration plans.

metadata.title: St Neots prostate screening event could set world record with 122 men tested
metadata.contentSnippet: A prostate cancer awareness event in St Neots could set a new world record for the most men tested in a single day.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots prostate screening event could set world record with 122 men tested
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A prostate cancer awareness event in St Neots could set a new world record for the most men tested in a single day. The event, held at Eaton Socon Health Centre, saw 122 men screened by a team from North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust, led by surgeon Jyoti Shah MBE. Miss Shah said: "Prostate cancer is a silent killer, but it is a cancer that we can cure if we pick it up early enough. "It is the most common cancer in men in the UK, with one in eight being diagnosed at some point in their lives – and for men of Afro-Caribbean heritage, the risk is one in four." PSA blood tests were provided during the community event (Image: NHS) Campaigner Dave Young and the St Neots Prostate Cancer Support Group organised the event with support from Purple Horizons, attracting around 100 men. An application has been submitted to Guinness World Records to verify the achievement. Miss Shah praised Mr Young and the team for their efforts. She said: "The campaign was an enormous success and huge kudos to Dave Young and Purple Horizons for organising such a well-attended event. "I am so very proud of and grateful to my team for their dedication and giving their time to support this important community event – and to our Hospitals’ Charity for meeting the cost of the PSA tests." The PSA blood tests, funded by the North West Anglia Hospitals' Charity, typically cost £3.50 each. The awareness campaign was held at Eaton Socon Health Centre (Image: NHS) A handful of men have already been identified as needing a GP referral or hospital appointment. St Neots Town Councillor Sarah Pitt, who attended the event, spoke about the importance of raising awareness within the transgender community. Cllr Pitt said: "By speaking openly about having a PSA test, I hope I can encourage more people who still have a prostate, including trans women, to find out about PSA testing and consider whether it is appropriate for them." The current registered Guinness World Records mark is 258 men signed up for testing in eight hours, set in Egypt in 2024. Patients were due to receive their results directly, with their GPs notified and follow-up information provided where needed.

metadata.title: Community sustainability and supply chain champions invited to enter awards
metadata.contentSnippet: Entries are open for the Community Champion of the Year and the Supply Chain Business of the Year awards at the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Community sustainability and supply chain champions invited to enter awards
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Organisations, businesses and individuals making a positive environmental impact are being encouraged to enter two prestigious categories in this year's East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027. The Community Champion of the Year award celebrates those driving sustainability initiatives at a local level, while the Supply Chain Business of the Year award recognises organisations embedding environmental responsibility throughout their operations. Together, the awards shine a spotlight on the people and businesses leading the way in innovation, collaboration and sustainable change, while delivering measurable benefits for communities and the environment. COMMUNITY CHAMPION OF THE YEAR The Community Champion of the Year award recognises individuals, groups and organisations making a lasting difference through local sustainability initiatives. This category celebrates those who are leading environmental change in their communities through action, innovation and engagement. From grassroots projects and educational programmes to large-scale environmental initiatives, the award highlights efforts that deliver measurable benefits while inspiring others to get involved. Judges will be looking for nominees who have made an exceptional contribution to sustainability at a local level. Entries should demonstrate clear community impact, showing how work has improved environmental outcomes and created lasting change. Leadership and initiative will also play an important role. Entrants should show how they have driven projects forward, encouraged participation and championed sustainability within their communities. Evidence of collaboration with residents, schools, businesses, voluntary groups or public bodies will strengthen an application. Judges want to see innovative approaches to environmental challenges alongside measurable outcomes that demonstrate the value of the work undertaken. Last year’s award was won by PSH Environmental. The Rackheath-based recycling and waste management company was recognised for its community engagement and environmental initiatives. Reflecting on the win, managing director Nigel Parker said: “It’s really good to win this award. It’s a lot of hard work and effort and a case of doing the job properly!” CRITERIA The judges will be looking for an individual, group or organisation that has made an exceptional contribution to sustainability within their community. The winner should demonstrate leadership, innovation and a commitment to creating positive environmental change at the local level. The ability to inspire and engage others in sustainability efforts will be a key factor. The Supply Chain Business of the Year award celebrates organisations that are reducing environmental impact through sustainable supply chain management, innovation and collaboration (Image: Getty Images) SUPPLY CHAIN BUSINESS OF THE YEAR The Supply Chain Business of the Year award recognises organisations that are driving sustainability throughout their supply chains and demonstrating how environmental responsibility can go hand in hand with commercial success. This category highlights those taking meaningful action across sourcing, logistics, operations and supplier relationships. Judges will be looking for organisations that have successfully integrated sustainable practices across their supply chains while continuing to innovate and grow. Entries should show how environmental considerations influence decision making and operational processes, from procurement through to delivery. Strong applications should demonstrate the use of new technologies, systems or working practices that reduce environmental impact while improving efficiency. Collaboration with suppliers, partners and other stakeholders will also play an important role in the judging process. The award also recognises businesses that can demonstrate long-term impact. Judges will want to see measurable improvements in sustainability performance, together with evidence that their approach can be scaled or replicated elsewhere. Last year’s winner was Beccles-based Radical Waste, a waste management company recognised for integrating sustainability throughout its operations. The business was praised for its zero-waste model, investment in technology and broader environmental initiatives. Reflecting on the award, managing director Julian Knights said: “It’s game changing for us and an absolute honour and privilege to be awarded Supply Chain Business of the Year.” CRITERIA The judges will be seeking a company or initiative that has successfully integrated sustainability into its supply chain. Innovation, collaboration with partners and the long-term impact of the changes made will be key. The scalability of the model and measurable improvements in sustainability will also be assessed. Submit your entries before the deadline, which is midnight on Sunday, November 8. To enter the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk To find out more about all categories, please click here.

metadata.title: Recognising the businesspeople making a positive difference
metadata.contentSnippet: Find out what the Apprentice of the Year and Behaviour Change Campaign of the Year judges will be looking for at the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards 2027.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Recognising the businesspeople making a positive difference
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The East Anglia Clean & Green Awards are back! For this edition of the awards, innovation is the top priority, and both the Apprentice of the Year and Behaviour Change Campaign of the Year awards will celebrate businesses and individuals who are making an impact on sustainability in their sector. Here, the judges for these two awards tell us more about what they will be looking for from entrants. Elizabeth Conboy, executive director, commercial, RenewableUK, which sponsors Apprentice of the Year (Image: RenewableUK) Sponsored by RenewableUK Sponsor judge: Elizabeth Conboy, executive director, commercial, RenewableUK What do you bring to the judging process? I work closely with organisations across the renewable energy supply chain, from developers and manufacturers to technology providers and SMEs. That gives me a broad perspective on the skills, behaviours and leadership qualities that help individuals and businesses succeed in a fast-growing sector. Have you ever been judged for an award yourself? Yes, both personally and through the organisations I’ve been involved with. I understand the effort that goes into preparing an entry and how important recognition can be for individuals and teams. How will you use that experience when judging this award? I’ll look beyond polished submissions and focus on the substance of the achievement. Having been through the process myself, I understand the importance of giving every entry fair consideration and recognising different forms of success and impact. What will you be looking for in the winner? I’ll be looking for evidence of impact, a commitment to learning, and a genuine contribution to their organisation or the wider sector. I’m particularly interested in individuals who demonstrate initiative, collaboration and a desire to make a positive difference. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? Be authentic and don’t underestimate your achievements. Focus on the difference you’ve made, the challenges you’ve overcome and the lessons you’ve learned. The strongest entries clearly demonstrate impact and bring the individual’s story to life. Why is innovation an important judging consideration for this award? Whether it’s finding new ways of working, solving challenges or improving processes, innovative thinking helps organisations stay competitive and accelerates progress towards our net zero ambitions. Adam Tucker, account manager, Clarksons Port Services, which sponsors Behaviour Change Campaign of the Year (Image: Clarksons Port Services) Sponsored by Clarksons Port Services Sponsor judge: Adam Tucker, account manager, Clarksons Port Services Why were you keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards? I was keen to get involved in the Clean & Green Awards because they celebrate the organisations and individuals who are making a genuine difference to sustainability across our region. The campaigns recognised by these awards demonstrate how effective communication, collaboration and innovation can inspire people to make more sustainable choices and create lasting environmental impact. The awards are also an opportunity to celebrate success, share best practice and learn from one another. What do you bring to the judging process? In my role at Clarksons Port Services, I work closely with clients across offshore wind and the wider energy sector, giving me insight into the diverse approaches organisations are taking to support the energy transition. I’ll be looking at entries from both a commercial and practical perspective, recognising campaigns that have not only been creative but have also delivered measurable outcomes and genuine value for the audiences they were designed to influence. What will you be looking for in the winner? For me, the winning campaign will be one that can clearly demonstrate it has changed behaviours, not simply raised awareness. I’ll be looking for strong evidence of impact, supported by a creative, audience-focused approach that has inspired people to take meaningful, lasting action. What advice would you give to anyone that’s considering entering? I’d definitely encourage anyone who’s considering entering to do it. Don’t assume your campaign isn’t significant enough or that someone else has achieved more. If you’ve made a positive difference and can demonstrate the impact you’ve had, it’s worth sharing your story. Having been both an award entrant and a judge, I know that authenticity goes a long way. You don’t need to overcomplicate your submission; be honest, provide clear evidence and let the impact of your campaign speak for itself. Why should creative or innovative behavioural change strategies be celebrated? Behaviour change is rarely straightforward, which is why creative and innovative approaches deserve to be recognised. The most successful campaigns find new ways to connect with people, challenge established habits and make sustainable choices easier, more relevant and more achievable. The deadline for entries to the East Anglia Clean & Green Awards is Sunday, November 8 at midnight. For more information or to enter, please visit cleanandgreenawards.co.uk

metadata.title: Disgraced ex-Cambs copper to be sentenced over 'toxic' Whatsapp culture
metadata.contentSnippet: Disgraced celebrity police officer Paul Street, who created a “toxic” WhatsApp culture, will be sentenced later for misconduct in a public office.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Disgraced ex-Cambs copper to be sentenced over 'toxic' Whatsapp culture
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A disgraced celebrity police officer from Cambridgeshire who created a “toxic” WhatsApp culture will be sentenced later for misconduct in a public office. Ex-police sergeant Paul Street, 41, found fame in television crime shows on the BBC and Channel 4 and was known for getting “impressive results” through his “robust” style. However, anti-corruption officers began investigating him and uncovered his two WhatsApp groups in 2021 after a new police officer reported him. He encouraged colleagues to “bully” a teenage detainee and asked a workmate to send him a sex video of a female suspect, the Old Bailey had heard. The offences were committed while working at Cambridgeshire Constabulary leading a unit at Cambourne Police Station, mainly dealing with county lines drug supply and organised crime. Following an Old Bailey trial in June, Street, of Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, was found guilty of two charges of misconduct in a public office. Street had previously admitted two offences of unlawful disclosure of personal data relating to information and screenshots he sent to his partner in 2020. He will be sentenced alongside Josh Williams, 38, from Huntingdon, who pleaded guilty to misconduct in public office. The pair will appear at the Old Bailey before Judge Mark Lucraft KC on Wednesday morning. Eleven other officers were investigated over their conduct arising from the “toxic” culture Street had fostered. Of those, two resigned, one was dismissed for gross misconduct, one received a final warning, two received written warnings, and five others were dealt with for low level performance issues. During the trial, prosecutor Anne Whyte KC had described how Street “created a culture of bragging and intolerance towards suspects”, and a “zero-tolerance attitude to anyone on his team who disagreed with his methods and sentiments”. She had said: “He was not just promoting inappropriate attitudes, he was positively creating a toxic culture which junior officers would find difficult to challenge and likely to adopt.” In April 2020, Street called on his team to “bully” 17-year-old detainee Robiul Islam, encouraging them to “please hit him” and “smash his head in”. In the autumn of 2020, Williams was tasked with examining the phone of a female suspect he told Street was “quite fit”. Street asked him if there were “any nudes”, and Williams replied there was a video of the woman committing a sexual act. Williams went on to send Street a photo from the woman’s phone depicting her in underwear. The following year, Street asked on WhatsApp if Williams still had the intimate private video because he wanted to show it to “the lads from footy”. When he was interviewed about it, Street claimed he wanted to see the images to reassure himself the woman, who was released without charge, was not the victim of exploitative behaviour. But jurors were told it was not Williams’s job to discuss or share the private images, and neither was it Street’s job to ask for nudes or the sex video. Giving evidence, Street admitted his messages on WhatsApp were “poor” but said the language was “gallows humour” and part of the culture at the time. He also told jurors that being successful in his job had made him “arrogant”. Street had previously appeared on BBC show Britain’s Teenage Drug Runners in 2017, and in 2019 was on Channel 4’s Famous And Fighting Crime documentary. The prosecution asserted Street was more than a “maverick” officer with unorthodox methods and having good arrest rates did not justify his “out of control” behaviour.

metadata.title: New 20-year Hunts parking plan set for debate as demand set to rise
metadata.contentSnippet: A new long-term parking strategy could soon shape the future of car parks and town centres across Huntingdonshire.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New 20-year Hunts parking plan set for debate as demand set to rise
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Huntingdonshire District Council's cabinet is set to discuss a new 20-year parking strategy aimed at supporting town centres, improving customer experience and planning for future growth. Huntingdonshire District Council’s cabinet will consider the proposed plan when it meets today (Tuesday September 15). Work on the new parking strategy began in early October 2025 after a procurement exercise. The strategy will run from 2026 to 2046 and focus on economic growth, customer service and future demand. Read more Man arrested after young boy thrown into crocodile pit has bail extended Electric car charging stations could replace spaces at Hunts car park Six arrested after 'violent disorder' which seriously injured two men School council creates banner urging safer parking outside Hunts primary school Discover stunning National Trust site with 'something for everyone' The strategy will not set parking charges but will guide future decisions on tariffs and management. It outlines a vision for a "well-managed, balanced and future-focused parking service" that supports economic growth while promoting integration with public transport, walking, cycling, and electric vehicle infrastructure. The strategy has four aims: supporting thriving town centres, delivering a modern service, linking parking to sustainable transport and managing its assets responsibly. The council runs 25 off-street car parks with 3,149 spaces, according to evidence gathered for the strategy. Capacity is generally sufficient, but some town-centre car parks come under pressure at peak times. The council hired Ethos to study occupancy, assess parking and gather public views. The first survey drew 1,546 responses and the second drew 1,472. The second consultation found that 72 per cent backed the overall vision, while 95 per cent supported its focus on town centres and economic activity. The strategy warns that parking demand is expected to rise over the next two decades. By 2045, some car parks—particularly in Ramsey, Huntingdon and St Neots—could be under severe pressure, while others still have spare capacity. The plan proposes reviewing charges, stay limits and accessibility, improving signs and walking and cycling links, and adding more electric vehicle charging points. If approved, officers will draw up a phased plan, with some “quick win” measures expected within 12 to 18 months. The council said the first phase of engagement took place in December last year, before the second consultation sought views on the emerging vision, objectives and policy direction.

metadata.title: Inquest into death of Cambs killer Ian Huntley suspended pending murder trial
metadata.contentSnippet: An inquest into the death of Soham killer Ian Huntley will remain suspended pending the outcome of the murder trial of a fellow prisoner.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Inquest into death of Cambs killer Ian Huntley suspended pending murder trial
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An inquest into the death of Soham killer Ian Huntley remains suspended pending the outcome of the trial of a fellow prisoner charged with his murder. Huntley was allegedly attacked with a metal bar in a workshop at the maximum security Frankland Prison near Durham on February 26. Huntley was taken to the Royal Victoria Infirmary, Newcastle, where he died on March 7. A brief inquest hearing in Crook, County Durham, was held where coroner Jeremy Chipperfield was told criminal proceedings had begun and a trial was due to start on November 23. Anthony Russell, 44, has been charged with murder and has appeared in court previously. Mr Chipperfield asked whether Russell had entered pleas and was told by his coroner’s officer that psychiatric assessments have been carried out on behalf of the prosecution and defence. The coroner said the inquest will remain suspended until the completion of the criminal proceedings and it will then be considered whether it was necessary to complete the inquest. Mr Chipperfield said: “That cannot happen until we know the shape of any trial.” He adjourned the inquest proceedings until December 16 for a further brief hearing. Huntley was serving a life sentence for the 2002 murders of 10-year-olds Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman. The ex-school caretaker killed the best friends after they left a family barbecue to buy sweets in Soham, Cambridgeshire, on August 4 2002. He dumped their bodies in a ditch 10 miles away. They were not found for 13 days despite a search involving hundreds of police officers. At the time, Huntley lived with Maxine Carr who was a teaching assistant at Holly and Jessica’s primary school. He denied murdering the girls but was convicted after a trial at the Old Bailey in 2003. He was jailed for life with a recommended minimum term of 40 years.

news.title: Ramsey fraudster jailed for £40,000 theft from employer
news.summary: Kirsty Payne, 44, of Taverners Drive, Ramsey, has been sentenced to 18 months in prison for defrauding her Cambridge-based employer, Marshall Thermo King, of over £40,000. She spent the stolen funds on a skiing holiday and had a previous fraud conviction.
news.content: Cambs fraudster stole £40,000 from employer and spent it on skiing holiday A second-time fraudster has been jailed for stealing more than £40,000 from her employer and spending it on a skiing holiday. Kirsty Payne, 44, of Taverners Drive, Ramsey, admitted defrauding her Cambridge-based employer, Marshall Thermo King, which trades as Marshall Fleet Solutions. In February 2025, she processed a £400,410 payment through the company system—£40,383 more than the legitimate amount. The extra funds were traced to an account belonging to one of Payne’s family members. The discrepancy went unnoticed until April, when Payne was signed off work because of her deteriorating mental health. During a wellbeing check with the company’s head of HR, she suddenly confessed to the fraud and resigned. She first claimed the money paid for a relative’s medical treatment, but later told police it funded a skiing holiday in the French Alps. Payne said the theft was a "spur of the moment" decision. However, she had a previous conviction for fraud by false representation and said she was experiencing financial difficulties despite earning around £80,000 a year. Payne told officers she had been struggling mentally, especially due to a family member’s terminal illness. But she could not explain why she took the money. Detective Constable Valentin Radulescu, who investigated the case, said: "Payne gave little thought to the impact of defrauding her employer out of tens of thousands of pounds. "By committing fraud for a second time she showed she had not learned her lesson, and this was looked on negatively by the courts, who imposed a custodial sentence which she had initially avoided. "I hope her time behind bars allows her to reflect on her actions and hopefully, this case also serves as a warning to anyone else hoping to turn a profit through deception." Payne pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation at Cambridge Magistrates’ Court in July. On September 10, she was sentenced to 18 months in prison at Peterborough Crown Court. The sentence included ten months for the latest fraud, plus extra time for breaching a suspended sentence for a previous similar offence.

metadata.title: Additional police presence after boy, 14, suffers knife injury near school
metadata.contentSnippet: There will be an additional police presence in Peterborough today after a 14-year-old boy suffered a knife injury near Ormiston Bushfield Academy in Orton Goldhay.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Additional police presence after boy, 14, suffers knife injury near school
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: There will be an additional police presence in Peterborough today after a 14-year-old boy suffered a knife injury. The 14-year-old was injured in Orton Goldhay, Peterborough, at around 4pm on Monday, September 14. Emergency crews attended and police cordoned off playing fields beside Ormiston Bushfield Academy. The victim was taken to Peterborough City Hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. Two 14-year-old boys from Peterborough have been arrested in connection with the incident. One remains in custody on suspicion of grievous bodily harm, possessing a knife and theft. The second was arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm and assisting an offender before being bailed until December 14. Cambridgeshire Police said on the morning of September 15: "There will be an additional policing presence in the area today."
